currentEntries.definition: The watcher-tree and the priesthood's sign — first tree to wake, from shaqad, to watch: “I will watch over my word.” Aaron's dead rod budded, blossomed, and yielded almonds overnight — the house of Levi chosen by a resurrection sign — and the sanctuary lampstand is carved of almond cups: the watcher-tree bears the lamp.
currentEntries.citations: (Jer 1:11-12; Num 17:8; Ex 25:33-34) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Watchfulness or wakefulness—especially God’s vigilant readiness to fulfill his word. This symbolism rests on the Hebrew wordplay between šāqēd (“almond”) and šōqēd (“watching”), reinforced by the almond tree’s early blossoming.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: God's watchfulness and vigilance—specifically His wakeful attentiveness to His word so as to fulfill it swiftly. This rests on the Hebrew wordplay in Jeremiah between 'shaqed' (almond) and 'shoqed' (watching/wakeful), reinforced by the natural fact that the almond is the first tree to blossom in the Levantine spring (often called the 'awake' or 'watchful' tree), making it an emblem of divine alertness, promptness, and the hastening of God's purposes.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Watchfulness, the hastening or fulfillment of God's word, and resurrection or new life.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: divine watchfulness / vigilance (God promptly watching over and fulfilling His word)

currentEntries.term: Assembly of the wicked / synagogue of Satan
currentEntries.definition: The counterfeit congregation — an edah (the covenant-assembly word) claiming covenant standing while gathered against the covenant's Lord: God names the rebel camp “this evil congregation… gathered together against me,” Korah's company declares all the congregation holy, and at the cross the assembly encloses the Messiah from inside the camp while the dogs compass from without — “the synagogue of Satan, which say they are Jews, and are not.”
currentEntries.citations: (Ps 22:16; Num 14:35; 16:3; Ps 1:5; 26:5; Acts 4:27; Rev 2:9; 3:9) · see What Is the Point?, ch. 25

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A community that claims religious legitimacy or covenant identity but, through opposition to God, Christ, or faithful believers, functions as an instrument of Satan. In Christian interpretation, the expression usually signifies false or hostile religion rather than a building or an assembly openly dedicated to Satan.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching the phrase denotes a counterfeit covenant community: a group that claims the identity and privileges of God's people while in fact opposing God and persecuting the faithful, thereby serving Satan rather than God. In its original setting in Revelation, the dominant historical-critical reading takes it as the local Jewish synagogue communities in Smyrna and Philadelphia who denounced or slandered Christians to Roman authorities; the theological point drawn from it in Christian interpretation is that outward religious identity without allegiance to Christ is a false claim, so that the 'assembly' stands symbolically for false or apostate religion in opposition to the true people of God. The related phrase 'assembly of the wicked' (Psalm 22:16) is traditionally read christologically as the hostile crowd surrounding the suffering righteous one, applied in Christian exegesis to those who condemned and crucified Christ.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: A religious group or institution that claims to serve God and hold true covenantal authority, but actively opposes Christ and persecutes true believers. In its original biblical context, it specifically refers to local Jewish communities in Asia Minor who rejected Jesus as Messiah and persecuted the early Christians, while 'assembly of the wicked' prophetically describes those who orchestrated the crucifixion.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: A group falsely claiming to be God's true people (Jews) who actually serve Satan by opposing and persecuting faithful Christians

currentEntries.definition: The self-made kingdom that builds a name against heaven — an empire raised over many kingdoms, the covenant counterfeit.
currentEntries.citations: (Gen 11:4; Jer 51:7; Rev 17:18) · see The Bow, ch. 44, and The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Babel/Babylon most commonly symbolizes proud, idolatrous, oppressive human civilization organized in rebellion against God—especially worldly empire, corrupt power, and false religion destined for divine judgment.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, Babel/Babylon functions as the archetypal symbol of human pride, self-exaltation, and organized rebellion against God — the 'city of man' or godless world system standing in deliberate contrast to the city of God (Jerusalem/Zion). Babel represents humanity's attempt to make a name for itself and reach heaven by its own power (resulting in confusion and scattering), and Babylon extends this into the image of an idolatrous, oppressive, seductive world power destined for divine judgment. In Revelation, 'Babylon the great' is the culminating symbol of this anti-God civilization, whose fall is contrasted with the descent of the New Jerusalem.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Human pride, rebellion against God, systemic idolatry, and an oppressive, worldly anti-God system or empire.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Prideful human rebellion against God (exalting self/city to heaven without God), producing confusion, scattering, and judgment; more broadly the archetypal worldly empire/system (idolatrous, immoral, oppressive) that captivates and persecutes God's people and stands opposed to His kingdom, destined for divine overthrow.

currentEntries.definition: The firstfruits — the first and humblest grain, reaped in spring; the sheaf waved before the LORD, which is Christ risen.
currentEntries.citations: (Ex 9:31; Lev 23:10; Ruth 1:22; 2 Kgs 4:42; 1 Cor 15:20) · see Grass, ch. 42

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Barley has no universally settled Christian symbolic meaning. Where a broad symbolism is assigned, it most often represents humble or inexpensive sustenance through which God provides—especially provision for ordinary or poor people.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In most Christian teaching, barley symbolizes humble, lowly provision — the bread of the poor — through which God works and provides. Because barley was the cheaper grain eaten by the poor (about half the value of wheat), it is read as a picture of humility, lowliness, and God's use of small or despised means, most famously in the boy's five barley loaves with which Jesus feeds the five thousand. Closely intertwined with this is a second widely taught meaning: barley as the firstfruits grain of the early (Passover-season) harvest, and therefore a type of resurrection and of the 'firstfruits' people of God.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Firstfruits of the harvest symbolizing the resurrection of Christ, as well as humility, poverty, and God's provision for the lowly.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Christ as the firstfruits of the resurrection (linked to the wave-sheaf offering)

currentEntries.definition: A nation or kingdom of the world — the wild, predatory figure of a people, as the tree is its rooted figure; different beasts are different kingdoms, and the unclean beasts are the Gentile nations God cleanses in Peter's vision.

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: In apocalyptic Christian interpretation, a beast or wild animal most commonly symbolizes brutal, idolatrous political power—an empire, kingdom, or ruler that opposes God, arrogates divine authority, and persecutes God’s people.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian interpretation, the symbolic 'beast' or wild animal represents earthly political power in opposition to God — specifically kingdoms, empires, and their rulers that persecute God's people. Daniel's four beasts are explicitly interpreted within the text as four kings/kingdoms (traditionally Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome), and the beast(s) of Revelation are read as a climactic God-opposing world power and/or its ruler, frequently identified with the figure of the Antichrist. The core consensus idea is that 'beast' signifies brutal, arrogant, idolatrous human government or a tyrannical ruler animated by satanic power, in contrast to the humane, God-given rule symbolized by the 'one like a son of man.'

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Oppressive, anti-God political powers, worldly empires, or a specific eschatological Antichrist that persecutes God's people.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: An antichristian empire, ruler, or system of political/religious power opposed to God and empowered by Satan (commonly identified as the Antichrist or his kingdom)

currentEntries.definition: Receiving God's testimony as governing truth in a response that submits to it. Bare assent can recognize a fact — demons believe and tremble — but saving belief obeys the word believed, and persistent refusal to obey exposes unbelief.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: personal trust in Christ, not mere assent — the instrument that receives salvation.
currentEntries.citations: (Mark 1:27; John 3:36; 12:42-43; Rom 10:16; Heb 3:18-19; Jas 2:19-22) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Belief is most commonly understood not as a symbolic image but as faith: accepting the truth of God’s revelation and personally trusting, relying upon, and committing oneself to God—especially to Jesus Christ—for salvation.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'belief' or 'to believe' (Greek pisteuo, Hebrew aman) is understood not as mere intellectual acknowledgment but as saving faith: personal trust in, reliance upon, and commitment to God and specifically to Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior. It is treated as the divinely appointed means of receiving salvation, justification, and eternal life, involving assent to the truth of the gospel, trust of the heart, and entrustment of oneself to Christ. Classical Protestant theology often analyzes it into three elements: notitia (knowledge of the content), assensus (assent that it is true), and fiducia (personal trust). Belief is thus the relational counterpart of God's grace: grace offers, faith receives.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Personal trust/reliance upon God (especially Jesus Christ) for salvation, eternal life, and relationship with God, going beyond mere intellectual assent to include commitment and dependence

currentEntries.definition: What a people is strung together by — a kingdom's covenant, and the might that is that covenant's outward face: one word (qesheth) carries weapon, might, and covenant-token, and to break the bow is to unstring the kingdom.

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: When “bow” denotes the weapon, it most commonly symbolizes warfare, military power, conquest, or divine/human judgment. A broken bow correspondingly symbolizes defeated power or the ending of war.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching and biblical interpretation, the bow is most commonly read as a symbol of military power, strength, and warfare — and by extension of God's judgment when God is depicted bending or drawing his bow against the wicked. Correspondingly, the breaking or removal of the bow symbolizes the end of war, the humbling of human might, and the peace God establishes.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: God's covenant, mercy, and faithfulness, specifically representing His promise of peace and His pledge not to destroy the earth by flood (the rainbow).

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Sign of God's covenant promise of mercy and faithfulness (the rainbow set in the clouds after the flood)

currentEntries.definition: The curse-ground's crop — those consumed by “the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches”: fruitless, choking the word, offering a false shadow, and ending in fire.
currentEntries.citations: (Gen 3:18; Matt 13:22; Judg 9:15; 2 Sam 23:6-7; Heb 6:8) · see The Parables of the Kingdom, ch. 2

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The effects of the fall—especially sin, curse, fruitlessness, hardship, and divine judgment. In Christian interpretation, thorns and related plants most broadly signify what corrupts or frustrates good fruit and what grows under God's curse or judgment.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, thorns, thistles, and briers primarily symbolize the curse pronounced on creation because of sin — the painful, frustrating consequences of the Fall, and by extension sin itself, unfruitfulness, and divine judgment. The ground bringing forth thorns after Adam's transgression (Genesis 3:17-18) is treated as the paradigm text, so that thorny growth throughout Scripture is read as a sign of a cursed, unproductive, or judged condition.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The curse of sin, divine judgment, and the hardship resulting from the Fall.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The curse of sin and its painful, obstructive consequences in a fallen creation (toil, barrenness, judgment, and hindrance to fruitfulness)

currentEntries.definition: The members of a nation — broken off, or grafted in, while the tree itself stands.
currentEntries.citations: (Rom 11:17) · see Trees, ch. 41

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: People belonging to God—especially disciples or believers whose spiritual life and fruitfulness depend on union with Christ, the vine.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, 'branches' most commonly symbolize believers (disciples) in living union with Christ, who is the vine; the branches derive spiritual life from him and are expected to bear fruit, while fruitless branches face removal and judgment.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Believers or groups of people in covenant relationship with God, deriving their spiritual life, sustenance, and fruitfulness from Christ or the covenant root.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Believers/disciples who must remain united to Christ (the true vine) in order to live and bear fruit; unfruitful branches are pruned or cast away

currentEntries.definition: The word of God.
currentEntries.citations: (Deut 8:3; Matt 4:4) · see Orphans, Widows & the Fatherless, ch. 14

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Bread most commonly symbolizes God-given life, provision, and spiritual nourishment, understood supremely in Christian teaching as Jesus Christ, the “bread of life.”

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, bread primarily symbolizes Jesus Christ himself as the source of spiritual life and divine sustenance — the 'Bread of Life' — a meaning concentrated in and reinforced by the Eucharist/Lord's Supper, where bread represents (or, in sacramental traditions, becomes) Christ's body given for believers. Behind this stands the broader biblical motif of bread as God's life-giving provision, typified by the manna in the wilderness, which Christian interpreters read as foreshadowing Christ.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The body of Christ and ultimate spiritual sustenance, specifically representing Jesus as the 'Bread of Life' and his sacrifice in the Eucharist/Communion.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The body of Christ (Eucharistic presence and sacrificial life given for believers)

currentEntries.definition: The word churned solid — milk worked by labor into sound doctrine: the diet that teaches to “refuse the evil, and choose the good,” the remnant's food, the wash of the walking feet (“I washed my steps with butter”). Its counterfeit is speech “smoother than butter” with war beneath.
currentEntries.citations: (Prov 30:33; Isa 7:15, 22; Job 29:6; 2 Sam 17:29; Ps 55:21) · see Butter, ch. 47

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Rich nourishment, material abundance, and prosperity—often understood as a sign of God's generous provision. This is a broad contextual association rather than a fixed biblical symbol.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: Abundance, prosperity, and the richness of God's blessing. In most Christian teaching and commentary, butter/curds (Hebrew chemah) functions as an emblem of plenty — the fatness of the land and the overflow of divine provision — since curdled milk was a staple luxury of pastoral abundance in the ancient Near East.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Abundance, divine provision, and the richness of the land, often coupled with honey; alternatively, it symbolizes a diet of pastoral simplicity forced by national judgment and agricultural devastation.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Prosperity, abundance, or richness of blessing

currentEntries.term: Cast into the sea (a stone, mountain, or millstone sinking)
currentEntries.definition: The fall of Babylon — a ruling power irreversibly destroyed, sunk into the sea of peoples, never to rise. A phrase-symbol, not a single word.
currentEntries.citations: (Jer 51:63-64; Rev 18:21; Ex 15:4-5) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Decisive and often irreversible divine judgment: the condemned person, city, kingdom, or hostile power is violently overthrown, removed, and made unable to rise again.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: Irreversible, total divine judgment: to be cast into the sea (like a stone, millstone, or mountain sinking) most commonly symbolizes complete, final, and unrecoverable destruction or removal by God's judgment. The sinking object disappears beyond retrieval, so the image signals a doom from which there is no rising again.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Irrevocable, violent, and total judgment or destruction, permanently removing an entity so that it never rises again.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Sudden, violent, complete, and irreversible destruction or divine judgment

currentEntries.definition: The towering tree — a power of great height and majesty, whoever bears it: Assyria was “a cedar in Lebanon”; the house of David the “high cedar” whose tender twig God replants to become “a goodly cedar”; the righteous “grow like a cedar.” The symbol is the stature, not the nation's identity.

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Strength, majesty, lofty stature, and enduring stability. The cedar—especially the cedar of Lebanon—is commonly used as an image of impressive, durable greatness; in positive contexts it characterizes the flourishing righteous or divinely established rule.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching the cedar—especially the cedar of Lebanon—primarily symbolizes strength, majesty, and enduring stature, applied most often to the flourishing and stability of the righteous person who is planted and grows under God's blessing. The tree's great height, longevity, deep rooting, and incorruptible fragrant wood make it the standard biblical image of noble, God-given greatness.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Strength, majesty, enduring stature, and the flourishing of the righteous.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: strength, majesty, durability, and the flourishing of the righteous

currentEntries.definition: The empty husk winnowed off the grain and driven away by the wind — what the wicked are likened to: weightless, rootless, blown off and burned. Not to be confused with the tares.
currentEntries.citations: (Ps 1:4; Matt 3:12) · see Grass, ch. 42

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Chaff most commonly symbolizes the wicked, ungodly, or unrepentant—people who lack enduring spiritual substance and are separated from the righteous under divine judgment, often pictured as being scattered or burned.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, chaff overwhelmingly symbolizes the wicked, the worthless, and the unrepentant who are separated from the righteous and destroyed in divine judgment. The image derives from the ancient winnowing process, in which the light, useless husks are blown away by the wind (or burned) while the valuable grain is retained. Thus chaff stands for people (or things) that lack substance and value before God, are unstable and transient, and are ultimately swept away or consumed at judgment—most famously in John the Baptist's picture of Christ burning the chaff 'with unquenchable fire.'

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The wicked, ungodly, or unfruitful individuals who are separated from the righteous and destined for divine judgment and destruction.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: the wicked/ungodly (or worthless people) who are separated from the righteous and destined for judgment or destruction

currentEntries.definition: To cleanse is to remove the defilement that bars proper contact, approach, or use; clean describes what is free of that defilement and fit for its permitted place. Uncleanness may be physical, ceremonial, or moral and does not always mean guilt: childbirth, marital relations, and touching the dead all make unclean without being called sin. Cleansing removes what makes a vessel unfit; sanctification places the cleansed vessel under a holy claim and appointed use.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly treated either as hygiene and obsolete ritual regulation, or as a synonym for moral purity and holiness.
currentEntries.citations: (Lev 10:10; 12:2; 15:18; Num 19:11; Ps 51:2, 10; Eph 5:26; 1 John 1:7, 9) · see Uncommon Sanctification, Justification, and Cleanliness

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual and moral purity or impurity before God: “unclean” commonly symbolizes sin, defilement, and unfitness for God’s holy presence, while cleansing symbolizes forgiveness, purification, sanctification, and restoration to fellowship with God.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'clean/unclean' is understood as ritual-purity language that symbolizes moral and spiritual condition before God: uncleanness represents sin, defilement, and unfitness to approach a holy God, while cleanness represents holiness, moral purity, and acceptable standing in God's presence. Correspondingly, 'cleanse/cleansing' symbolizes God's forgiveness of sin and the sanctification of the believer, accomplished ultimately through the atoning blood of Christ (with the Old Testament washings and purification rites read as types or foreshadowings of that spiritual cleansing). A closely joined sub-theme is Jesus' relocation of defilement from external ritual to the inner heart (Mark 7), and the New Testament's declaration that former ritual categories (foods, Gentiles) are now 'cleansed,' opening covenant access to all peoples.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual and moral purity versus defilement by sin, with 'clean' denoting holiness and fitness for God's presence, 'unclean' denoting sin-induced impurity or separation from God, and 'cleansing/cleanse' denoting divine purification and forgiveness (especially through Christ's atoning blood, the Spirit, or the word), of which OT ritual categories are types.

currentEntries.definition: The vehicle of heaven — “who maketh the clouds his chariot” — and its cargo is the word: “my doctrine shall drop as the rain.” The pillar that led Israel, the cloud that received Him and brings Him back in like manner, the transport of the caught-up saints; risen from the sea of peoples, a multitude airborne — the cloud of witnesses. Its counterfeit is the cloud without water.
currentEntries.citations: (Ps 104:3; Ex 13:21; Acts 1:9-11; Dan 7:13; 1 Thess 4:17; Heb 12:1) · see Clouds, ch. 37 | (Ps 104:3; Ex 13:21; Acts 1:9-11; Dan 7:13; 1 Thess 4:17; Heb 12:1) · see Clouds, in the free digital edition at TimeTested.Bible

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The presence, glory, and majesty of God—often simultaneously revealing God and concealing the fullness of the divine presence.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching and biblical interpretation, the cloud is most commonly understood as a symbol of the divine presence and glory of God (often called the Shekinah glory) — the visible manifestation of God's presence that simultaneously reveals and conceals Him, guiding, protecting, and accompanying His people, and associated with theophany and, in the New Testament, with Christ's ascension and return.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The presence, glory, and guidance of God (often referred to as the Shekinah glory), representing both His divine revelation and the veiling of His overwhelming majesty.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Divine presence and glory of God (theophanic cloud / Shekinah)

currentEntries.definition: The stamped image — a person as the owner's minted image-bearer: dug from the field, refined in the fire, struck with the NAME; priced by the law, ransomed at a flat half-shekel when counted, lost and sought by lamplight. Man's mint valued the Shepherd at slave-damages; God's scales weigh the widow's whole living above all abundance.

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Money or material value, especially as a symbol of wealth and the believer’s responsibility to use material resources faithfully rather than serve them as an idol.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, the coin most commonly functions as a symbol of image, ownership, and allegiance: because a coin bears the image and inscription of its issuer, it belongs to that issuer. In the dominant homiletic and patristic reading of the tribute-money episode ('render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's'), the coin stamped with Caesar's image represents what is owed to earthly authority, while the human being—stamped with God's image (Genesis 1:26-27)—belongs wholly to God. The coin thus symbolizes the question of ultimate ownership and where one's allegiance is due.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Earthly wealth, secular authority, and temporal obligations, often serving as a contrast to divine authority and spiritual devotion.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: a lost sinner (or soul of value) who is diligently sought and joyfully recovered by God

currentEntries.definition: Concealed disobedience — deeds hidden from the light.
currentEntries.citations: (John 3:19-20) · see Light and Darkness, ch. 21

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Moral and spiritual evil—especially sin, unbelief, ignorance of God, and alienation from God—contrasted with God, truth, holiness, and salvation as “light.”

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, darkness primarily symbolizes evil, sin, and spiritual separation from God — the moral and spiritual condition opposed to God, who is symbolized by light. It encompasses spiritual ignorance or blindness, the realm and power of Satan, and life apart from the truth and salvation revealed in Christ. Believers are described as being delivered 'out of darkness' into God's light, and unbelief or wickedness is portrayed as 'walking in darkness.'

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Sin, spiritual blindness, evil, death, and separation from God, often representing the domain of Satan in contrast to the light of God.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: evil, sin, spiritual blindness/ignorance, death, and separation from or opposition to God (as the antithesis of divine light)

currentEntries.definition: The time of light — exposure and accountability, when deeds are seen and tested; the season to walk, work, and watch. The children of light are the children of the day. In the prophets’ counts the day is a unit that scales: a day for a year in judgment, and one day with the Lord as a thousand years.
currentEntries.citations: (Gen 1:5; John 9:4; 1 Thess 5:5; Num 14:34; Ezek 4:6; 2 Pet 3:8) · see Light and Darkness, ch. 21

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: In symbolic day–night imagery, “day” most commonly signifies light, divine revelation, moral clarity, righteous life, and the sphere of God’s saving activity, in contrast with the darkness of ignorance, sin, or evil.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, 'day' most commonly carries the symbolic sense of a divinely appointed period of time rather than a fixed 24-hour unit — above all a period of God's decisive action in judgment and salvation, epitomized in the phrase 'the Day of the Lord.' Closely tied to this is the widely cited principle that with God a 'day' is not measured by human clocks (a day as a thousand years), and, in prophetic interpretation, the frequently invoked day-for-a-year equivalence.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The realm of spiritual light, truth, and righteousness, often contrasted with the darkness or 'night' of sin, ignorance, and evil.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Light, righteousness, divine presence/truth, or the sphere of godly living (in explicit contrast to night as darkness, evil, or ignorance)

currentEntries.definition: One in whom the law is sealed — “seal the law among my disciples” — proven by continuing in the word, love, and fruit; three times Jesus says cannot of those who will not leave their own, bear the cross, and forsake all. Baptized into the Name, the disciple is perfected “as his master” — the Head whose Name carries the Word, the covenant law, and the fruitful priesthood.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: a learner and follower of Jesus — any believer, entered by faith and baptism, growing lifelong in Christlikeness.
currentEntries.citations: (Isa 8:16; Luke 6:40; Ex 23:21; Jer 31:33; John 8:31; Luke 14:26-33; Rev 14:1) · see The Disciple, ch. 9

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A disciple most commonly signifies a committed follower and learner of Jesus—one who receives his teaching, imitates his way of life, obeys him, and participates in his mission. In Christian application, the disciple often functions as the model or representative of Christian believers generally.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'disciple' (Greek mathētēs, 'learner') primarily signifies a committed follower of Jesus Christ — one who learns from him, obeys his teaching, imitates his life, denies self, takes up the cross, and is being formed into his likeness. It functions as the normative identity of every Christian: to be a Christian is to be a disciple, a lifelong apprentice of Jesus marked by obedience, love, and fruit-bearing.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: A dedicated follower, learner, or apprentice of Jesus Christ who submits to His teachings, imitates His life, and is committed to lifelong spiritual growth and obedience.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: A committed learner and follower of Jesus Christ who adheres to His teachings, imitates His way of life, and often incurs personal cost or self-denial

currentEntries.definition: The covenant lawsuit executed — the wife sent out of the house: exile and scattering. Hated when it betrays the wife of the covenant; commanded when the union is itself fornication — a marriage God never joined. God gave Israel the bill, and answered His own no-return rule at the cross.
currentEntries.citations: (Jer 3:8; Isa 50:1; Deut 24:1-4; Ezra 10:3; Mal 2:11-16) · see Marriage and Divorce, ch. 12

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: When treated symbolically, divorce or a bill of divorcement most commonly represents the rupture of a covenant relationship because of persistent unfaithfulness—especially God’s judicial separation from unfaithful Israel, whose idolatry and apostasy are portrayed as marital adultery.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching and biblical interpretation, the 'bill of divorcement' functions symbolically as God's judicial severance of His covenant relationship with unfaithful Israel. Building on the pervasive marriage metaphor in which God is the husband and Israel the wife, divorce represents the rupture of the covenant caused by Israel's 'spiritual adultery' — idolatry and apostasy. The most cited instance is Jeremiah 3:8, where God says He gave the northern kingdom of Israel a certificate of divorce and sent her away because of her adulteries, while faithless Judah did not learn from this. The symbol thus communicates covenant judgment: exile and rejection as the legal consequence of persistent unfaithfulness, while also setting up the prophetic hope of restoration and remarriage (Hosea 2; Isaiah 54; Isaiah 62:4-5).

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: God's judgment and temporary covenantal separation from unfaithful Israel due to spiritual adultery (idolatry).

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Metaphor for God's judgment and temporary putting-away of unfaithful Israel (or Judah) for spiritual adultery/idolatry

currentEntries.definition: The Gentile power — an unclean beast outside the covenant table, fed on the crumbs that fall from it until brought in; at the cross it was the dogs that compassed and pierced, and at the end, without are dogs.
currentEntries.citations: (Matt 15:26-27; Mark 7:28; Ps 22:16; Rev 22:15) · see Trees, ch. 41

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A dog most commonly symbolizes what is unclean, contemptible, morally corrupt, or excluded from the holy community. Applied to people, the image commonly denotes wicked persons, hostile outsiders, or false teachers rather than one fixed class in every passage.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the dog is a predominantly negative symbol of uncleanness, contempt, and moral impurity. It represents those outside the covenant community or hostile to what is holy: the profane, the wicked, unbelievers, and (in the Gospels) Gentiles as viewed from a Jewish covenantal perspective. By extension it commonly symbolizes false teachers and apostates who return to their sin.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Impurity, wickedness, false teachers, and those outside the covenant (the unholy).

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: unclean, despised, or contemptible persons (especially Gentiles, false teachers, apostates, or the wicked)

currentEntries.definition: The destination of the way — the entrance to the house of God, marked on the posts.
currentEntries.citations: (Ex 12:7; Deut 6:9; John 10:9) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Access, entrance, or passage—most characteristically, access to God, salvation, and eternal life through Christ. A door or gate may therefore represent both the offered way of entry and the decisive boundary between those admitted and those excluded.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the door/gate primarily symbolizes access to God and salvation, with Christ himself identified as the exclusive door or gateway through which believers enter eternal life, safety, and fellowship with God. The image conveys both entrance (admission into salvation, the kingdom, the flock) and exclusivity (there is one legitimate way in).

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Christ as the exclusive means of access to salvation, eternal life, and fellowship with God; more broadly, the transition point or entrance into the Kingdom of God.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Jesus Christ himself as the exclusive entrance or means of access to salvation, the sheepfold of God's people, and eternal life

currentEntries.definition: A devouring kingdom.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: Satan himself, per Revelation 12:9.
currentEntries.citations: (Pharaoh, Ezek 29:3; Babylon, Jer 51:34) · see The Sign of Jonah, ch. 4

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Satan—the devil as the chief personal power of evil, enemy of God, accuser and persecutor of God’s people.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching the dragon is overwhelmingly understood as a symbol of Satan (the devil), the primordial adversary of God and persecutor of God's people. The Book of Revelation makes this identification explicit, calling the great red dragon 'that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan,' thereby also linking the dragon to the serpent of Eden. By extension the dragon symbolizes cosmic evil and the chaotic, God-opposing power that stands behind hostile earthly kingdoms.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Satan (the Devil), the ancient serpent and adversary of God who opposes Christ and persecutes the people of God

currentEntries.definition: The front of the compass — Hebrew qedem, “east” and “ancient” in one word: Eden planted eastward, the glory returning “from the way of the east,” the lightning of the coming, the kings of the east crossing the dried river. Where beginnings and returns come from.
currentEntries.citations: (Gen 2:8; Ezek 43:2; Matt 24:27; Rev 16:12; Ezek 46:1) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: When “east” is given a positive symbolic meaning in Christian interpretation, it most commonly represents the manifestation or coming of God—especially Christ’s return—and, by association, light, resurrection, and paradise. This underlies the traditional Christian practice of facing east in prayer and worship.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the east is most commonly understood as the direction associated with God's presence, glory, and salvation — the direction of the rising sun (dawn/light), of Eden, and of the expected coming (and return) of Christ. This underlies the historic Christian practice of praying and orienting churches toward the east.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Exile, separation from God's presence, and judgment.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: direction of divine glory/presence, paradise (Eden), light, and the coming/advent of Christ (rising sun/resurrection)

currentEntries.definition: Spiritually, the whore of Babylon that rides the beast — the city that kills the prophets, “where also our Lord was crucified”: Jerusalem.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: bondage to sin, and the world-system out of which God redeems.
currentEntries.citations: (Rev 11:8; 18:24; Matt 23:37; Gal 4:25; Isa 1:10) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Bondage to sin and to an oppressive, godless world-system, from which God delivers his people in an exodus. In common Christian typology, Egypt is the realm of slavery, Pharaoh represents enslaving power, and departure from Egypt prefigures salvation and liberation.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, Egypt is primarily a symbol of bondage and slavery — specifically the world of sin and oppression from which God delivers His people. The Exodus narrative is treated as the paradigm of salvation, so 'Egypt' becomes shorthand for the old life of enslavement (to sin, to the world, to worldly powers) that believers are redeemed out of, with the Exodus itself typologically foreshadowing redemption in Christ. Leaving Egypt = conversion/deliverance; longing to return to Egypt = backsliding toward the old sinful life or worldliness.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: bondage/slavery to sin and the world system opposed to God, from which God delivers His people

currentEntries.definition: Babel’s confederate — allied with Shinar in Scripture's first war, judged under Babylon's own sentence (“I will break the bow of Elam”), its oracle the prologue to Babylon's fall.
currentEntries.citations: (Gen 14:1, 9; Jer 49:35; 51:56) · see The Bow, ch. 44

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Elam has no settled, term-specific symbolic meaning in Christian interpretation. It is primarily understood historically and geographically as the ancient people and territory east of Mesopotamia, associated with a son of Shem and later with the region of Persia/Iran.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: Elam has no strong single symbolic meaning in mainstream Christian interpretation; it is overwhelmingly treated as a literal ancient nation (east of Babylon, in the region of modern southwestern Iran, capital Susa/Shushan). Where a broader theological or typological significance is drawn, the most commonly assigned meaning is that Elam represents distant Gentile nations under God's sovereign judgment who are nevertheless promised restoration and inclusion in God's redemptive plan — judgment followed by mercy on the nations 'in the latter days,' with the presence of Elamites at Pentecost often cited as a fulfillment or foreshadowing of Gentile inclusion in the gospel.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Distant Gentile nations that are subject to God's severe judgment but are ultimately included in His eschatological grace and the universal outpouring of the Holy Spirit.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: No settled or commonly assigned symbolic meaning; treated primarily as a historical people and nation (descendants of Shem, located east of Babylon/Mesopotamia)

currentEntries.definition: The leaders of the assemblies, seated among the host of heaven — the court round about the throne, the named and brightest of the stars.
currentEntries.citations: (1 Kgs 22:19; Isa 24:23; Rev 4:4; Matt 19:28; Ps 89:5-7) · see Sun, Moon & Stars, ch. 29

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Elders most commonly signify mature, authorized leaders and representative guardians of God’s covenant community. In Revelation, the twenty-four elders are commonly understood as heavenly representatives of the redeemed people of God, expressing their worship, priestly status, and royal participation in God’s reign.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, 'elders' most commonly carry the symbolic meaning of the representative leadership of God's covenant people — mature, authoritative figures who stand for and govern the whole community. When the term is treated symbolically (most notably the twenty-four elders of Revelation 4–5), the dominant interpretation is that they represent the totality of the redeemed people of God across both covenants: the twelve tribes of Israel plus the twelve apostles (12 + 12 = 24), depicted as enthroned, crowned, and worshiping — i.e., the church/people of God glorified and reigning with God.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The complete body of the redeemed people of God, often specifically representing the union of Old and New Covenant believers (represented by the 12 Patriarchs and 12 Apostles), as well as spiritual maturity, wisdom, and pastoral authority.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Representatives of the redeemed people of God (the Church and/or Israel) in the heavenly throne room

currentEntries.definition: The scattered firstborn whose seed becomes the fulness of the nations.
currentEntries.citations: (Gen 48:19) · see Jacob, Israel & Ephraim, ch. 45

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Ephraim most commonly functions as a representative name for the northern kingdom of Israel—often emphasizing its idolatry, covenant unfaithfulness, judgment, and hoped-for restoration. This usage arises because Ephraim became the leading tribe of the northern kingdom.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching and biblical scholarship, 'Ephraim' functions primarily as a symbolic name (synecdoche) for the northern kingdom of Israel as a whole — the ten tribes that split from Judah — because Ephraim was the largest and politically dominant northern tribe. In the prophets, especially Hosea, Ephraim represents Israel in its unfaithfulness, idolatry, and pride, yet simultaneously as the wayward 'son' whom God still loves and promises to restore. Thus the settled symbolic core is: apostate-yet-beloved Israel, an object of both judgment and covenant compassion. A closely joined secondary layer comes from the name's etymology, 'fruitful' (Genesis 41:52), so Ephraim is also frequently expounded as fruitfulness or blessing granted by God, especially blessing in the land of affliction.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The Northern Kingdom of Israel, often symbolizing a rebellious, idolatrous, or backsliding people whom God still deeply loves and desires to restore.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The northern kingdom of Israel (the ten tribes), often as a figure of apostate or idolatrous Israel

currentEntries.definition: The lamp of the body — a burning light within a person, shining as the stars shine; the good eye gives its bread to the poor, the evil eye withholds; His eyes are flames of fire, running to and fro through all the earth.
currentEntries.citations: (Matt 6:22-23; Prov 22:9; 23:6; Zech 4:10; Rev 1:14; 5:6) · see Sun, Moon & Stars, ch. 29

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual perception or understanding—the capacity to recognize divine truth, with clear or opened eyes representing faith and insight, and blindness or darkened eyes representing unbelief, ignorance, or moral corruption.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the eye most commonly symbolizes spiritual perception and the moral/spiritual condition of the inner person: the eye is the 'lamp of the body,' so that a 'healthy' or 'single' eye represents an enlightened, undivided, rightly-oriented heart, while a 'bad' or 'evil' eye represents inner darkness, moral corruption, or misdirected desire. The eye functions as the gateway or index of the soul—what and how one 'sees' reveals and shapes one's spiritual state.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual perception, understanding, and the moral focus or desires of the heart.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: spiritual perception, insight, or understanding (the capacity to receive light/truth or remain in darkness)

currentEntries.definition: Trusting faithfulness — reliance on God's unseen promise held steady through obedience. Works do not purchase the promise; they enact and bring faith to maturity, and faith without them is dead.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: confident trust in God and His promises — the sole instrument of justification.
currentEntries.citations: (Hab 2:4; Heb 11:1, 8; Jas 2:17, 22; Rom 4:4-5; Eph 2:8-10) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Trusting reliance on God—especially confidence in Jesus Christ and his saving work—expressed through commitment, obedience, and hope rather than mere intellectual agreement.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'faith' (Greek pistis, Hebrew emunah) primarily denotes personal trust in and reliance upon God — and, in the New Testament, specifically trust in Jesus Christ and his saving work — rather than mere intellectual agreement. It is standardly defined as confident assurance in God's character and promises, the divinely enabled means by which a person receives salvation and is counted righteous ('justification by faith'), and the posture of dependence that characterizes the whole Christian life ('walking by faith, not by sight').

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Trusting reliance and confident assurance in God and His promises, centered on Jesus Christ for salvation and life (not mere intellectual assent)

currentEntries.definition: The Messiah — the one who bears the Father's light unchanged through the night; the moon is that name written in the sky, His throne established in the heavens.
currentEntries.citations: (Ps 89:37; Rev 1:5; 3:14; Isa 55:4) · see Sun, Moon & Stars, ch. 29

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A Christological title signifying Jesus Christ as the perfectly trustworthy revealer and representative of God, whose testimony is confirmed by his obedient life, death, and resurrection.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'Faithful Witness' (Greek: ho martys ho pistos) is understood primarily as a Christological title: it designates Jesus Christ as the one who perfectly and reliably testifies to God's truth and character — revealing God, confirming God's promises, and remaining true to that testimony even to the point of death. The title carries the double sense of the Greek word martys: 'witness' in the legal/testimonial sense and, by extension, 'martyr,' since Christ's witness culminated in his crucifixion. His resurrection ('firstborn of the dead' in the same verse) vindicates that witness.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: A Christological title referring to Jesus Christ, symbolizing his perfect, unwavering testimony to God's truth, his role as the ultimate revealer of the Father, and his obedience even unto the point of death.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: A christological title for Jesus as the reliable, true, and ultimate revealer/testifier of God's character, will, and truth (even unto death)

currentEntries.definition: God's covenant people left without their Father — the remnant.
currentEntries.citations: (Lam 5:3) · see Orphans, Widows & the Fatherless, ch. 14

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Symbolically, “fatherless” or “orphan” most commonly represents a state of vulnerability, abandonment, and lack of protective care, together with dependence on God as defender and Father. Christian teaching often uses the image to emphasize that God protects the defenseless and does not leave his people spiritually abandoned.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching the 'fatherless' or 'orphan' functions as the paradigmatic figure of the defenseless and socially vulnerable person who lacks a human protector and provider, and who therefore stands under God's special guardianship. Together with the widow and the sojourner/stranger, the orphan forms a stock triad representing all who are powerless, so that treatment of the fatherless becomes the biblical test of true justice and true religion: God is portrayed as 'father of the fatherless,' Israel is commanded to protect and provide for them, and oppressing them invites divine judgment.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The vulnerable, defenseless, and marginalized in society who are under God's special protection, often representing humanity's helpless spiritual state without God.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The vulnerable, helpless, and marginalized who stand under God's special protective care and fatherhood, and whose defense is a mark of true righteousness and pure religion

currentEntries.definition: Reverent awe expressed as keeping the commandments and departing from evil.
currentEntries.citations: (Eccl 12:13) · see The Fear of the Lord, ch. 23

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Reverent awe of God—recognition of his holiness, majesty, authority, and accountability before him—which produces humble worship, trust, rejection of evil, and obedient living. Christian teaching commonly distinguishes this from mere panic or servile terror, while allowing a genuine awareness of divine judgment.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'the fear of the LORD' is understood not primarily as terror but as reverent awe, worshipful respect, and humble submission before God — an attitude of devotion and obedience that Scripture presents as the foundation ('beginning') of wisdom and knowledge and the proper posture of covenant relationship with God.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Profound reverence, awe, and respectful submission to God, which leads to obedience, worship, and the shunning of evil.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Reverential awe, profound respect, and loving obedience toward God that constitutes the foundation of true wisdom, knowledge, and righteous living

currentEntries.definition: The walk — a man's conduct, his way; washed clean while the body stays bathed.
currentEntries.citations: (John 13:10) · see Garments & Armor, ch. 43

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Most commonly, “feet” symbolize a person’s practical walk—conduct, direction, and manner of life. They can therefore represent whether someone follows God’s way, stands securely, or is prepared to carry out a calling. This is a broad contextual association rather than a fixed biblical symbol.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, feet most commonly symbolize a person's 'walk'—that is, one's conduct, moral direction, and course of life. To have one's feet on a right path, kept from stumbling, or set upon a rock is read as living faithfully and obediently before God, while straying or slipping feet represent sin and moral failure.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Moral conduct, the path of life, readiness to spread the Gospel, and humility or servanthood (particularly in the context of foot-washing).

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: the walk, path, or moral conduct of life

currentEntries.definition: The world — Jesus’ own decoding — sown with the seed of the word and reaped at the harvest; its unreaped edge is where the poor and stranger glean, and its hidden treasure is bought whole to be mined.
currentEntries.citations: (Matt 13:38; Lev 19:9-10) · see Grass, ch. 42

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The world—the human sphere in which God’s kingdom, gospel, and final judgment operate. This is the most recognizable Christian symbolic meaning because Jesus explicitly says, “the field is the world” in the parable of the wheat and weeds.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, the field most commonly symbolizes the world — the whole realm of humanity in which God's kingdom is sown, where good and evil grow together until the final judgment/harvest. This meaning is treated as authoritative because Jesus himself supplies it in his explanation of the parable of the wheat and the tares: 'The field is the world' (Matthew 13:38). Closely bound to this is the derivative missionary sense: the world as a harvest field of souls ready to be gathered.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The world (the broad sphere of human existence where God's word is sown and spiritual forces operate)

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: the world

currentEntries.definition: Self-made righteousness — a covering of one's own cut, all show and no substance; the cursed fig tree bore leaves but no fruit.
currentEntries.citations: (Gen 3:7; Matt 21:19) · see Garments & Armor, ch. 43

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, the fig leaves sewn by Adam and Eve most commonly symbolize humanity’s self-made attempt to conceal the shame and guilt of sin. They are often portrayed as an inadequate covering, sometimes extended typologically to human works or self-righteousness in contrast with God’s provision.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, fig leaves most commonly symbolize humanity's inadequate self-effort to cover sin and shame — human-made righteousness or self-justification that cannot truly atone. The image comes from Adam and Eve sewing fig leaves together after the Fall, a covering routinely contrasted in sermons and commentaries with the garments of skin God later provides (often read as pointing to divinely provided atonement through sacrifice, and typologically toward Christ). Closely bound up with this is the meaning of shame and the newly awakened consciousness of sin.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Human attempts to cover sin, shame, and guilt through self-righteousness or inadequate human efforts, rather than relying on God's provision.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Inadequate human attempts to cover personal sin, guilt, or shame through self-made efforts (often contrasted with God's later provision of covering)

currentEntries.definition: God's own consuming presence — “the LORD thy God is a consuming fire”: never a chamber, always the encounter. The same fire sustains the bush, refines the silver, walks the covered out of the furnace, and consumes the uncovered; the difference is never the fire but the covering.
currentEntries.citations: (Deut 4:24; Heb 12:29; Ex 3:2; Dan 3:25-27; Mal 3:3; 1 Cor 3:15) · see Heaven and Hell, ch. 16

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Divine judgment: fire most commonly symbolizes God’s holy action against sin, including punishment, destruction, and—where the context permits—purification.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, fire is primarily a symbol of God's presence and holiness, which manifests in two closely linked ways: divine judgment upon sin and purifying refinement of God's people. The dominant summary formula is that fire represents the holy presence of God that both consumes what is evil and purifies what is to be preserved ('our God is a consuming fire').

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: God's holy presence, purifying judgment, and consuming wrath against sin.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Divine judgment and wrath (including eschatological punishment)

currentEntries.definition: The divider God set between the two seas of people — the restless nations below and the gathered waters above, the heavenly assembly — and the place where the lights are hung.
currentEntries.citations: (Gen 1:6-8, 14-17; Ps 148:4; Rev 17:15) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The heavenly or divine realm: a symbol of God’s transcendence, glory, sovereignty, and ordered rule over creation.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the 'firmament' (Hebrew raqia, named 'Heaven' in Genesis 1:8) is understood as the expanse or vault God created on the second day to separate the waters above from the waters below. Symbolically it stands for God's power to order and divide chaos into a structured cosmos, and it functions as the visible boundary between the earthly realm and the heavenly realm—the sky/heavens that 'declare the glory of God' and point worshippers upward to God's transcendent dwelling and throne.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The boundary between the earthly realm and God's heavenly throne, symbolizing divine sovereign order, protection from chaos, and the majestic declaration of God's glory.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The celestial expanse or vault of the sky that God creates to separate the waters above from the waters below (and which He names Heaven), symbolizing the ordered boundary between the earthly realm and the divine realm as well as the visible display of God's creative glory and majesty.

currentEntries.definition: Men in the sea of nations — and the redeemed drawn out of it, the catch of the fishers of men gathered in the net.
currentEntries.citations: (Hab 1:14; Matt 4:19; 13:47-48) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: In broad Christian symbolism, the fish most commonly signifies Jesus Christ and, by extension, Christian faith and Christian identity. This association is especially tied to the early Christian ichthys emblem and the Greek acrostic interpreted as “Jesus Christ, God’s Son, Savior.”

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the fish most commonly symbolizes people (souls/converts) gathered into the kingdom of God through evangelism, encapsulated in Jesus' call to become 'fishers of men.' Closely intertwined with this, and often treated as the primary meaning in historical Christian tradition, is the fish as a symbol of Christ himself and of Christian identity, via the Greek word ICHTHYS (fish) used as an acronym for 'Iesous Christos Theou Yios Soter' (Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior) — an early Christian confessional emblem. In exegesis of the biblical text itself, the 'souls caught for the kingdom' meaning is primary; in devotional/iconographic tradition, the Christ/ICHTHYS meaning is primary.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Evangelism, winning souls, and Christian discipleship, famously derived from Jesus calling his disciples to be fishers of men.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Jesus Christ (as Savior/Son of God, via the ΙΧΘΥΣ/Ichthys acrostic)

currentEntries.definition: An army in motion — a nation invading, or the Lord's own host sweeping the enemy away.
currentEntries.citations: (Isa 8:7; Jer 47:2; Dan 9:26) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Divine judgment upon pervasive human sin and corruption, especially as represented by Noah’s flood; it is commonly paired with God’s preservation of a faithful remnant and the beginning of a renewed creation.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the Flood (Noah's flood) primarily symbolizes God's judgment upon human sin combined with the salvation/preservation of a righteous remnant, and—via explicit New Testament typology—it prefigures Christian baptism, in which the believer passes through the waters of judgment into cleansing and new life.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Divine judgment upon global sin and wickedness, simultaneously serving as a vehicle for the salvation of the righteous and acting as a typology for Christian baptism.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: God's righteous judgment on human wickedness and the merciful salvation of a faithful remnant via the ark

currentEntries.definition: One who hears God's word and will not do it — the lawless, not the unintelligent.
currentEntries.citations: (Ps 14:1; Matt 7:26) · see The Fool and the Wise, ch. 20

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A “fool” most commonly represents a morally and spiritually undiscerning person—one who rejects God’s wisdom and consequently lives in unbelief, wickedness, pride, or disobedience. In biblical interpretation, the term usually concerns character and relationship to God rather than low intelligence.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching and biblical interpretation, the 'fool' primarily symbolizes moral and spiritual rebellion against God rather than intellectual deficiency. The fool is one who lives as if God does not exist or does not matter—rejecting divine wisdom, despising instruction, and ordering life around self rather than the fear of the LORD. Folly is thus treated as a moral-religious category (practical godlessness), the antithesis of the wise person who fears God.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: A person who is morally and spiritually deficient, rejecting God's authority, ignoring divine wisdom, and living in practical atheism or rebellion, rather than merely lacking intellectual intelligence.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: A person of moral and spiritual deficiency who rejects divine wisdom, instruction, or God Himself (practical ungodliness or denial of God), rather than mere intellectual incapacity

currentEntries.definition: The blocking flesh — “the body of the sins of the flesh,” Scripture's own decode — covering a covenant member and stopping its work: the uncircumcised heart cannot be humbled or love, the uncircumcised ear “cannot hearken,” uncircumcised lips cannot be heard, and a young tree's fruit is “uncircumcised” until the covenant year. Cut it away, or be cut off.

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: When used symbolically, “uncircumcised” most commonly denotes a person or human nature not inwardly consecrated to God—especially a hardened, disobedient, spiritually insensitive heart that remains identified with the “flesh” rather than covenant faithfulness.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the foreskin (and the state of being 'uncircumcised') symbolizes the unregenerate, sinful human nature ('the flesh') and, correspondingly, a heart that is closed, stubborn, and unresponsive to God. To be 'uncircumcised' is to stand outside God's covenant — impure, alienated, and spiritually insensible — while removal of the foreskin symbolizes the cutting away of sin and the cleansing/consecration of the person to God. This is developed into the metaphor of 'circumcision of the heart': physical foreskin removal typifies the inward removal of sinful resistance, accomplished ultimately (in Christian reading) by the Spirit through union with Christ rather than by the physical rite.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The unregenerate human nature, the flesh, or spiritual impurity representing a heart not yielded to God that requires spiritual cleansing.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual uncleanness, hardness of heart, or exclusion from God's covenant people (contrasted with the need for heart-circumcision)

currentEntries.definition: Spiritual unfaithfulness — breaking covenant with God to go after other gods and kingdoms; not merely the physical sin. The out-of-covenant union is itself the whoredom.
currentEntries.citations: (Ex 34:15-16; Hos 1:2; Jer 3:9; Rev 17:2) · see Marriage and Divorce, ch. 12

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual or covenant unfaithfulness to God—especially idolatry, apostasy, and devotion to rival gods or powers. Israel, the church, or a religious community is portrayed as an unfaithful spouse or prostitute.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching and biblical interpretation, 'fornication' or 'whoredom' (Hebrew zanah/zenut; Greek porneia) used symbolically refers to spiritual unfaithfulness to God — most specifically idolatry and apostasy. Because the covenant between God and His people is portrayed as a marriage, worshiping other gods, trusting foreign alliances, or mixing pagan practices with true worship is depicted as adultery or prostitution against the divine Husband. The unfaithful people (Israel, Judah, or apostate 'Babylon') are personified as a harlot.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual unfaithfulness to God, specifically through idolatry, apostasy, or worshiping false gods.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual unfaithfulness or idolatry (covenant adultery against God, often depicted as Israel or the people of God acting as a harlot by pursuing false gods or worldly powers)

currentEntries.definition: The four spirits of heaven — God's executing agents, shown as the four horsemen.
currentEntries.citations: (Zech 6:5) · see The Four Winds, ch. 34

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The four winds most commonly symbolize the four quarters or cardinal directions of the world and, by extension, worldwide extent, totality, or universality.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching and biblical scholarship, 'the four winds' is understood primarily as an idiom for the four cardinal directions (north, south, east, west) and thus for the totality or universality of the earth. Phrases such as 'from the four winds' or 'to the four winds' mean 'from every direction / to everywhere,' expressing the worldwide scope of God's action—whether gathering (the elect, exiles) or scattering (nations, kingdoms). Secondarily, the winds are frequently read as agents or forces under God's sovereign control operating across the whole earth.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The totality of the earth, representing all four points of the compass (North, South, East, West) and signifying global or universal scope.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The four cardinal directions (north, south, east, west), representing the whole earth, all nations, or universal scope

currentEntries.definition: A nation's works, by which it is judged — “every good tree bringeth forth good fruit”.
currentEntries.citations: (Matt 7:17; 21:43) · see Trees, ch. 41

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The visible outcome or evidence produced by a person’s inner spiritual condition—especially character, conduct, and good works. In Christian teaching, “good fruit” commonly denotes righteousness and the virtues produced by the Holy Spirit, while “bad fruit” denotes sinful conduct revealing a corrupt source.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'fruit' primarily symbolizes the visible outward product or evidence of a person's inner spiritual condition — that is, character, conduct, and works that flow from the heart. When applied to believers, it most often refers to Christlike character and good works produced by the Holy Spirit through a life united to Christ (the 'fruit of the Spirit'), and it serves as the test by which genuine faith or true versus false teachers are recognized ('by their fruits you shall know them').

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Outward actions, character traits, and spiritual virtues that result from one's inner relationship with God, particularly the Holy Spirit.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Outward evidence or produce of inward spiritual condition, especially virtues, character, and good works generated by faith or the Holy Spirit

currentEntries.definition: A planted stand of trees — a grouping of nations.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: paradise and fellowship with God — Eden lost and restored.
currentEntries.citations: (Ezek 31:9) · see Trees, ch. 41

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Paradise: the ordered, life-giving presence of God in which humanity enjoys communion with God, often extended to the hope of creation restored.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the garden symbolizes paradise as the place of God's presence and unbroken communion between God and humanity. Rooted in the Garden of Eden, it represents the original blessed state of creation—provision, fellowship with God, and life (the tree of life)—which is lost through sin (expulsion from Eden) and finally restored in the new creation, where Revelation deliberately returns to garden imagery (tree of life, river of life). The garden thus frames the whole canonical arc: paradise created, paradise lost, paradise regained.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The Garden of Eden as paradise: the original place of perfect creation, innocence, abundance, and unhindered communion with God, later associated with the Fall and eschatological restoration

currentEntries.definition: Righteousness — the righteous acts of the saints.
currentEntries.citations: (Rev 19:8, ASV) · see Garments & Armor, ch. 43

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A garment most commonly symbolizes a person’s spiritual or moral condition—especially righteousness, salvation, or acceptance bestowed by God. Clean, white, or festal garments typically signify righteousness and redeemed status, while stained or filthy garments signify guilt or defilement.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, a garment most commonly symbolizes a person's spiritual state or standing before God — above all, righteousness. Being clothed in clean, white, or fine garments represents righteousness (whether imputed righteousness received from God/Christ or the righteous deeds of the saints), salvation, and acceptance before God; conversely, soiled, filthy, or inadequate garments represent sin, guilt, and unrighteousness. The dominant reading is 'the garment of salvation / robe of righteousness' — the believer is stripped of sin-stained clothing and clothed by God with righteousness, often expressed as being 'clothed with Christ.'

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual state, character, righteousness, and standing before God, often contrasting human sinfulness with God's imputed righteousness or salvation.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Righteousness, purity, or salvation as a divine covering (especially white garments representing Christ's righteousness or the saints' holy standing)

currentEntries.definition: The judgment — the valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem's wall, where the carcases of the transgressors burn: “their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched.” What destroys “both soul and body,” distinct from Sheol, the grave that holds all alike.
currentEntries.citations: (Matt 10:28; Isa 66:24; Jer 7:32; Mark 9:43-48) · see Heaven and Hell, ch. 16

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Gehenna/hell/the lake of fire most commonly symbolizes the final divine judgment of the unrepentant wicked: irreversible exclusion from blessed life with God and punishment traditionally understood as eternal conscious suffering.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, Gehenna (rendered 'hell' in most English Bibles) and the 'lake of fire' in Revelation are understood as symbols or names for the place/state of final, post-judgment punishment of the unrepentant wicked — traditionally conceived as eternal conscious torment, separation from God, and irreversible condemnation. The imagery derives from the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a site of child sacrifice denounced by the prophets, which became in Second Temple Judaism a byword for divine judgment by fire.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The state or place of ultimate, eternal judgment and punishment for the wicked, typically understood as eternal conscious torment and complete separation from God.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: the final place of eternal fiery punishment and torment for the wicked after divine judgment (hell)

currentEntries.definition: The rage of the wicked at the righteous — what the excluded do at the sight of the kingdom they forfeited, sorrow and hatred in one face; then they melt away. Defined on the wicked against the just, staged at Stephen's trial, templated in the psalm: he shall see, be grieved, gnash, and perish.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the anguish of the damned under conscious, everlasting torment.
currentEntries.citations: (Ps 112:10; Ps 37:12; Luke 13:28; Acts 7:54; Matt 8:12) · see The Weeping and the Gnashing | (Ps 112:10; Ps 37:12; Luke 13:28; Acts 7:54; Matt 8:12) · see The Weeping and the Gnashing, in the free digital edition at TimeTested.Bible

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Severe anguish, despair, and sometimes enraged regret experienced under divine judgment—especially exclusion from God’s kingdom and, in traditional Christian teaching, the punishment of hell.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'gnashing of teeth' (nearly always paired with 'weeping') symbolizes the extreme anguish, despair, and suffering of those who are excluded from God's kingdom and consigned to final judgment or hell. It functions as a stock formula in Jesus' teaching for the conscious misery and regret of the condemned — the pain of eschatological loss.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Intense anguish, sorrow, and regret experienced by those excluded from God's kingdom and consigned to eschatological punishment (outer darkness or hell)

currentEntries.definition: The gospel of the kingdom — the renewed covenant, the law going forth from Zion.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the good news that Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again.
currentEntries.citations: (Isa 52:7; 2:3; Jer 31:33; Heb 4:2) · see Gospel, ch. 5

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The “Gospel” primarily means the good news that God’s saving reign has come through Jesus Christ—especially through his death and resurrection—calling people to faith, repentance, forgiveness, and new life.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, 'Gospel' (Greek: euangelion, 'good news') primarily denotes the announcement of salvation accomplished by God through Jesus Christ — specifically his death for sins, burial, resurrection, and lordship — offered to all who believe. It is understood less as a symbol than as a proclamation: the message that in Christ, God has acted decisively to redeem humanity, forgive sin, and inaugurate his kingdom.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The 'good news' (euangelion) of salvation, the forgiveness of sins, and the inauguration of the Kingdom of God through the incarnation, life, atoning death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: the good news of salvation through the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ

currentEntries.definition: The wild branch — the stranger, the Gentile — received into the covenant tree.
currentEntries.citations: (Rom 11:17) · see Trees, ch. 41

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The grafting image most commonly symbolizes Gentile believers being incorporated by faith into the covenant people of God and sharing in the spiritual blessings rooted in Israel’s patriarchal promises. They are depicted as wild olive branches grafted into a cultivated olive tree, while being warned against pride toward Jewish branches.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: The inclusion of Gentile believers into God's covenant people. In Paul's olive tree metaphor, Gentiles are 'wild olive branches' grafted contrary to nature into the cultivated olive tree (rooted in the patriarchs and God's promises to Israel), sharing the nourishing root while some natural branches (unbelieving Israel) were broken off through unbelief. The image teaches Gentile participation in Israel's covenant blessings by faith, coupled with a warning against Gentile arrogance and an affirmation that natural branches can be grafted back in.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The inclusion of Gentiles into the covenant promises and people of God, sharing in the spiritual heritage and root of Israel.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Gentile believers being incorporated (as wild olive branches) into the cultivated olive tree representing the covenant people of God / Israel, thereby sharing in the root and rich sap of the Abrahamic promises and blessings while some natural branches are broken off for unbelief (with the possibility of re-grafting).

currentEntries.definition: A nation's works ripened into its people — persons as the vineyard's yield: God looked for grapes — judgment and righteousness — and found men: Israel “like grapes in the wilderness,” the good man the missing cluster, the remnant the blessing left in it. Pressed, the grape gives blood — the cup of the covenant, or the cup of wrath, as the vintage is grapes or wild grapes.
