glossaryEntries.definition: One in whom the law is sealed — “seal the law among my disciples” — proven by continuing in the word, love, and fruit; three times Jesus says cannot of those who will not leave their own, bear the cross, and forsake all. Baptized into the Name, the disciple is perfected “as his master” — the Head whose Name carries the Word, the covenant law, and the fruitful priesthood.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: a learner and follower of Jesus — any believer, entered by faith and baptism, growing lifelong in Christlikeness.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Isa 8:16; Luke 6:40; Ex 23:21; Jer 31:33; John 8:31; Luke 14:26-33; Rev 14:1) · see The Disciple, ch. 9

glossaryEntries.definition: The covenant lawsuit executed — the wife sent out of the house: exile and scattering. Hated when it betrays the wife of the covenant; commanded when the union is itself fornication — a marriage God never joined. God gave Israel the bill, and answered His own no-return rule at the cross.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Jer 3:8; Isa 50:1; Deut 24:1-4; Ezra 10:3; Mal 2:11-16) · see Marriage and Divorce, ch. 12

glossaryEntries.definition: The Gentile power — an unclean beast outside the covenant table, fed on the crumbs that fall from it until brought in; at the cross it was the dogs that compassed and pierced, and at the end, without are dogs.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Matt 15:26-27; Mark 7:28; Ps 22:16; Rev 22:15) · see Trees, ch. 41

glossaryEntries.definition: The destination of the way — the entrance to the house of God, marked on the posts.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ex 12:7; Deut 6:9; John 10:9) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7

glossaryEntries.definition: A devouring kingdom.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: Satan himself, per Revelation 12:9.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Pharaoh, Ezek 29:3; Babylon, Jer 51:34) · see The Sign of Jonah, ch. 4

glossaryEntries.definition: The front of the compass — Hebrew qedem, “east” and “ancient” in one word: Eden planted eastward, the glory returning “from the way of the east,” the lightning of the coming, the kings of the east crossing the dried river. Where beginnings and returns come from.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 2:8; Ezek 43:2; Matt 24:27; Rev 16:12; Ezek 46:1) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

glossaryEntries.definition: Spiritually, the whore of Babylon that rides the beast — the city that kills the prophets, “where also our Lord was crucified”: Jerusalem.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: bondage to sin, and the world-system out of which God redeems.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Rev 11:8; 18:24; Matt 23:37; Gal 4:25; Isa 1:10) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

glossaryEntries.definition: Babel’s confederate — allied with Shinar in Scripture's first war, judged under Babylon's own sentence (“I will break the bow of Elam”), its oracle the prologue to Babylon's fall.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 14:1, 9; Jer 49:35; 51:56) · see The Bow, ch. 44

glossaryEntries.definition: The leaders of the assemblies, seated among the host of heaven — the court round about the throne, the named and brightest of the stars.
glossaryEntries.citations: (1 Kgs 22:19; Isa 24:23; Rev 4:4; Matt 19:28; Ps 89:5-7) · see Sun, Moon & Stars, ch. 29

glossaryEntries.definition: The scattered firstborn whose seed becomes the fulness of the nations.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 48:19) · see Jacob, Israel & Ephraim, ch. 45

glossaryEntries.definition: The lamp of the body — a burning light within a person, shining as the stars shine; the good eye gives its bread to the poor, the evil eye withholds; His eyes are flames of fire, running to and fro through all the earth.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Matt 6:22-23; Prov 22:9; 23:6; Zech 4:10; Rev 1:14; 5:6) · see Sun, Moon & Stars, ch. 29

glossaryEntries.definition: Trusting faithfulness — reliance on God's unseen promise held steady through obedience. Works do not purchase the promise; they enact and bring faith to maturity, and faith without them is dead.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: confident trust in God and His promises — the sole instrument of justification.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Hab 2:4; Heb 11:1, 8; Jas 2:17, 22; Rom 4:4-5; Eph 2:8-10) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

glossaryEntries.definition: The Messiah — the one who bears the Father's light unchanged through the night; the moon is that name written in the sky, His throne established in the heavens.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ps 89:37; Rev 1:5; 3:14; Isa 55:4) · see Sun, Moon & Stars, ch. 29

glossaryEntries.definition: God's covenant people left without their Father — the remnant.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Lam 5:3) · see Orphans, Widows & the Fatherless, ch. 14

glossaryEntries.definition: Reverent awe expressed as keeping the commandments and departing from evil.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Eccl 12:13) · see The Fear of the Lord, ch. 23

glossaryEntries.definition: The walk — a man's conduct, his way; washed clean while the body stays bathed.
glossaryEntries.citations: (John 13:10) · see Garments & Armor, ch. 43

glossaryEntries.definition: The world — Jesus’ own decoding — sown with the seed of the word and reaped at the harvest; its unreaped edge is where the poor and stranger glean, and its hidden treasure is bought whole to be mined.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Matt 13:38; Lev 19:9-10) · see Grass, ch. 42

glossaryEntries.definition: Self-made righteousness — a covering of one's own cut, all show and no substance; the cursed fig tree bore leaves but no fruit.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 3:7; Matt 21:19) · see Garments & Armor, ch. 43

glossaryEntries.definition: God's own consuming presence — “the LORD thy God is a consuming fire”: never a chamber, always the encounter. The same fire sustains the bush, refines the silver, walks the covered out of the furnace, and consumes the uncovered; the difference is never the fire but the covering.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Deut 4:24; Heb 12:29; Ex 3:2; Dan 3:25-27; Mal 3:3; 1 Cor 3:15) · see Heaven and Hell, ch. 16

glossaryEntries.definition: The divider God set between the two seas of people — the restless nations below and the gathered waters above, the heavenly assembly — and the place where the lights are hung.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 1:6-8, 14-17; Ps 148:4; Rev 17:15) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40

glossaryEntries.definition: Men in the sea of nations — and the redeemed drawn out of it, the catch of the fishers of men gathered in the net.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Hab 1:14; Matt 4:19; 13:47-48) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40

glossaryEntries.definition: An army in motion — a nation invading, or the Lord's own host sweeping the enemy away.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Isa 8:7; Jer 47:2; Dan 9:26) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40

glossaryEntries.definition: One who hears God's word and will not do it — the lawless, not the unintelligent.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ps 14:1; Matt 7:26) · see The Fool and the Wise, ch. 20

glossaryEntries.definition: The blocking flesh — “the body of the sins of the flesh,” Scripture's own decode — covering a covenant member and stopping its work: the uncircumcised heart cannot be humbled or love, the uncircumcised ear “cannot hearken,” uncircumcised lips cannot be heard, and a young tree's fruit is “uncircumcised” until the covenant year. Cut it away, or be cut off.
Spiritual unfaithfulness — breaking covenant with God to go after other gods and kingdoms; not merely the physical sin. The out-of-covenant union is itself the whoredom.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ex 34:15-16; Hos 1:2; Jer 3:9; Rev 17:2) · see Marriage and Divorce, ch. 12

glossaryEntries.definition: The four spirits of heaven — God's executing agents, shown as the four horsemen.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Zech 6:5) · see The Four Winds, ch. 34

glossaryEntries.definition: A nation's works, by which it is judged — “every good tree bringeth forth good fruit”.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Matt 7:17; 21:43) · see Trees, ch. 41

glossaryEntries.definition: A planted stand of trees — a grouping of nations.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: paradise and fellowship with God — Eden lost and restored.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ezek 31:9) · see Trees, ch. 41

glossaryEntries.definition: Righteousness — the righteous acts of the saints.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Rev 19:8, ASV) · see Garments & Armor, ch. 43

glossaryEntries.definition: The judgment — the valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem's wall, where the carcases of the transgressors burn: “their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched.” What destroys “both soul and body,” distinct from Sheol, the grave that holds all alike.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Matt 10:28; Isa 66:24; Jer 7:32; Mark 9:43-48) · see Heaven and Hell, ch. 16

glossaryEntries.definition: The rage of the wicked at the righteous — what the excluded do at the sight of the kingdom they forfeited, sorrow and hatred in one face; then they melt away. Defined on the wicked against the just, staged at Stephen's trial, templated in the psalm: he shall see, be grieved, gnash, and perish.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the anguish of the damned under conscious, everlasting torment.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ps 112:10; Ps 37:12; Luke 13:28; Acts 7:54; Matt 8:12) · see The Weeping and the Gnashing | (Ps 112:10; Ps 37:12; Luke 13:28; Acts 7:54; Matt 8:12) · see The Weeping and the Gnashing, in the free digital edition at TimeTested.Bible

glossaryEntries.definition: The gospel of the kingdom — the renewed covenant, the law going forth from Zion.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the good news that Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Isa 52:7; 2:3; Jer 31:33; Heb 4:2) · see Gospel, ch. 5

glossaryEntries.definition: Favor that moves first — “while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” — and then goes to work: “teaching us that, denying ungodliness… we should live soberly, righteously, and godly.” Its counterfeit turns it into license (Jude 4).
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: unmerited favor — “getting what you don't deserve” — with no office afterward.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Rom 5:8; Titus 2:11-12; Ex 34:6) · see Grace, Mercy & the Gift, ch. 24

glossaryEntries.definition: The wild branch — the stranger, the Gentile — received into the covenant tree.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Rom 11:17) · see Trees, ch. 41

glossaryEntries.definition: A nation's works ripened into its people — persons as the vineyard's yield: God looked for grapes — judgment and righteousness — and found men: Israel “like grapes in the wilderness,” the good man the missing cluster, the remnant the blessing left in it. Pressed, the grape gives blood — the cup of the covenant, or the cup of wrath, as the vintage is grapes or wild grapes.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Isa 5:2-7; Hos 9:10; Mic 7:1-2; Isa 65:8; Gen 49:11; Rev 14:18-20) · see The Parable of the Vineyard | (Isa 5:2-7; Hos 9:10; Mic 7:1-2; Isa 65:8; Gen 49:11; Rev 14:18-20) · see The Parable of the Vineyard, in the free digital edition at TimeTested.Bible

glossaryEntries.definition: The individual mortal — a man, flesh; and the field God farms unto harvest.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Isa 40:6-8; Matt 13:38) · see Grass, ch. 42

glossaryEntries.definition: A great ruler among the sea of peoples — the personal head who can stand for the kingdom, state, and administration acting through him. Pharaoh stands for Egypt, Nebuchadnezzar for Babylon, and Caesar for Rome: the ruler swallows through the body he heads, and is forced to give back what he swallowed.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: God's appointed rescue-instrument, a type of the three days in the tomb.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ezek 29:3; 32:2; Jer 51:34, 44; Dan 7:17, 23; John 19:15-16) · see The Sign of Jonah, ch. 4

glossaryEntries.definition: The covenant-breaker who wears the form of covenant without its substance — “that great city,” spiritually Sodom, Egypt, Babylon: Jerusalem unfaithful.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: spiritual adultery; in Revelation, an apostate religious world-system — Rome, not Jerusalem.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Rev 17:18; 11:8; Ezek 23:19) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

glossaryEntries.definition: The end of the age, when the field of mankind is reaped — the wheat gathered, the chaff burned.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Joel 3:13; Matt 13:39) · see Grass, ch. 42

glossaryEntries.definition: To un-choose — the repudiation of a covenant partner or claim, never a mere feeling: the un-favored wife, the ground of divorce, the King refused. Scripture glosses it by its enactments — sent away, driven out of the house, “did not choose,” “I will love them no more” — and keeps the grudge in other words (satam, natar); Jesus' parallel saying translates the hard text: “hate not” father and mother is “he that loveth father or mother more than me.”
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: an emotion — hostility, bitterness — softened in the famous texts to “love less.”
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 29:30-31; Prov 1:29; Hos 9:15; Luke 14:26) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

glossaryEntries.definition: Jerusalem — the navel and heart of the land.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the grave or Hades, where Christ lay three days.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Matt 12:40; Ezek 5:5; 38:12) · see The Sign of Jonah, ch. 4, and The Ship

glossaryEntries.definition: The jurisdiction where God's will is already done — the visible sky and the seat of rule in one dual word (shamayim), over against the earth, the realm delegated to men where His will must yet be done. God's motion is downward — rain, fire, the Son, the city; the climb up is Babel's. The hope is heaven come down, not man gone up.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ps 115:16; Isa 66:1; Matt 6:10; John 3:13; Rev 21:2-3) · see Heaven and Hell, ch. 16

glossaryEntries.definition: One English word laid over two different things — Sheol/Hades, the grave that swallows righteous and wicked alike, and Gehenna, the judgment that destroys. The doctrine changes with the word beneath.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the place of eternal conscious punishment and separation from God.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ps 16:10 with Matt 10:28) · see Heaven and Hell, ch. 16

glossaryEntries.definition: The head covered with yeshuah — Yeshua: God's own war-dress, put on when there was no man, and lent to the soldier; David's form of it — “thou hast covered my head in the day of battle.” The head of every man is Christ, and the counterfeit is issued for the same forehead.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Isa 59:16-17; Eph 6:11, 17; Ps 140:7; 1 Cor 11:3; 1 Thess 5:8; Rev 22:4) · see Garments & Armor, ch. 43

glossaryEntries.definition: The way of holiness — the prepared road home.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Isa 35:8) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7

glossaryEntries.definition: The mount of an executing spirit; the conqueror who wins the nations by the bow.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Rev 6:2) · see The Four Winds, ch. 34

glossaryEntries.term: Image of metals (gold, silver, brass, clay)
glossaryEntries.definition: The succession of gentile world-kingdoms, shattered by the stone-kingdom of God.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Dan 2:32-45) · see Mountain, ch. 39

glossaryEntries.definition: The discipline of the law, received and kept — what only fools despise.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Prov 1:7; 23:23) · see The Fool and the Wise, ch. 20

glossaryEntries.definition: The fourth kingdom — Rome: Daniel named Medo-Persia and Greece outright, and the iron that breaks in pieces all before it is the empire that held the world when He came.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Dan 2:40; 8:20-21) · see The Sign of Jonah, ch. 4

glossaryEntries.definition: A set-apart, sanctified people — the covenant-rock risen out of the sea of nations (a mountain breaking the surface), waiting for the law that sanctifies it; “the island of the innocent,” delivered to safety while the kingdoms fall.
The new name of the one who prevails with God — covenant and character, not blood.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 32:28; Rom 9:6) · see Jacob, Israel & Ephraim, ch. 45

glossaryEntries.definition: The crooked, supplanting human heart that God transforms.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 27:36; Jer 17:9) · see Jacob, Israel & Ephraim, ch. 45

glossaryEntries.definition: In covenant contexts, one in the covenant — “he is a Jew, which is one inwardly,” while some “say they are Jews, and are not.” The name is Judah's, and Judah means praise — “Now will I praise the LORD” — so Paul's definition lands on the name itself: the Jew inwardly is he “whose praise is not of men, but of God.” The word also walks in plain dress, ethnic and religious; context decides which coat it wears.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Rom 2:28-29; Gen 29:35; Rev 3:9; Rom 9:6; Zech 8:23) · see Jacob, Israel & Ephraim, ch. 45

glossaryEntries.definition: The law's ruling and the ruler's office — what God declares due, kept like a commandment and owed first to the widow, the fatherless, the stranger, and the poor. To judge is to rule and deliver by the law (the judges were saviours; “a king to judge us… and fight our battles”), so the righteous pray for judgment and creation rejoices at its coming; condemnation is one verdict of the office, not the office.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Deut 10:18; Ps 119:160; Matt 23:23; 1 Sam 8:20; Isa 33:22; Dan 7:22) · see Justice and Judgment, ch. 18

glossaryEntries.definition: Righteousness under a second English name — one Hebrew word behind both renderings: the commandments done where a neighbor can be wronged or righted.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 18:19/Jer 22:3; Ps 89:14/97:2) · see Justice and Judgment, ch. 18

glossaryEntries.definition: To judge, declare, or demonstrate a person, word, deed, or cause right against a question or charge; the opposite is to condemn. God answers the charge against the sinner by grace through Christ, forgiving rather than renaming ungodliness righteousness. Deeds may vindicate a claimed faith, but they cannot purchase the Judge's mercy or place God in debt.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught in Protestant theology: God's once-for-all legal declaration that a believer is righteous through Christ's imputed righteousness, received by faith apart from works.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Deut 25:1; Prov 17:15; Matt 11:19; Luke 7:29; Rom 3:24-26; 4:4-8; 8:33; Jas 2:21-25) · see Uncommon Sanctification, Justification, and Cleanliness, and The End of the Law for Paul's law, works, wages, and debt vocabulary

glossaryEntries.definition: Covenant relationship proven by obedience — the intimate “knew” of marriage; a stranger is one not known.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 4:1; Hos 4:6; Matt 7:23; 1 John 2:3-4) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

glossaryEntries.definition: One of the flock — a covenant person, not by itself Christ: Nathan's ewe lamb is a poor man's beloved, Jeremiah is “like a lamb… brought to the slaughter,” the disciples are sent “as lambs among wolves.” The Lamb of God is Christ — the one lamb “without blemish,” taken “out from the sheep”: the perfect lamb of the flock.
glossaryEntries.citations: (2 Sam 12:3; Jer 11:19; Isa 53:6-7; Ex 12:5; Luke 10:3; John 1:29) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7 — derived in the digital edition’s symbol study at TimeTested.Bible

glossaryEntries.definition: The commandment.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Prov 6:23) · see Light and Darkness, ch. 21

glossaryEntries.definition: Bread soured — the word made impure, embittered, and puffed up; the hidden corruption that ferments through the whole lump, purged before Passover and forbidden on God's altar. The NT names it the corrupt doctrine of the Pharisees.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Lev 2:11; Matt 16:12; 1 Cor 5:7-8) · see Grass, ch. 42

glossaryEntries.definition: The King's jubilee release — out of the slaver's house (sin, Egypt, Babylon) and home to the household, inheritance, and service of God; a change of masters, never the absence of one. Its constitution is the perfect law of liberty; its counterfeit, liberty as license, is a return to bondage.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Lev 25:10; Isa 61:1; Jas 1:25; 2 Pet 2:19) · see Liberty, ch. 19

glossaryEntries.definition: Covenant existence — the life the law produces.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: Christ Himself, and the eternal life imparted to believers.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Deut 30:19-20; Lev 18:5; John 14:6; Matt 7:14) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7

glossaryEntries.definition: The law lived visibly — good works others can see.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Prov 6:23; Matt 5:16) · see Light and Darkness, ch. 21

glossaryEntries.definition: The devouring ruler or empire — the beast-kingdom at its most royal and most predatory: “as a roaring lion… so is a wicked ruler”; the princes are lions, and Assyria and Babylon “the lions” that scattered the sheep. The figure's rightful holder is the Lion of the tribe of Juda — and in His kingdom the lion is tamed.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Prov 28:15; Zeph 3:3; Jer 50:17; Ezek 19; Rev 5:5) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7 — derived in the digital edition’s symbol study at TimeTested.Bible

glossaryEntries.definition: A nation — as the beasts of Daniel's sea are kingdoms, the living creatures in Revelation's sea are peoples.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Dan 7:3, 17; Rev 8:9; 16:3) · see The Bow, ch. 44

glossaryEntries.definition: The Spirit and word of God going out to give life.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Jer 2:13; John 7:38) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40

glossaryEntries.definition: The scattered house of Israel, sought and regathered.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Matt 15:24) · see Jacob, Israel & Ephraim, ch. 45

glossaryEntries.definition: Self-giving covenant allegiance embodied, for those under God's authority, in commandment-keeping. Obedience without love can be empty sacrifice, but claimed love that persistently refuses His commands is false — “this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments”.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: self-giving devotion or benevolence toward God and neighbor, with obedience as its necessary fruit and evidence rather than love's defining form.
glossaryEntries.citations: (John 14:15; 1 Cor 13:3; 1 John 4:8-10; 5:3; 2 John 4-6; Rom 13:10) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

glossaryEntries.definition: The covenant union of God and His people — the one-flesh bond God joins: the wife called by the Husband's name, brought under His wing.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 2:24; Ezek 16:8; Eph 5:31-32; Rev 19:7) · see Marriage and Divorce, ch. 12

glossaryEntries.definition: The word obeyed to completeness — “My meat is to do the will of him that sent me, and to finish his work”; and the will is the word: where Matthew hears “do the will of my Father,” Luke records the same saying as “hear the word of God, and do it.” Milk and meat are one substance in two states — the word received, and the word done: chewed and tasted as the ear tries words, served in due season, its fruit senses exercised to discern.
glossaryEntries.citations: (John 4:34; 6:55; 7:17; Matt 12:50; Luke 8:21; Ps 40:8; Job 34:3; Heb 5:14; Matt 24:45) · see Introduction, ch. 1

glossaryEntries.definition: Covenant loyalty — the Hebrew is chesed, the word beneath most of the Bible's “mercy”: the debt canceled for the one who “confesseth and forsaketh,” kept “with them that love him and keep his commandments,” and required of the pardoned — “blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy.”
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: not getting the punishment you do deserve — a one-way transaction, no conditions named.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Deut 7:9; Prov 28:13; Matt 18:27-35; 5:7) · see Grace, Mercy & the Gift, ch. 24

glossaryEntries.definition: The word received — teaching another has already digested, swallowed without work; the right first food of babes, given to grow them, and meant to be outgrown at weaning. Churned, it becomes butter — the word worked toward solid food.
glossaryEntries.citations: (1 Pet 2:2; 1 Cor 3:1-2; Isa 28:9; 7:15; Prov 30:33; Heb 5:12-13) · see Introduction, ch. 1

glossaryEntries.definition: The instant of decisive action, built on the image of an eye's wink — the unit in which judgment and mercy alike are done, never a slow process: Babylon falls “in a moment… in one day,” and the dead are raised “in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye.”
glossaryEntries.citations: (Isa 47:9; Job 34:20; 1 Cor 15:52) · see The Moment, ch. 38 | (Isa 47:9; Job 34:20; 1 Cor 15:52) · see The Moment, in the free digital edition at TimeTested.Bible

glossaryEntries.definition: The faithful witness — the Son, who shines with no light of His own but the Father's reflected, the light that shineth in the world's night; the lesser light that rules the night and marks the appointed times.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the church reflecting Christ's light as the moon reflects the sun.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ps 89:37; Rev 1:5; John 1:5; 5:19) · see Sun, Moon & Stars, ch. 29

glossaryEntries.definition: A kingdom — the seat of ruling authority.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Jer 51:25; Dan 2:35) · see Mountain, ch. 39

glossaryEntries.definition: Without covenant covering — exposed in one's breach.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ezek 16:8; Gen 3:7) · see Garments & Armor, ch. 43

glossaryEntries.definition: The covenant identity of a house, consisting of 3 things appointed and provided by its Head: the Word (the manna), the covenant law (the stone tables), and the fruitful priesthood (Aaron's budded rod). A counterfeit Name substitutes a different word, covenant, or priesthood; a Name is taken in vain when any one is rejected, replaced, or removed. A bride takes her Husband's Name by entering His house, coming under His authority, and obeying Him.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the person's character, authority, and reputation.

glossaryEntries.definition: The gospel’s gathering of all kinds out of the sea of peoples.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Matt 13:47-48) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40

glossaryEntries.definition: The renewed moon — chodesh, from chadash, to renew: the phase of the moon that serves as the sign of the start of the month, and so the name of the month itself. A sign must be watched for: the east gate opens on it for worship, commerce resents it, and Paul files it among the shadows of things to come; which phase renews the month, the Pearl chapter weighs from the letters.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ps 81:3; 1 Sam 20:5, 18; Isa 66:23; Ezek 46:1-3; Amos 8:5; Col 2:16-17) · see The Pearls of Wisdom, ch. 31

glossaryEntries.definition: A newly conferred covenant identity under its giver — known, received, and kept only by the one who bears it.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: a new God-given identity and character bestowed on the overcomer.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 32:28; Isa 62:2-5; 65:15; Rev 2:17) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

glossaryEntries.definition: The time of darkness — hiding and sleep, when opportunity closes; the children of the night sleep and are drunken, doing their deeds in the dark.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 1:5; 1 Thess 5:5-7) · see Light and Darkness, ch. 21

glossaryEntries.definition: A great city of the sea — gentile peoples who repent and rise in judgment.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Matt 12:41) · see The Sign of Jonah, ch. 4

glossaryEntries.definition: The hidden quarter — tsaphon, from the root to hide, to lurk: the dark side of the sky, the door the ambush comes by. In the north country the spoilers of Babylon gather — “an assembly of great nations,” the ten allied kings who turn on the seven the whore rules — and in its uttermost recesses, the “sides of the north,” the enemy set his seat.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Jer 1:14; 50:9, 41; 51:48; Ps 48:2; Isa 14:13; Rev 17:16-18) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35, and Lucifer's Declared Plan, ch. 30

glossaryEntries.definition: The commandment's truth and correction received and laid up inwardly until they govern the life — the tested, pressed fruit of the Spirit stored as proven obedience; light is that obedience made visible as an example to others.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the Holy Spirit — anointing, consecration, and empowering.

glossaryEntries.definition: Israel, the covenant people.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Jer 11:16; Hos 9:10) · see Trees, ch. 41

glossaryEntries.definition: The covenant made whole — shalom, from a root meaning to complete, restore, repay: the work of righteousness, the great peace of them that love the law — not the world’s truce and not a feeling (“not as the world giveth”). What the gospel publishes is this peace restored; the counterfeit pronounces it twice over an unkept covenant — “Peace, peace; when there is no peace.”

The one complete light — under the KJV's “rubies” (peninim, Strong's pearl), wisdom and the bride are priced above pearls; and the night sky's one pearl is the full moon (keseh, “fulness,” the letters under “throne” and “time appointed”), governor of the appointed times, the one-pearl gates of the city — the merchant's entry at the King's gate.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the kingdom of heaven, worth surrendering everything to gain — or the church, purchased by Christ.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Prov 3:15; 31:10; Ps 81:3; Prov 7:20; Job 26:9; Ps 104:19; Rev 21:21) · see The Pearls of Wisdom, ch. 31

glossaryEntries.definition: The bowed-humble before God — one Hebrew word family behind “poor” and “meek,” and “needy” (evyon) its constant companion; empty-handed toward Him, and so able to receive: the gospel’s hearers and heirs of the kingdom.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ps 37:11/Matt 5:5; Isa 61:1/Luke 4:18; Isa 66:2; Jas 2:5; Ps 72:12-13) · see Orphans, Widows & the Fatherless, ch. 14

glossaryEntries.definition: The faithful few who glean the edge — widow, fatherless, stranger, as Ruth did; small by design, refined like gold out of dross, at a fixed ratio traceable from the gleaning law's own geometry to Elijah's seven thousand.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ruth 2; 1 Kgs 19:18; Zech 13:8-9; Rom 11:5) · see The Remnant, ch. 15

glossaryEntries.definition: The self-sufficient who “have need of nothing” — full of self, and so unable to receive; Laodicea's boast, and Smyrna's opposite. The true wealth is being “rich toward God”: faith tried in the fire, and the garment of righteousness.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Rev 3:17-18; Rev 2:9; Prov 13:7; Luke 12:21) · see Orphans, Widows & the Fatherless, ch. 14

glossaryEntries.definition: Right-living. God is Right-Living by definition — His ways and works are the measure of right. For those under His authority, right-living is the doing of His commandments: the law kept, worn as the garment of righteous acts. Romans 4 excludes wage-work that would put God in debt, not obedience; even complete obedience earns no wage because the servant has only done his duty. Righteousness is given and reckoned by grace, but the gift never renames wrong-living right.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: primarily right standing before God — Christ's imputed righteousness received by faith apart from works — with right-living as its subsequent fruit and evidence.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Deut 32:4; 6:25; Ps 119:172; 145:17; Luke 17:7-10; Rom 4:4-8; Phil 3:9; Heb 11:8; 1 John 3:7) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6, for the dependent definitions; The End of the Law for Paul's wage, debt, law, and obedience vocabulary; and Garments & Armor, ch. 43, for righteousness given and worn

glossaryEntries.definition: The covenant — the Rock that followed Israel “was Christ,” the covenant in person; the stone the builders refused, made the cornerstone.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Deut 32:4; Isa 42:6; 1 Cor 10:4; Ps 118:22) · see Mountain, ch. 39

glossaryEntries.definition: The complete seven — six-and-one as a single whole, at every scale the law counts it: the week whose seventh day is the rest, the seventh year that rests the land, the seven-sevens that ring in jubilee. Scripture counts “seven sabbaths complete” and calls the week itself the sabbath; the rest-day is the crown of the unit, one-seventh of what the word names.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Lev 23:15 with Deut 16:9; Lev 25:2-8; 2 Chr 36:21; Luke 18:12; Matt 28:1; Heb 4:9) · see The Sabbath, ch. 32 | (Lev 23:15 with Deut 16:9; Lev 25:2-8; 2 Chr 36:21; Luke 18:12; Matt 28:1; Heb 4:9) · see The Sabbath, in the free digital edition at TimeTested.Bible

glossaryEntries.definition: To cause, appoint, or acknowledge as holy — removing someone or something from common status, placing it under an owner's claim for an appointed purpose, and treating or preparing it accordingly. God sanctifies by claiming for Himself and fitting for His use; people sanctify God and His Name by treating and displaying Him as holy. Moral cleansing and obedient living fit a person to that holy calling, but they are not the word's entire meaning.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: God's progressive work of inward renewal, by which believers die more and more to sin and live in righteousness.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ex 13:2; Num 8:17; Isa 8:13; Ezek 36:23; John 10:36; 17:19; 1 Cor 7:14; 1 Thess 4:3-7; 2 Tim 2:21; Heb 10:10, 29) · see Uncommon Sanctification, Justification, and Cleanliness

glossaryEntries.definition: The countless multitude — grains of the shore beyond number; and so a shifting foundation: to build on the sand is to build on the crowd, not the covenant-rock.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 22:17; Hos 1:10; Rev 20:8; Matt 7:26) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40

glossaryEntries.definition: Covenant blood made wearable — and counterfeited by those who wear the form without the substance.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Isa 1:18; Josh 2:18; Heb 9:19; Rev 17:4) · see Garments & Armor, ch. 43 — derived in the digital edition’s symbol study at TimeTested.Bible

glossaryEntries.definition: Peoples and nations — the restless, unrooted mass below the firmament; and, above it, the gathered waters of heaven: the still sea of glass where the angels and the redeemed stand.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Rev 17:15; Gen 1:6-8; Ps 148:4; Rev 4:6; 15:2) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40

glossaryEntries.definition: The NAME impressed on its owner — the signet-plate the law sets on the priest's forehead (HOLINESS TO THE LORD), the law bound on hand and between the eyes, stamped by the Spirit on God's servants before judgment; the inscription is quoted: the Lord knoweth them that are his — let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity. The counterfeit takes the same two places.
The word of God, sown in the hearts of men.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Luke 8:11) · see Grass, ch. 42

glossaryEntries.definition: The deceiver; the one who strips the covenant covering.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 3:1) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40 — derived in the digital edition’s symbol study at TimeTested.Bible

glossaryEntries.definition: The covering of a greater presence — refuge under the Almighty's wings, a kingdom's protection over its people, the outline a coming body casts ahead of itself. Good to dwell in — not the gloom it is read as; the KJV itself renders the word “defence”.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ps 91:1; Num 14:9; Col 2:17) · see Shadow, ch. 17

glossaryEntries.definition: The covenant people, who hear the Shepherd's voice and follow.
glossaryEntries.citations: (John 10:27) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

glossaryEntries.definition: The demanding place — from sha'al, to demand: mortality's claim on all flesh, swallowing righteous and wicked alike, personified with a mouth, gates, and bars. Its dead sleep in silence until it is made to give them back; then it is itself destroyed — “O grave, I will be thy destruction.” Distinct from Gehenna, the judgment.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 37:35; Ps 16:10; Eccl 9:5; Isa 5:14; Hos 13:14; Rev 20:13-14) · see Heaven and Hell, ch. 16

glossaryEntries.definition: An earthly kingdom, city, state, or governed political body riding upon the sea of peoples: its rulers guide it, its inhabitants and servants crew it, its armies defend it, and its wealth is carried as cargo. Christ needs no constructed body beneath Him: He walks upon the sea directly, and when He sails with His disciples the vessel comes under its true Head. The ship may be broken while its people survive.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the Church — a vessel of salvation carrying believers through the dangers of the world.

glossaryEntries.definition: A prophecy given in advance — often a prophet's lived story — whose fulfillment testifies; not a wonder performed on demand.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: a miraculous act pointing to God's power and Christ's identity.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Isa 7:14; Ezek 24:24; Luke 11:30) · see Signs and Similitudes, ch. 3

glossaryEntries.definition: The transgression of the law — Scripture's own definition: “sin is the transgression of the law”; where no law is, there is no transgression, and by the law is the knowledge of sin.
glossaryEntries.citations: (1 John 3:4; Rom 4:15; 3:20; 7:7) · see Grace, Mercy & the Gift, ch. 24

glossaryEntries.definition: A spiritual name of Jerusalem — the prophets address her rulers so to their faces: “Hear the word of the LORD, ye rulers of Sodom… ye people of Gomorrah”; Ezekiel calls Sodom her sister and Jerusalem the worse; and Revelation writes the name on “the great city… where also our Lord was crucified.”
glossaryEntries.citations: (Isa 1:10; Ezek 16:46-48; Rev 11:8) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

glossaryEntries.definition: The righteous, who rule the night with the Son — “they that be wise shall shine… as the stars for ever”; the twelve stars are the twelve tribes, gathered into the twelve constellations, the Mazzaroth.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Dan 12:3; Ps 136:9; Gen 37:9; Rev 12:1; Job 38:32) · see Sun, Moon & Stars, ch. 29

glossaryEntries.definition: A covenant cut by God — for a covenant is cut (Hebrew karat) — grown into the kingdom that breaks the world-empires and fills the earth.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Dan 2:34-35, 44-45; Gen 15:17-18; Deut 9:10; Col 2:11) · see Mountain, ch. 39

glossaryEntries.definition: The nations in turmoil — the raging sea, stilled at Christ's word, “Peace, be still”.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: divine judgment, and the trials of life which Christ has power to calm.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ps 65:7; Isa 17:12-13; Mark 4:39; Luke 21:25) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40

glossaryEntries.definition: A non-citizen of God's commonwealth — one outside the covenant, drawn in, or, once in, made a stranger to the world.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Eph 2:12, 19) · see Orphans, Widows & the Fatherless, ch. 14

glossaryEntries.definition: The Father, the source of light, from which every lesser light is drawn; the righteous shall shine as the sun in His kingdom.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ps 84:11; Gen 37:9; Matt 13:43) · see Sun, Moon & Stars, ch. 29

glossaryEntries.definition: The unclean beast par excellence — the one beast in the law wearing the outward sign without the inward work: the hoof parted, the cud never chewed. The nation outside the covenant that tramples what is holy — pearls under their feet, the holy city under the Gentiles, the washed sow back in the mire.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Lev 11:7; Deut 14:8; Matt 7:6; Rev 11:2; Isa 66:17; 2 Pet 2:22) · see The Other White Meat, ch. 48

glossaryEntries.definition: War and the word of judgment — the great sword that takes peace from the earth; the flaming sword that guards the way.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Rev 6:4; Gen 3:24) · see The Four Winds, ch. 34

glossaryEntries.definition: The prophet that teacheth lies — Isaiah's own decode, with head and tail already defined by the covenant: obedience makes Israel “the head, and not the tail,” and the curse inverts it. The dragon fells a third of the stars with its tail — the led destroyed by the misleading — and the trumpet armies' serpent-tails “had heads”: the liar enthroned. Moses is told to seize the serpent exactly there.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Isa 9:15-16; Deut 28:13, 44; Rev 12:4; 9:19; Ex 4:4) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

glossaryEntries.definition: The counterfeit sown among the wheat by the enemy — a weed that mimics the true grain until the harvest, then is bound in bundles and burned; the children of the wicked one, distinct from the winnowed chaff.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Matt 13:25-30, 38-40) · see Grass, ch. 42

glossaryEntries.definition: The stronghold raised by a Name around its house — refuge, watchtower, and lighthouse in one: high to see danger, giving light to guide the house, and covered to shelter those who come inside. A strong tower is an intact Name protecting its people; an unfinished tower is a Name begun without depth to endure its cost; a fallen tower is a covenant stronghold broken, emptied, or judged.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Prov 18:10; Ex 13:21; Isa 4:5-6; Hab 2:1; Gen 11:1-8; Luke 14:28-30; Matt 13:20-21; Luke 13:4-5) · see The Tower | (Prov 18:10; Ex 13:21; Isa 4:5-6; Hab 2:1; Gen 11:1-8; Luke 14:28-30; Matt 13:20-21; Luke 13:4-5) · see The Tower

glossaryEntries.definition: A nation or people.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Dan 4:22; Rom 11:17) · see Trees, ch. 41

glossaryEntries.definition: God's law — the standard.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: Christ Himself, and God's word — the gospel that sets free.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ps 119:142; 2 John 4) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7

glossaryEntries.definition: The tassels bound to the corners of the garment; looking upon them reminds the wearer of all the LORD's commandments, to do them.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Num 15:38-39) · see Wings, ch. 13

glossaryEntries.definition: Discernment of good from evil, gained by departing from evil — “a good understanding have all they that do his commandments”.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Job 28:28; Ps 111:10) · see The Fool and the Wise, ch. 20

glossaryEntries.definition: The low and humbled — the opposite of the mountain-kingdom; “every valley shall be exalted”.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the low seasons of trial and death, set against the mountaintop.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Isa 40:4) · see Mountain, ch. 39 — derived in the digital edition’s symbol study at TimeTested.Bible

glossaryEntries.definition: The espoused — betrothed to one husband with the wedding still ahead: covenant standing, not attainment; the law counts a betrothed virgin already a wife, the prophets call the ten-tribe house re-espoused after her divorce “the virgin of Israel,” and virgins plural are the bride’s companions who follow her in — the opposite of the harlot who goes after many.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Deut 22:23-24; Joel 1:8; Jer 31:4, 21; Amos 5:2; Ps 45:14-15; 2 Cor 11:2; Matt 25:1) · see The Fool and the Wise, ch. 20

glossaryEntries.definition: The words of the one who speaks; the Shepherd's voice is His words.
glossaryEntries.citations: (John 10:27) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

glossaryEntries.definition: Salvation — the covenant's enclosure: “thou shalt call thy walls Salvation”; God Himself “a wall of fire round about.” The counterfeit is self-built — wealth's high wall “in his own conceit,” and the whitewashed wall of false peace that the storm flattens.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Isa 60:18; Zech 2:5; Prov 18:11; Ezek 13:10-15) · see The Parable of the Vineyard | (Isa 60:18; Zech 2:5; Prov 18:11; Ezek 13:10-15) · see The Parable of the Vineyard, in the free digital edition at TimeTested.Bible

glossaryEntries.definition: Covenant conduct — the walk.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: Jesus Himself as the one way to the Father; the narrow way against the broad.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Jer 6:16; Matt 7:14) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7

glossaryEntries.definition: A seven — shavua, a unit of sevens, and not only of days: Laban decodes it in the text — “Fulfil her week… yet seven other years” — and Jacob serves seven years for the week named; the jubilee is counted as “seven sabbaths of years,” and Daniel’s seventy weeks are sevens of years — unpointed, seventy sevens that open into seventy jubilees. The Feast of Weeks runs the same count in days — seven sevens to the fiftieth — the jubilee modeled a day for a year.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 29:27-28; Lev 23:15-16; 25:8; Dan 9:24-25) · see Daniel Unsealed, ch. 36

glossaryEntries.definition: The sea at the back — the Hebrew for west is “sea” (yam): Israel faces east, so the west is “the hinder sea,” what lies behind; and as far as the east is from the west, so far are the transgressions removed.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Zech 14:8; Joel 2:20; Ps 103:12) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

glossaryEntries.definition: The children of the kingdom — the good grain gathered into the barn at the harvest.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Matt 13:38; 3:12) · see Grass, ch. 42

glossaryEntries.definition: God's covenant people cut off from their Husband.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Lam 1:1; Isa 54:5) · see Orphans, Widows & the Fatherless, ch. 14

glossaryEntries.definition: Spirit — ruach.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Zech 6:5) · see The Four Winds, ch. 34

glossaryEntries.definition: The vineyard's reckoning — where the fruit a people has borne is pressed out and rendered to the Owner, in one of two vintages: presses that “burst out with new wine” when the grapes are good; the growers themselves trodden — “the great winepress of the wrath of God” — and blood for wine, when the vintage is wickedness.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Isa 5:2, 7; Prov 3:10; Joel 2:24; 3:13; Lam 1:15; Isa 63:3; Rev 14:19-20) · see The Parable of the Vineyard | (Isa 5:2, 7; Prov 3:10; Joel 2:24; 3:13; Lam 1:15; Isa 63:3; Rev 14:19-20) · see The Parable of the Vineyard, in the free digital edition at TimeTested.Bible

glossaryEntries.definition: The covenant edge — wing, skirt, border, corner — where the reminder of the law is bound and refuge is found.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ezek 16:8) · see Wings, ch. 13

glossaryEntries.definition: The fear of the LORD lived out — the doing of the commandments; “the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom”.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Prov 9:10; Ps 111:10; Deut 4:6) · see The Fool and the Wise, ch. 20

glossaryEntries.definition: One who hears God's word and does it, who fears the LORD.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Matt 7:24; Ps 111:10) · see The Fool and the Wise, ch. 20

glossaryEntries.definition: Deeds — not a synonym for obedience. A work becomes obedience when it executes a legitimate command; it becomes disobedience when the command or deed conflicts with God's command. Romans 4 uses the laborer's work offered for wages and debt; James 2 uses Abraham's work as faith made visible. Complete obedience still earns no wage: the servant has only done his duty.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: in Paul's salvation texts, “works” broadly includes human obedience and effort set against faith; good works then follow salvation as its fruit and evidence.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ex 18:20; Ps 111:7; Mic 6:16; Luke 17:7-10; Rom 4:4-5; Jas 2:21-22) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6, for faith and works, and The End of the Law for Paul's works, wages, and duty vocabulary

glossaryEntries.definition: Paul's phrase for deeds considered in relation to law. It is not a synonym for obedience and does not identify one unchanging class of deeds. The surrounding passage may identify God's law, a circumcision-party application, or leave the particular acts unnamed. What remains consistent is the rejected claim made for those deeds: they cannot purchase justification, produce the Spirit, establish covenant standing, or place God in debt. The context identifies the work; the phrase denies it as the purchase price.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Rom 3:20, 28; 9:32 KJV/TR; Gal 2:16; 3:2, 5, 10) · see The End of the Law

glossaryEntries.definition: To bow down and serve — homage in the body, allegiance in the life; the fear of the LORD made visible, kept at His appointed times, on His terms. Not the song service: Scripture separates worship from singing in single scenes.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ex 20:5; Matt 4:10/Deut 6:13; 2 Chr 20:18-19; Rev 14:7) · see Worship, ch. 22

glossaryEntries.definition: A turning — shanah, written on the root to change, repeat, return: one complete cycle of time, at whatever scale the count is running — Jeremiah’s seventy “years” close only as seventy jubilees, and a thousand years pass as a day.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Jer 25:11-12; Dan 9:2, 24; Ps 90:4) · see Daniel Unsealed, ch. 36

judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, lamp oil is most commonly interpreted as a symbol of the Holy Spirit — the indwelling presence, grace, and enabling power of God's Spirit in the believer's life. This reading is anchored above all in the Parable of the Ten Virgins, where the wise virgins' possession of oil (and the foolish virgins' lack of it) is taken to represent having or lacking the Spirit's presence and the spiritual life He produces, which cannot be borrowed or transferred from another person at the last moment. The interpretation is reinforced by the wider biblical pattern in which anointing oil accompanies or represents the Spirit's coming upon prophets, priests, and kings, and by the lampstand vision of Zechariah, where oil-fed lamps are explicitly linked to the word 'not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.'

entries.definition: Receiving God's testimony as governing truth in a response that submits to it. Bare assent can recognize a fact — demons believe and tremble — but saving belief obeys the word believed, and persistent refusal to obey exposes unbelief.
entries.commonView: Commonly taught: personal trust in Christ, not mere assent — the instrument that receives salvation.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'belief' or 'to believe' (Greek pisteuo, Hebrew aman) is understood not as mere intellectual acknowledgment but as saving faith: personal trust in, reliance upon, and commitment to God and specifically to Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior. It is treated as the divinely appointed means of receiving salvation, justification, and eternal life, involving assent to the truth of the gospel, trust of the heart, and entrustment of oneself to Christ. Classical Protestant theology often analyzes it into three elements: notitia (knowledge of the content), assensus (assent that it is true), and fiducia (personal trust). Belief is thus the relational counterpart of God's grace: grace offers, faith receives.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'disciple' (Greek mathētēs, 'learner' or 'pupil') primarily denotes a committed follower of Jesus Christ — one who learns from him, obeys his teaching, imitates his life, and is bound to him in personal allegiance. Symbolically, discipleship stands for the whole Christian life: self-denial, cross-bearing, obedience to Jesus' word, love for fellow believers, and fruit-bearing. In this dominant reading, 'disciple' is functionally equivalent to 'Christian' (cf. Acts 11:26), describing not merely intellectual students but apprentices whose lives are being conformed to their Master.

judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching the dragon is overwhelmingly understood as a symbol of Satan (the devil), the primordial adversary of God and persecutor of God's people. The Book of Revelation makes this identification explicit, calling the great red dragon 'that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan,' thereby also linking the dragon to the serpent of Eden. By extension the dragon symbolizes cosmic evil and the chaotic, God-opposing power that stands behind hostile earthly kingdoms.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, Egypt is primarily a symbol of bondage and slavery — specifically the world of sin and oppression from which God delivers His people. The Exodus narrative is treated as the paradigm of salvation, so 'Egypt' becomes shorthand for the old life of enslavement (to sin, to the world, to worldly powers) that believers are redeemed out of, with the Exodus itself typologically foreshadowing redemption in Christ. Leaving Egypt = conversion/deliverance; longing to return to Egypt = backsliding toward the old sinful life or worldliness.

judges.label: Grok

The fish thus symbolizes divine preservation through death-like descent and the certainty of resurrection.

judges.consensusMeaning: Paradise: the ordered, life-giving presence of God in which humanity enjoys communion with God, often extended to the hope of creation restored.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the garden symbolizes paradise as the place of God's presence and unbroken communion between God and humanity. Rooted in the Garden of Eden, it represents the original blessed state of creation—provision, fellowship with God, and life (the tree of life)—which is lost through sin (expulsion from Eden) and finally restored in the new creation, where Revelation deliberately returns to garden imagery (tree of life, river of life). The garden thus frames the whole canonical arc: paradise created, paradise lost, paradise regained.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The Garden of Eden as paradise: the original place of perfect creation, innocence, abundance, and unhindered communion with God, later associated with the Fall and eschatological restoration

entries.definition: The rage of the wicked at the righteous — what the excluded do at the sight of the kingdom they forfeited, sorrow and hatred in one face; then they melt away. entries.commonView: Commonly taught: the anguish of the damned under conscious, everlasting torment.

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Severe anguish, despair, and sometimes enraged regret experienced under divine judgment—especially exclusion from God’s kingdom and, in traditional Christian teaching, the punishment of hell.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'gnashing of teeth' (nearly always paired with 'weeping') symbolizes the extreme anguish, despair, and suffering of those who are excluded from God's kingdom and consigned to final judgment or hell. It functions as a stock formula in Jesus' teaching for the conscious misery and regret of the condemned — the pain of eschatological loss.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Intense anguish, sorrow, and regret experienced by those excluded from God's kingdom and consigned to eschatological punishment (outer darkness or hell)

entries.definition: The gospel of the kingdom — the renewed covenant, the law going forth from Zion.

entries.citations: (Isa 52:7; 2:3; Jer 31:33; Heb 4:2) · see Gospel, ch. 5

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The “Gospel” primarily means the good news that God’s saving reign has come through Jesus Christ—especially through his death and resurrection—calling people to faith, repentance, forgiveness, and new life.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'Gospel' (Greek euangelion, 'good news') primarily denotes the message of salvation accomplished by God through the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ — the announcement that God has acted in Christ to forgive sin, reconcile humanity to himself, and inaugurate his kingdom, received by faith. It is less a symbol than a technical term for the core Christian proclamation (kerygma).

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: the good news of salvation through the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ

entries.definition: The covenant-breaker who wears the form of covenant without its substance — “that great city,” spiritually Sodom, Egypt, Babylon: Jerusalem unfaithful.
entries.commonView: Commonly taught: spiritual adultery; in Revelation, an apostate religious world-system — Rome, not Jerusalem.
entries.citations: (Rev 17:18; 11:8; Ezek 23:19) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual or covenantal unfaithfulness—especially idolatry, apostasy, and reliance on corrupt political powers—is the most common symbolic meaning of “harlot.” The image portrays a people, city, or religious body abandoning loyalty to God for other gods, powers, wealth, or alliances.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the harlot is the dominant biblical symbol of spiritual unfaithfulness to God — specifically idolatry and apostasy by a people covenanted to God. Israel/Judah are repeatedly portrayed as an unfaithful wife who 'plays the harlot' by worshiping other gods and trusting foreign alliances. In the New Testament the image culminates in 'Babylon the Great, mother of harlots' (Revelation 17–18), understood as a corrupt religious, political, and economic system seducing the nations away from God. Thus 'harlot' symbolically = a covenant community or world system that abandons faithfulness to God for idolatry, worldly power, and illicit alliances.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: spiritual unfaithfulness/idolatry (covenantal adultery against God)

entries.definition: Jerusalem — the navel and heart of the land.
entries.commonView: Commonly taught: the grave or Hades, where Christ lay three days.
entries.citations: (Matt 12:40; Ezek 5:5; 38:12) · see The Sign of Jonah, ch. 4

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Jesus’ death and burial—his being in the grave or, more broadly, in the state/realm of the dead before his resurrection.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, 'heart of the earth' is Jesus's own phrase (Matthew 12:40) prophesying His burial in the tomb/grave — the period between His death and resurrection, typologically paralleled with Jonah's three days and nights in the belly of the great fish. The dominant reading takes it as the grave itself, often with the extended sense of entering the realm of the dead (Sheol/Hades).

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The grave or tomb (place of burial/death) of Jesus, paralleling Jonah's confinement in the fish as a sign of death and subsequent deliverance/resurrection

entries.definition: One English word laid over two different things — Sheol/Hades, the grave that swallows righteous and wicked alike, and Gehenna, the judgment that destroys. The doctrine changes with the word beneath.
entries.commonView: Commonly taught: the place of eternal conscious punishment and separation from God.
entries.citations: (Ps 16:10 with Matt 10:28) · see Heaven and Hell, ch. 16

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Hell most commonly signifies the final condition or realm of divine judgment: irreversible exclusion from blessed communion with God and punishment of unrepentant evil. Biblical images such as fire, outer darkness, the undying worm, and the second death express the horror and finality of that judgment, though traditions differ over how literally those images should be understood.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'Hell' primarily signifies the final state or place of divine punishment and separation from God for the unrepentant wicked after death and final judgment. It is symbolically depicted through images of unquenchable fire, darkness, weeping and gnashing of teeth, and destruction (drawing on the Greek term Gehenna, itself derived from the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a site associated with idolatrous burning and later with fiery judgment). The dominant traditional reading takes this as eternal conscious punishment and exclusion from God's presence.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The final place or state of eternal conscious punishment, torment, and separation from God for the unrighteous after judgment

entries.definition: Covenant existence — the life the law produces.
entries.commonView: Commonly taught: Christ Himself, and the eternal life imparted to believers.
entries.citations: (Deut 30:19-20; Lev 18:5; John 14:6; Matt 7:14) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Divine or eternal life given by God in and through Jesus Christ—salvation understood as restored communion with God, spiritually present now and fulfilled in resurrection.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'life' or 'the life' symbolically denotes eternal, divine life (Greek zoe) that comes from God and is embodied in and given through Jesus Christ — a qualitatively new spiritual existence in communion with God, as opposed to mere biological existence (bios) or spiritual death. In Johannine usage especially, Christ himself is identified as 'the life,' so the term functions both as the gift (eternal life for believers) and the giver (Christ as the source and embodiment of that life).

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Jesus Christ himself as the personal source, embodiment, and giver of spiritual/eternal life (zoe)

entries.definition: The faithful witness — the Son, who shines with no light of His own but the Father's reflected, the light that shineth in the world's night; the lesser light that rules the night and marks the appointed times.
entries.commonView: Commonly taught: the church reflecting Christ's light as the moon reflects the sun.
entries.citations: (Ps 89:37; Rev 1:5; John 1:5; 5:19) · see Sun, Moon & Stars, ch. 29

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: In prophetic and apocalyptic interpretation, the moon most commonly functions as part of the divinely ordered cosmos; its darkening, turning to blood, or otherwise failing symbolizes the Day of the Lord, divine judgment, and the upheaval of the present world order.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In the broadest stream of Christian teaching, the moon is most commonly interpreted as the 'lesser light' that has no light of its own but reflects the light of the sun — symbolically, the Church (or the individual believer) reflecting the light of Christ, who is figured by the sun. This reading runs from patristic writers (e.g., Augustine, Ambrose, Origen) through medieval and modern devotional teaching. Bound up with this is the moon's role as a fixed, faithful witness in the heavens, a sign of God's ordered creation and covenant faithfulness.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: the Church (or people of God) as a lesser light reflecting the light of Christ/the Sun

entries.definition: The covenant itself — taken as a bride takes her husband's: to be called by His name is to be brought under His wing, whose corners carry the reminder of the commandments.
entries.commonView: Commonly taught: the person's character, authority, and reputation.
entries.citations: (2 Sam 7:13; Ex 20:7; Isa 4:1; Ruth 3:9) · see The Name, ch. 8

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A “name” most commonly symbolizes the identity and revealed character of the person who bears it; in biblical usage it can therefore represent the person himself or herself, including that person’s presence, reputation, and authority. judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching and biblical interpretation, a 'name' symbolizes the essential character, nature, and identity of the person who bears it — the name stands for the person themselves. This is most emphasized with the divine name: God's name represents God's own being, character, authority, and presence, so that to know, call on, praise, or profane the name is to know, call on, praise, or profane God himself. By extension, acting 'in the name' of someone means acting in their person, character, and delegated authority.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The name of a person (especially God or Jesus) stands for their full identity, character, authority, power, and presence, so that invoking or acting 'in the name' means acting by that person's authority and under their protection.

entries.definition: The renewed covenant, known — kept — only by the one who receives it.
entries.commonView: Commonly taught: a new God-given identity and character bestowed on the overcomer.

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A “new name” most commonly symbolizes a new, God-given identity and status—often associated with transformation, belonging to God, vindication, and a new vocation or destiny.

judges.label: Grok

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The kingdom of heaven (or the gospel of salvation/Christ) as a treasure of supreme, inestimable worth for which everything else should be sacrificed

judges.label: Claude

judges.label: Grok

entries.definition: Right-living. God is Right-Living by definition — His ways and works are the measure of right. Righteousness is given and reckoned by grace, but the gift never renames wrong-living right.

entries.definition: Right-living. God is Right-Living by definition — His ways and works are the measure of right. For those under His authority, right-living is the doing of His commandments: the law kept, worn as the garment of righteous acts. Romans 4 excludes wage-work that would put God in debt, not obedience; even complete obedience earns no wage because the servant has only done his duty. Righteousness is given and reckoned by grace, but the gift never renames wrong-living right.

entries.definition: To cleanse is to remove the defilement that bars proper contact, approach, or use; clean describes what is free of that defilement and fit for its permitted place. Uncleanness may be physical, ceremonial, or moral and does not always mean guilt: childbirth, marital relations, and touching the dead all make unclean without being called sin. Cleansing removes what makes a vessel unfit; sanctification places the cleansed vessel under a holy claim and appointed use.
entries.commonView: Commonly treated either as hygiene and obsolete ritual regulation, or as a synonym for moral purity and holiness.
entries.citations: (Lev 10:10; 12:2; 15:18; Num 19:11; Ps 51:2, 10; Eph 5:26; 1 John 1:7, 9) · see Uncommon Sanctification, Justification, and Cleanliness

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'clean/unclean' is understood as ritual-purity language that symbolizes moral and spiritual condition before God: uncleanness represents sin, defilement, and unfitness to approach a holy God, while cleanness represents holiness, moral purity, and acceptable standing in God's presence. Correspondingly, 'cleanse/cleansing' symbolizes God's forgiveness of sin and the sanctification of the believer, accomplished ultimately through the atoning blood of Christ (with the Old Testament washings and purification rites read as types or foreshadowings of that spiritual cleansing). A closely joined sub-theme is Jesus' relocation of defilement from external ritual to the inner heart (Mark 7), and the New Testament's declaration that former ritual categories (foods, Gentiles) are now 'cleansed,' opening covenant access to all peoples.

entries.definition: To judge, declare, or demonstrate a person, word, deed, or cause right against a question or charge; the opposite is to condemn. God answers the charge against the sinner by grace through Christ, forgiving rather than renaming ungodliness righteousness. Deeds may vindicate a claimed faith, but they cannot purchase the Judge's mercy or place God in debt.
entries.commonView: Commonly taught in Protestant theology: God's once-for-all legal declaration that a believer is righteous through Christ's imputed righteousness, received by faith apart from works.
entries.citations: (Deut 25:1; Prov 17:15; Matt 11:19; Luke 7:29; Rom 3:24-26; 4:4-8; 8:33; Jas 2:21-25) · see Uncommon Sanctification, Justification, and Cleanliness, and The End of the Law for Paul's law, works, wages, and debt vocabulary

In classic Protestant formulation this is a declarative act in which Christ's righteousness is imputed to the believer (justification by grace alone through faith alone). entries.definition: To cause, appoint, or acknowledge as holy — removing someone or something from common status, placing it under an owner's claim for an appointed purpose, and treating or preparing it accordingly. God sanctifies by claiming for Himself and fitting for His use; people sanctify God and His Name by treating and displaying Him as holy. Moral cleansing and obedient living fit a person to that holy calling, but they are not the word's entire meaning.

entries.definition: Deeds — not a synonym for obedience. A work becomes obedience when it executes a legitimate command; it becomes disobedience when the command or deed conflicts with God's command. Romans 4 uses the laborer's work offered for wages and debt; James 2 uses Abraham's work as faith made visible. Complete obedience still earns no wage: the servant has only done his duty.
entries.commonView: Commonly taught: in Paul's salvation texts, “works” broadly includes human obedience and effort set against faith; good works then follow salvation as its fruit and evidence.
entries.citations: (Ex 18:20; Ps 111:7; Mic 6:16; Luke 17:7-10; Rom 4:4-5; Jas 2:21-22) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6, for faith and works, and The End of the Law for Paul's works, wages, and duty vocabulary

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: “Works” most commonly means a person’s deeds or conduct as the outward expression and moral fruit of inward faith, character, and allegiance. Good works are acts of obedience, love, justice, and mercy; evil works are sinful acts that manifest unbelief or corrupt desire. They are frequently portrayed as evidence by which persons are known and judged, although Christian traditions differ over their precise relation to salvation.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'works' are understood as the outward deeds or actions of a person that express and evidence the inner spiritual condition — good works being the visible fruit of genuine faith, God's grace, and a regenerated heart, and evil works being the visible fruit of unbelief, the sinful nature ('the flesh'), or alignment with darkness. Works function as evidence or fruit rather than as the root: they reveal what a person truly is (a tree known by its fruit), and they will be the basis of divine assessment at judgment because they manifest the heart. In the dominant Protestant framing, good works are distinguished from saving faith — believers are saved by grace through faith, not by works, yet are saved 'unto' good works which necessarily follow true faith.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Human deeds/actions (good works as righteous fruit of genuine faith that evidence salvation and glorify God; evil works as sinful deeds of the flesh that reveal unbelief and bring judgment)

entries.definition: Paul's phrase for deeds considered in relation to law. It is not a synonym for obedience and does not identify one unchanging class of deeds. The surrounding passage may identify God's law, a circumcision-party application, or leave the particular acts unnamed. What remains consistent is the rejected claim made for those deeds: they cannot purchase justification, produce the Spirit, establish covenant standing, or place God in debt. The context identifies the work; the phrase denies it as the purchase price.
entries.citations: (Rom 3:20, 28; 9:32 KJV/TR; Gal 2:16; 3:2, 5, 10) · see The End of the Law

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Deeds done in obedience to “the law,” ordinarily understood as the commandments of the Mosaic Torah, especially when relied upon as the basis or means of being justified before God. In much Christian teaching, the phrase consequently represents human law-keeping or religious achievement contrasted with justification by faith.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, especially in the Reformation/Protestant tradition, 'works of the law' (Greek: erga nomou) refers to deeds performed in obedience to the Mosaic law—understood broadly as any human effort or moral/ritual performance undertaken to earn or establish righteousness before God. The phrase functions in Paul's letters as the negative pole in the faith-versus-works contrast: no one is justified by works of the law, but only through faith in Jesus Christ. Symbolically, the term stands for legalism, self-reliant human achievement, and works-righteousness as opposed to justification received by grace through faith.

judges.label: Grok

The context identifies the work; the phrase denies it as the purchase price.

entries.definition: The watcher-tree and the priesthood's sign — first tree to wake, from shaqad, to watch: “I will watch over my word.” Aaron's dead rod budded, blossomed, and yielded almonds overnight — the house of Levi chosen by a resurrection sign — and the sanctuary lampstand is carved of almond cups: the watcher-tree bears the lamp.
entries.citations: (Jer 1:11-12; Num 17:8; Ex 25:33-34) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Watchfulness or wakefulness—especially God’s vigilant readiness to fulfill his word. This symbolism rests on the Hebrew wordplay between šāqēd (“almond”) and šōqēd (“watching”), reinforced by the almond tree’s early blossoming.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: God's watchfulness and vigilance—specifically His wakeful attentiveness to His word so as to fulfill it swiftly. This rests on the Hebrew wordplay in Jeremiah between 'shaqed' (almond) and 'shoqed' (watching/wakeful), reinforced by the natural fact that the almond is the first tree to blossom in the Levantine spring (often called the 'awake' or 'watchful' tree), making it an emblem of divine alertness, promptness, and the hastening of God's purposes.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Watchfulness, the hastening or fulfillment of God's word, and resurrection or new life.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: divine watchfulness / vigilance (God promptly watching over and fulfilling His word)

entries.term: Assembly of the wicked / synagogue of Satan
entries.definition: The counterfeit congregation — an edah (the covenant-assembly word) claiming covenant standing while gathered against the covenant's Lord: God names the rebel camp “this evil congregation… gathered together against me,” Korah's company declares all the congregation holy, and at the cross the assembly encloses the Messiah from inside the camp while the dogs compass from without — “the synagogue of Satan, which say they are Jews, and are not.”
entries.citations: (Ps 22:16; Num 14:35; 16:3; Ps 1:5; 26:5; Acts 4:27; Rev 2:9; 3:9) · see What Is the Point?, ch. 25

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A community that claims religious legitimacy or covenant identity but, through opposition to God, Christ, or faithful believers, functions as an instrument of Satan. In Christian interpretation, the expression usually signifies false or hostile religion rather than a building or an assembly openly dedicated to Satan.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching the phrase denotes a counterfeit covenant community: a group that claims the identity and privileges of God's people while in fact opposing God and persecuting the faithful, thereby serving Satan rather than God. In its original setting in Revelation, the dominant historical-critical reading takes it as the local Jewish synagogue communities in Smyrna and Philadelphia who denounced or slandered Christians to Roman authorities; the theological point drawn from it in Christian interpretation is that outward religious identity without allegiance to Christ is a false claim, so that the 'assembly' stands symbolically for false or apostate religion in opposition to the true people of God. The related phrase 'assembly of the wicked' (Psalm 22:16) is traditionally read christologically as the hostile crowd surrounding the suffering righteous one, applied in Christian exegesis to those who condemned and crucified Christ.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: A religious group or institution that claims to serve God and hold true covenantal authority, but actively opposes Christ and persecutes true believers. In its original biblical context, it specifically refers to local Jewish communities in Asia Minor who rejected Jesus as Messiah and persecuted the early Christians, while 'assembly of the wicked' prophetically describes those who orchestrated the crucifixion.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: A group falsely claiming to be God's true people (Jews) who actually serve Satan by opposing and persecuting faithful Christians

entries.definition: The self-made kingdom that builds a name against heaven — an empire raised over many kingdoms, the covenant counterfeit.
entries.citations: (Gen 11:4; Jer 51:7; Rev 17:18) · see The Bow, ch. 44, and The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Babel/Babylon most commonly symbolizes proud, idolatrous, oppressive human civilization organized in rebellion against God—especially worldly empire, corrupt power, and false religion destined for divine judgment.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, Babel/Babylon functions as the archetypal symbol of human pride, self-exaltation, and organized rebellion against God — the 'city of man' or godless world system standing in deliberate contrast to the city of God (Jerusalem/Zion). Babel represents humanity's attempt to make a name for itself and reach heaven by its own power (resulting in confusion and scattering), and Babylon extends this into the image of an idolatrous, oppressive, seductive world power destined for divine judgment. In Revelation, 'Babylon the great' is the culminating symbol of this anti-God civilization, whose fall is contrasted with the descent of the New Jerusalem.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Human pride, rebellion against God, systemic idolatry, and an oppressive, worldly anti-God system or empire.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Prideful human rebellion against God (exalting self/city to heaven without God), producing confusion, scattering, and judgment; more broadly the archetypal worldly empire/system (idolatrous, immoral, oppressive) that captivates and persecutes God's people and stands opposed to His kingdom, destined for divine overthrow.

entries.definition: The firstfruits — the first and humblest grain, reaped in spring; the sheaf waved before the LORD, which is Christ risen.
entries.citations: (Ex 9:31; Lev 23:10; Ruth 1:22; 2 Kgs 4:42; 1 Cor 15:20) · see Grass, ch. 42

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Barley has no universally settled Christian symbolic meaning. Where a broad symbolism is assigned, it most often represents humble or inexpensive sustenance through which God provides—especially provision for ordinary or poor people.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In most Christian teaching, barley symbolizes humble, lowly provision — the bread of the poor — through which God works and provides.
