In mainstream teaching it represents salvation received as a gift from God ('take' the helmet) that guards the believer's thinking and secures hope of final deliverance in spiritual warfare.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The believer's assurance and present possession of salvation, as well as the future hope of final deliverance, which protects the mind and spiritual life from doubt and demonic attack.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Assurance/hope of salvation that protects the believer’s mind (thoughts, confidence, and resolve) against doubt, despair, and spiritual attack, as a piece of the Armor of God

entries.definition: The way of holiness — the prepared road home.
entries.citations: (Isa 35:8) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A divinely prepared way by which God comes to his people and leads the redeemed into salvation, holiness, restoration, and ultimately his presence.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the 'highway' functions primarily as a symbol of the prepared way of the Lord—God's route of salvation and deliverance by which He comes to His people and by which the redeemed return to Him. It is most often preached as the 'Highway of Holiness' (Isaiah 35:8): the sanctified path of salvation open to the redeemed and closed to the unclean, and, via Isaiah 40:3, as the way prepared for the coming of Christ, which the Gospels apply to John the Baptist's ministry.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The path of holiness, salvation, and right relationship with God; a prepared spiritual route for God's presence or the believer's journey of sanctification.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The prepared, straight path or way of the Lord (often messianic), enabling God's coming or the people's return/holiness

entries.definition: The mount of an executing spirit; the conqueror who wins the nations by the bow.
entries.citations: (Rev 6:2) · see The Four Winds, ch. 34

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Victory or conquest, especially victorious military or royal power. In Revelation 19 the white horse specifically represents Christ’s righteous, triumphant rule; in Revelation 6 the white horse and its crowned, bow-bearing rider signify conquest, though the rider’s identity is disputed.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching the horse is primarily a symbol of war, military power, and conquest, and the white horse specifically symbolizes victorious conquest. The most widely cited image is the white horse of Revelation 19:11, whose rider ('Faithful and True,' the Word of God) is universally understood as the victorious, returning Christ; white connotes victory, righteousness, and purity. The other famous white horse, the first of the four horsemen in Revelation 6:2, is also read as a figure of conquest, though the rider's identity is disputed (see alternatives). More broadly in Scripture, horses represent human military strength in contrast to trust in God.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Victory, righteous judgment, and conquest, most prominently symbolizing Jesus Christ's victorious return to defeat His enemies and establish His kingdom.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Victory, triumphant conquest, or the advance of Christ/the gospel

entries.term: Image of metals (gold, silver, brass, clay)
entries.definition: The succession of gentile world-kingdoms, shattered by the stone-kingdom of God.
entries.citations: (Dan 2:32-45) · see Mountain, ch. 39

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The metals in Nebuchadnezzar’s image symbolize a succession of earthly kingdoms or world empires. Their changing materials portray successive stages of imperial rule, culminating in a divided and unstable kingdom represented by iron mixed with clay; all are ultimately displaced by God’s everlasting kingdom.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: The great statue of Nebuchadnezzar's dream in Daniel 2 is most commonly understood as a prophetic symbol of a succession of world empires, decreasing in glory (gold to clay) from Babylon onward, which will ultimately be destroyed and replaced by God's everlasting kingdom (the stone cut without hands). In the traditional Christian scheme: the head of gold = Babylon (explicitly identified in the text as Nebuchadnezzar/Babylon), the silver chest and arms = Medo-Persia, the bronze belly and thighs = Greece (Alexander and successors), the iron legs = Rome, and the feet/toes of iron mixed with clay = a divided or weakened final form of that empire; the stone that smashes the image represents the kingdom of God (often identified with Christ and his kingdom/church).

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: A succession of worldly empires or kingdoms, traditionally identified as Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, and Rome, which will ultimately be destroyed and replaced by God's eternal kingdom.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Successive Gentile world empires (Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome, and a final divided kingdom) that dominate history until God's eternal kingdom destroys them and fills the earth

entries.definition: The discipline of the law, received and kept — what only fools despise.
entries.citations: (Prov 1:7; 23:23) · see The Fool and the Wise, ch. 20

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: God-given teaching or guidance that reveals how people should believe and live—especially divine law, wisdom, and moral direction. “Instruction” is generally treated as a direct concept rather than as a symbol with one fixed hidden meaning.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, 'instruction' is most commonly understood as divine teaching—God's word and guidance for righteous living. This tracks the Hebrew terms torah (teaching/law/instruction) and musar (instruction/discipline), so 'instruction' is regularly presented as God's revealed will communicated through Scripture, wisdom teaching, and parental/spiritual authority, functioning as the path to life and the beginning of wisdom.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: God's revealed will, divine guidance, and formative moral training that imparts wisdom and illuminates the path of life for the believer.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Divine teaching, guidance, or doctrine (especially Scripture or Torah) that forms wisdom, righteousness, and moral character

entries.definition: The fourth kingdom — Rome: Daniel named Medo-Persia and Greece outright, and the iron that breaks in pieces all before it is the empire that held the world when He came.
entries.citations: (Dan 2:40; 8:20-21) · see The Sign of Jonah, ch. 4

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Strength, hardness, and irresistible power—often specifically severe, crushing, or unyielding political or judicial power.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: Iron most commonly symbolizes strength, hardness, and unyielding power — especially severe, inflexible rule or judgment. The best-known expression is the messianic 'rod of iron,' denoting Christ's absolute, unbreakable authority over the nations, and more broadly iron connotes irresistible force, harshness, and severity (of rule, oppression, or affliction).

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Strength, unyielding power, severe judgment, and absolute rule (often represented by a rod of iron)

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: strength, hardness, and crushing or unyielding power (especially of kingdoms, rule, or military force)

entries.definition: A set-apart, sanctified people — the covenant-rock risen out of the sea of nations (a mountain breaking the surface), waiting for the law that sanctifies it; “the island of the innocent,” delivered to safety while the kingdoms fall.

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: When “islands” or “isles” carries representative force, it most commonly denotes distant coastlands and their peoples—especially remote Gentile nations or the farthest reaches of the inhabited world called to witness, worship, or receive God’s rule.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In most Christian teaching and biblical scholarship, 'island' or 'isle' (Hebrew 'iyyim, often rendered 'coastlands' in modern translations) is not primarily a fixed symbol but a figure for the distant Gentile nations and the farthest reaches of the earth. Symbolically it stands for remote peoples far from Israel who will nonetheless hear of, wait for, and receive God's salvation—hence it functions in prophetic and missionary interpretation as shorthand for the worldwide, universal scope of God's redemptive purpose extending to the Gentiles.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Distant nations, the Gentile world, or the ends of the earth

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Distant Gentile nations or remote coastlands of the earth that will receive God's law and salvation

entries.definition: The new name of the one who prevails with God — covenant and character, not blood.
entries.citations: (Gen 32:28; Rom 9:6) · see Jacob, Israel & Ephraim, ch. 45

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: God’s covenant people: a people chosen, formed, and called by God to belong to him, bear witness to him, and mediate his blessing. In Christian symbolism, “Israel” therefore commonly represents the people of God, although Christians disagree sharply over whether this designation refers primarily to ethnic Israel, the church, or both in different senses.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'Israel' primarily signifies the covenant people of God. In its most common symbolic/theological extension (found in patristic, Catholic, Orthodox, and Reformed traditions), the term is read as pointing beyond the ethnic nation to the Church as the 'true' or 'spiritual' Israel — the community of all who belong to God through faith in Christ, Jew and Gentile alike. The name itself, given to Jacob ('he strives with God,' Gen 32:28), is also frequently invoked as symbolizing the people who wrestle with and prevail with God.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The Church as the spiritual people of God or the New Israel, encompassing all believers in Christ, both Jew and Gentile.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The covenant people of God, fulfilled or continued as the Christian Church (spiritual/new Israel)

entries.definition: The crooked, supplanting human heart that God transforms.
entries.citations: (Gen 27:36; Jer 17:9) · see Jacob, Israel & Ephraim, ch. 45

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Jacob most commonly signifies Israel: the covenant patriarch whose renamed identity becomes the name and representative embodiment of the people descended from him. Thus biblical references to “Jacob” often denote the nation or covenant people collectively.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, Jacob primarily symbolizes the nation of Israel and, by extension, God's chosen covenant people. Because Jacob is renamed 'Israel' after wrestling with God, his name functions throughout Scripture as a synonym for the covenant nation, and his life story is read as the archetype of the flawed sinner ('supplanter/deceiver') transformed by God's grace into a bearer of the covenant promise.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The archetype of the natural, striving human (the supplanter) who is transformed by God's grace into a spiritual overcomer (Israel), as well as a corporate symbol for God's chosen, covenant people elected by grace.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: God's elect/covenant people (Israel/the Church as spiritual Israel)

entries.definition: In covenant contexts, one in the covenant — “he is a Jew, which is one inwardly,” while some “say they are Jews, and are not.” The name is Judah's, and Judah means praise — “Now will I praise the LORD” — so Paul's definition lands on the name itself: the Jew inwardly is he “whose praise is not of men, but of God.” The word also walks in plain dress, ethnic and religious; context decides which coat it wears.
entries.citations: (Rom 2:28-29; Gen 29:35; Rev 3:9; Rom 9:6; Zech 8:23) · see Jacob, Israel & Ephraim, ch. 45

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: When interpreted symbolically, “Jew” most commonly signifies a member of God’s covenant people—especially one whose covenant identity is inward and marked by faithfulness or “circumcision of the heart,” rather than merely by outward descent or observance. However, the term is ordinarily used literally in Scripture, and no single symbolic interpretation is settled across Christian traditions.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian symbolic interpretation, 'Jew' is most commonly taken to signify a member of God's covenant people, with the New Testament (especially Paul) redefining the 'true Jew' inwardly and spiritually: one whose heart is circumcised by the Spirit and who praises God, rather than one identified merely by ethnic descent or outward observance. On this reading, the term symbolizes authentic covenant belonging — faith-defined membership in the people of God — which many Christian traditions extend to believers in Christ regardless of ethnicity.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: A true or spiritual believer whose heart has been inwardly transformed by God, representing the spiritual people of God (often associated with the Church) as opposed to merely outward or ethnic descent.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: A true believer whose heart is circumcised by the Spirit (an inward Jew) rather than an ethnic descendant of Abraham alone

entries.definition: The law's ruling and the ruler's office — what God declares due, kept like a commandment and owed first to the widow, the fatherless, the stranger, and the poor. To judge is to rule and deliver by the law (the judges were saviours; “a king to judge us… and fight our battles”), so the righteous pray for judgment and creation rejoices at its coming; condemnation is one verdict of the office, not the office.
entries.citations: (Deut 10:18; Ps 119:160; Matt 23:23; 1 Sam 8:20; Isa 33:22; Dan 7:22) · see Justice and Judgment, ch. 18

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: God’s righteous evaluation of human persons, deeds, peoples, or powers, resulting in a just verdict—vindication or condemnation—and often in reward, punishment, or separation. In Christian teaching, “judgment” most commonly points especially to the final, eschatological judgment by God through Christ.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, 'Judgment' primarily refers to God's final eschatological judgment: the decisive act at the end of history in which God, exercised through Jesus Christ, holds all humanity accountable, evaluates every person's deeds and relationship to Christ, and renders a verdict that separates the righteous (destined for eternal life) from the wicked (destined for condemnation). It is symbolically depicted through courtroom imagery (books opened, a throne, a verdict), harvest imagery (reaping, winnowing, separating wheat from chaff), and shepherd imagery (separating sheep from goats). The 'Last Judgment' or 'Day of Judgment' is an article of the historic creeds ('he will come again to judge the living and the dead') and is affirmed across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Divine justice, the ultimate eschatological evaluation of deeds, the separation of the righteous from the wicked, and the final rectification of all wrongs.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: God's definitive evaluation of human lives and deeds (especially at the eschatological Last Judgment), resulting in eternal reward or condemnation

entries.definition: Righteousness under a second English name — one Hebrew word behind both renderings: the commandments done where a neighbor can be wronged or righted.
entries.citations: (Gen 18:19/Jer 22:3; Ps 89:14/97:2) · see Justice and Judgment, ch. 18

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: God’s righteous and impartial ordering of human life: judging rightly, giving people their due, restraining wrongdoing, and defending or restoring those who are oppressed or vulnerable. In Christian teaching, justice is commonly paired with righteousness and treated as both an attribute of God and a duty of God’s people.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'justice' (Hebrew mishpat/tsedaqah; Greek dikaiosyne) is understood primarily as an essential attribute of God's character and the corresponding moral demand He places on His people: rightly ordered relationships, faithfulness to covenant obligations, impartial judgment, and active protection of the vulnerable (the poor, widow, orphan, and foreigner). It is less a 'symbol' in the strict sense than a core theological concept: justice is the foundation of God's throne and rule, and doing justice is presented as inseparable from genuine worship and knowledge of God. In the New Testament it converges with 'righteousness' (the same Greek word family), so justice is also read as God's saving action to set things right, culminating in Christ.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: God's moral order applied to human relationships, characterized by restorative action, equitable treatment, and the active protection of the vulnerable (such as widows, orphans, and the poor).

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: God's righteous character and fair judgment that upholds moral order by vindicating the innocent, punishing wrongdoing, and requiring humans to act equitably especially toward the vulnerable

entries.definition: Covenant relationship proven by obedience — the intimate “knew” of marriage; a stranger is one not known.
entries.citations: (Gen 4:1; Hos 4:6; Matt 7:23; 1 John 2:3-4) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: When “know” carries theological or symbolic force, it most commonly denotes personal, experiential, and covenantal relationship—especially intimate communion with God—rather than mere possession of information. Such knowledge is often understood as involving recognition, love, trust, and obedience.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching and biblical scholarship, 'to know' (Hebrew yada'; Greek ginōskō) symbolizes intimate, experiential, relational knowledge rather than mere intellectual or factual awareness. Applied to God, 'knowing' God means being in a living covenant relationship with Him — personal communion, love, obedience, and fidelity — and God's 'knowing' a person signifies His personal, covenantal acknowledgment of them. This is routinely contrasted in commentaries and lexicons (e.g., TDNT, BDB, TWOT) with the Greek philosophical ideal of detached cognition.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Intimate, experiential relationship and personal fellowship, rather than merely intellectual or cognitive awareness.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Intimate, experiential, personal relationship or union (especially with God), as distinct from mere intellectual or propositional awareness

entries.definition: One of the flock — a covenant person, not by itself Christ: Nathan's ewe lamb is a poor man's beloved, Jeremiah is “like a lamb… brought to the slaughter,” the disciples are sent “as lambs among wolves.” The Lamb of God is Christ — the one lamb “without blemish,” taken “out from the sheep”: the perfect lamb of the flock.
entries.citations: (2 Sam 12:3; Jer 11:19; Isa 53:6-7; Ex 12:5; Luke 10:3; John 1:29) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7 — derived in the digital edition’s symbol study at TimeTested.Bible

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Jesus Christ as the innocent, sacrificial “Lamb of God,” whose death brings atonement, redemption, and deliverance; in Revelation, the slain Lamb is also the risen, victorious, and reigning Messiah.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, the lamb is overwhelmingly understood as a symbol of Jesus Christ as the innocent, sacrificial victim whose death atones for sin — the 'Lamb of God.' The image fuses the Passover lamb of the Exodus, the daily sacrificial lambs of the Levitical system, and the suffering servant led 'like a lamb to the slaughter,' all read typologically as fulfilled in Christ's crucifixion.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Jesus Christ as the ultimate, innocent, and unblemished sacrificial offering for the sins of humanity, fulfilling the Old Testament types of the Passover lamb and the Suffering Servant.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Jesus Christ as the sacrificial Lamb of God whose death atones for the sins of the world

entries.definition: The commandment.
entries.citations: (Prov 6:23) · see Light and Darkness, ch. 21

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: God’s truth—especially Scripture—as illumination and guidance for faithful living.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the lamp most commonly symbolizes God's Word (Scripture) as a source of guidance and illumination for the believer's life, and by close extension the light of divine truth and witness that believers are to display to the world.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: God's Word, truth, and divine guidance providing spiritual direction in darkness.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The Word of God as a source of spiritual illumination, guidance, and direction for the believer's path

entries.definition: Bread soured — the word made impure, embittered, and puffed up; the hidden corruption that ferments through the whole lump, purged before Passover and forbidden on God's altar. The NT names it the corrupt doctrine of the Pharisees.
entries.citations: (Lev 2:11; Matt 16:12; 1 Cor 5:7-8) · see Grass, ch. 42

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Leaven most commonly symbolizes a corrupting or morally harmful influence—especially sin, hypocrisy, or false teaching—that spreads through and affects a larger community.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In most Christian teaching, leaven symbolizes sin, corruption, or evil influence—especially false teaching and hypocrisy—whose defining characteristic is that a small amount spreads pervasively through the whole. This underlies the moral logic of removing leaven at Passover and the apostolic exhortation to purge sin from the community.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Sin, hypocrisy, false teaching, and corruption that spreads pervasively and contaminates the whole.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: sin, moral corruption, or evil/false influence that spreads and permeates

entries.definition: The King's jubilee release — out of the slaver's house (sin, Egypt, Babylon) and home to the household, inheritance, and service of God; a change of masters, never the absence of one. Its constitution is the perfect law of liberty; its counterfeit, liberty as license, is a return to bondage.
entries.citations: (Lev 25:10; Isa 61:1; Jas 1:25; 2 Pet 2:19) · see Liberty, ch. 19

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual freedom in Christ: liberation from bondage to sin, condemnation, death, and the enslaving misuse of the law, resulting in freedom to live by the Spirit in righteousness and loving service rather than self-indulgence.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'liberty' primarily symbolizes the spiritual freedom believers receive in Christ: emancipation from bondage to sin, death, condemnation, and the law as a means of justification. It is freedom for holiness and love, not autonomy or license — the redeemed state of the children of God enabled by the Spirit.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual freedom from the bondage of sin, death, and the condemnation of the law, granted through salvation in Jesus Christ and the indwelling of the Holy Spirit.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual freedom from bondage to sin, death, and the Mosaic law through Christ

entries.definition: Covenant existence — the life the law produces.
entries.commonView: Commonly taught: Christ Himself, and the eternal life imparted to believers.
entries.citations: (Deut 30:19-20; Lev 18:5; John 14:6; Matt 7:14) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Divine or eternal life given by God in and through Jesus Christ—salvation understood as restored communion with God, spiritually present now and fulfilled in resurrection.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'life' (especially 'the life,' Greek zōē) symbolizes eternal, divine life given by God through Jesus Christ — a qualitatively different existence from mere biological life, consisting in saving relationship and union with God, beginning now and consummated in resurrection. In Johannine usage 'the Life' is also a christological title: Christ himself is the embodiment and source of this life.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Eternal life, spiritual vitality, and the person of Jesus Christ Himself as the source of divine life and salvation (often distinguishing the Greek 'zoe' from mere physical 'bios').

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Jesus Christ himself as the personal source, embodiment, and giver of spiritual/eternal life (zoe)

entries.definition: The law lived visibly — good works others can see.
entries.citations: (Prov 6:23; Matt 5:16) · see Light and Darkness, ch. 21

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Light most commonly symbolizes God’s holy and life-giving presence as revealed truth and goodness: it discloses reality, guides people, brings salvation and life, and stands opposed to the darkness of sin, evil, ignorance, and death.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, light is the settled symbol of God's own nature and presence—His holiness, truth, and glory—and, derivatively, of Christ as the divine revelation and salvation given to the world. The core claim is twofold: God is light (utter purity and truth without any darkness), and Jesus Christ is 'the light of the world' who brings that divine life, truth, and salvation to humanity, dispelling the darkness of sin, ignorance, and death.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Divine presence, holiness, truth, and revelation, most fully realized in Jesus Christ as the source of salvation and spiritual life, standing in stark contrast to the darkness of sin, evil, and ignorance.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: God and especially Jesus Christ as the source of spiritual truth, holiness, life, salvation, and divine presence, opposed to darkness as evil, sin, and ignorance

entries.definition: The devouring ruler or empire — the beast-kingdom at its most royal and most predatory: “as a roaring lion… so is a wicked ruler”; the princes are lions, and Assyria and Babylon “the lions” that scattered the sheep. The figure's rightful holder is the Lion of the tribe of Juda — and in His kingdom the lion is tamed.
entries.citations: (Prov 28:15; Zeph 3:3; Jer 50:17; Ezek 19; Rev 5:5) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7 — derived in the digital edition’s symbol study at TimeTested.Bible

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Royal power, majesty, courage, and victory—most characteristically the Messiah/Christ as the “Lion of the tribe of Judah.”

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching the lion is most commonly a symbol of royal, sovereign power and majesty, applied above all to Jesus Christ as the 'Lion of the tribe of Judah'—the conquering messianic King descended from Judah and David. The image conveys kingship, strength, courage, and victorious authority.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Jesus Christ (the Lion of the Tribe of Judah), representing messianic kingship, divine power, victory, and authority.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Jesus Christ as the conquering Lion of the tribe of Judah, symbolizing royal power, strength, majesty, and victory

entries.definition: A nation — as the beasts of Daniel's sea are kingdoms, the living creatures in Revelation's sea are peoples.
entries.citations: (Dan 7:3, 17; Rev 8:9; 16:3) · see The Bow, ch. 44

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: In biblical visions, especially Ezekiel and Revelation, the “living creatures” are most commonly understood as exalted heavenly throne attendants—identified with or closely related to cherubim—who surround God’s throne, proclaim his holiness, and represent creation worshiping under his sovereign rule.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, 'living creature' (Hebrew chayyah/chayyot; Greek zōon/zōa) most commonly refers to the four living creatures of the divine throne visions, understood as an exalted order of angelic beings — identified with the cherubim — who attend God's throne and lead the worship of heaven. Symbolically, they are most often taken to represent the whole of animate creation (wild beasts, domestic animals, humanity, and birds, via the lion, ox, man, and eagle faces) gathered in ceaseless praise before God, testifying to God's sovereignty over all living things.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Exalted angelic beings (specifically cherubim) that continually surround God's throne, declaring His holiness and representing the apex of animate creation in worship.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The four living creatures of Ezekiel and Revelation symbolize the four Evangelists (or the four Gospels): man/angel for Matthew, lion for Mark, ox for Luke, and eagle for John.

entries.definition: The Spirit and word of God going out to give life.
entries.citations: (Jer 2:13; John 7:38) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: God’s life-giving gift—especially the Holy Spirit—imparting spiritual renewal, salvation, and eternal life.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'living water' primarily symbolizes the Holy Spirit given by Jesus Christ to believers, and closely bound up with that, the eternal life / salvation that Christ offers. Jesus is presented as the source of this water, which quenches spiritual thirst permanently and wells up to eternal life. John's Gospel itself supplies the dominant interpretive key by stating that the rivers of living water refer to the Spirit whom believers would receive.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The Holy Spirit, eternal life, and the spiritually satisfying, life-giving grace of God mediated through Jesus Christ.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: the Holy Spirit (who imparts eternal life and quenches spiritual thirst)

entries.definition: The scattered house of Israel, sought and regathered.
entries.citations: (Matt 15:24) · see Jacob, Israel & Ephraim, ch. 45

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A person who has wandered from God or is spiritually lost—especially a sinner whom God, represented by the shepherd, compassionately seeks and restores. The image emphasizes both human straying and divine concern for the individual.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the 'lost sheep' symbolizes the sinner who has strayed from God — and by extension straying humanity generally — whom God (or Christ the Good Shepherd) actively seeks out, finds, and joyfully restores. The image emphasizes divine initiative in seeking the lost, the value of each individual person to God, and heaven's joy over repentance.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: A person or group who has strayed from God, fallen into sin, or become spiritually lost and vulnerable, requiring rescue, repentance, and restoration by the Good Shepherd.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: A sinner (or spiritually straying person) who has gone astray from God and is sought out and restored by the divine Shepherd (Christ/God), illustrating God's rejoicing over one repentant sinner.

entries.definition: The covenant union of God and His people — the one-flesh bond God joins: the wife called by the Husband's name, brought under His wing.
entries.citations: (Gen 2:24; Ezek 16:8; Eph 5:31-32; Rev 19:7) · see Marriage and Divorce, ch. 12

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Marriage and bride imagery most commonly symbolizes the covenantal, loving, faithful, and ultimately consummated union between Christ and his people, especially the Church. Christ is the bridegroom, and the Church or redeemed people of God is the bride.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, marriage and the bride are understood as symbols of the covenant union between Christ and the Church: Christ is the bridegroom and the Church (the collective people of God) is his bride. The imagery expresses exclusive covenant loyalty, sacrificial love, purification, and the anticipated consummation of that union at the eschatological 'marriage supper of the Lamb.' This builds on the Old Testament portrayal of Israel as the wife of YHWH, with idolatry depicted as adultery or harlotry.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The covenantal relationship and ultimate spiritual union between Christ and the Church, representing God's redeeming love for His people.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The Church (or God's people) as the bride of Christ, with earthly marriage symbolizing the covenantal, loving union between Christ and the Church

entries.definition: The word obeyed to completeness — “My meat is to do the will of him that sent me, and to finish his work”; and the will is the word: where Matthew hears “do the will of my Father,” Luke records the same saying as “hear the word of God, and do it.” Milk and meat are one substance in two states — the word received, and the word done: chewed and tasted as the ear tries words, served in due season, its fruit senses exercised to discern.
entries.citations: (John 4:34; 6:55; 7:17; Matt 12:50; Luke 8:21; Ps 40:8; Job 34:3; Heb 5:14; Matt 24:45) · see Introduction, ch. 1

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Substantial or advanced spiritual teaching—truth suited to mature believers, contrasted with “milk” as elementary instruction for spiritual beginners.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, 'meat' (often rendered 'solid food' in modern translations) most commonly symbolizes advanced or mature spiritual teaching—deeper doctrine suited to spiritually grown believers—in explicit contrast to 'milk,' the elementary teaching given to spiritual infants.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Advanced spiritual teaching and deep theological truths requiring spiritual maturity, frequently contrasted with the 'milk' of basic foundational doctrines.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Mature or advanced Christian doctrine and spiritual teaching (solid food for the spiritually mature), as contrasted with elementary teachings (milk for infants in the faith)

entries.definition: The word received — teaching another has already digested, swallowed without work; the right first food of babes, given to grow them, and meant to be outgrown at weaning. Churned, it becomes butter — the word worked toward solid food.
entries.citations: (1 Pet 2:2; 1 Cor 3:1-2; Isa 28:9; 7:15; Prov 30:33; Heb 5:12-13) · see Introduction, ch. 1

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Basic spiritual nourishment—especially elementary Christian teaching suited to new or spiritually immature believers.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian interpretation, milk primarily symbolizes elementary or basic spiritual teaching — the foundational nourishment appropriate to new or immature believers, typically contrasted with 'solid food' (meat), which represents mature, advanced doctrine. The image carries two related inflections: a positive one (milk as the pure, life-giving Word of God that new converts should crave) and a corrective one (remaining on milk as a sign of stunted spiritual growth).

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Basic, foundational spiritual teachings or elementary truths suitable for new or spiritually immature believers.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: elementary Christian doctrine or pure spiritual nourishment for new/immature believers (in contrast to solid food for the mature)

entries.definition: The instant of decisive action, built on the image of an eye's wink — the unit in which judgment and mercy alike are done, never a slow process: Babylon falls “in a moment… in one day,” and the dead are raised “in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye.”
entries.citations: (Isa 47:9; Job 34:20; 1 Cor 15:52) · see The Moment, ch. 38 | (Isa 47:9; Job 34:20; 1 Cor 15:52) · see The Moment, in the free digital edition at TimeTested.Bible

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The term “moment” has no settled, technical symbolic meaning in Christian interpretation. When used symbolically, its most common broad sense is the brevity and transience of human experience, often contrasted with God’s eternity or the lasting significance of divine action.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, 'moment' is most commonly treated not as a fixed symbol but as a temporal figure for instantaneous divine action and the brevity of earthly experience measured against eternity. Its most prominent doctrinal use is Paul's 'in a moment (Greek: atomos, an indivisible instant), in the twinkling of an eye' describing the sudden, instantaneous transformation of believers at the resurrection/last trumpet. Closely joined to this is the contrast between 'momentary' affliction and eternal glory: present suffering is a 'moment' compared with the eternal weight of glory God prepares.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The fleeting nature of earthly time and afflictions when contrasted with eternity, as well as the suddenness of divine action and eschatological change.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: the fleeting or temporary character of earthly affliction, human life, or divine displeasure when set against eternal glory or favor

entries.definition: The faithful witness — the Son, who shines with no light of His own but the Father's reflected, the light that shineth in the world's night; the lesser light that rules the night and marks the appointed times.
entries.commonView: Commonly taught: the church reflecting Christ's light as the moon reflects the sun.
entries.citations: (Ps 89:37; Rev 1:5; John 1:5; 5:19) · see Sun, Moon & Stars, ch. 29

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: In prophetic and apocalyptic interpretation, the moon most commonly functions as part of the divinely ordered cosmos; its darkening, turning to blood, or otherwise failing symbolizes the Day of the Lord, divine judgment, and the upheaval of the present world order.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching the moon is most commonly interpreted as a symbol of derived or reflected light: it has no light of its own but reflects the sun, and is therefore read as a figure of the Church (or the individual believer) reflecting the light of Christ, who is symbolized by the sun. This reading is ancient (patristic writers such as Augustine and Ambrose spoke of the Church as 'luna,' waxing and waning through history while receiving all her light from Christ) and remains a staple of sermons and devotional teaching.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The Church, which possesses no innate light but reflects the divine light of Christ (the Sun of Righteousness), often associated with phases of waxing and waning through earthly history and persecution.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: the Church (or people of God) as a lesser light reflecting the light of Christ/the Sun

entries.definition: A kingdom — the seat of ruling authority.
entries.citations: (Jer 51:25; Dan 2:35) · see Mountain, ch. 39

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A mountain most commonly signifies a place or sphere of divine presence, revelation, worship, and encounter with God—often emphasizing holiness, transcendence, and nearness to heaven.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, a mountain primarily symbolizes the place of God's presence and divine revelation — the meeting point between heaven and earth where God discloses himself, gives covenant/law, and establishes his dwelling (his 'holy mountain,' Zion). By extension it frequently symbolizes God's kingdom or rule established over the earth.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: A place of divine encounter, transcendent revelation, and God's sovereign presence or established kingdom.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: A place of divine revelation, theophany, or encounter with the presence of God (often linked to covenant, law, temple, or the kingdom of God).

entries.definition: Without covenant covering — exposed in one's breach.
entries.citations: (Ezek 16:8; Gen 3:7) · see Garments & Armor, ch. 43

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Shameful exposure and vulnerability, especially the exposure of sin or guilt and the loss of innocence under divine judgment.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, nakedness primarily symbolizes shame, guilt, and the exposure of sin before God — the human condition after the Fall, in which people are spiritually destitute and need to be 'covered' or clothed by God (ultimately with Christ's righteousness). The movement from unashamed nakedness in Eden, to shame-filled awareness of nakedness after sin, to God clothing Adam and Eve, is treated as the paradigm: nakedness = exposed sinfulness and shame; divine clothing = grace, atonement, and imputed righteousness.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual exposure, shame, guilt, and moral vulnerability resulting from sin, as well as the absence of righteous covering.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: shame, humiliation, and exposure of sin/guilt (requiring covering or clothing in righteousness)

entries.definition: The covenant identity of a house, consisting of 3 things appointed and provided by its Head: the Word (the manna), the covenant law (the stone tables), and the fruitful priesthood (Aaron's budded rod). A counterfeit Name substitutes a different word, covenant, or priesthood; a Name is taken in vain when any one is rejected, replaced, or removed. A bride takes her Husband's Name by entering His house, coming under His authority, and obeying Him.
entries.commonView: Commonly taught: the person's character, authority, and reputation.

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A “name” most commonly symbolizes the identity and revealed character of the person who bears it; in biblical usage it can therefore represent the person himself or herself, including that person’s presence, reputation, and authority. God’s name especially signifies God as revealed and made known.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching and biblical interpretation, a 'name' symbolizes the essential character, identity, and authority of the person who bears it — not merely a label. Above all, the 'name of God' (or 'the name of the LORD' / 'the name of Jesus') stands for God's revealed nature, reputation, presence, and power, so that to know, call on, trust, hallow, or act 'in' the name is to engage with the person himself. Names in Scripture are consistently treated as disclosing or determining who someone truly is, which is why God's self-revelation, divine name-changes, and prayer/salvation 'in the name' carry such theological weight.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The character, authority, essence, and identity of the person to whom it belongs. In biblical symbolism, particularly regarding God or Jesus, a name is not merely a label but represents the totality of the person's revealed nature and sovereign power.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The name of a person (especially God or Jesus) stands for their full identity, character, authority, power, and presence, so that invoking or acting 'in the name' means acting by that person's authority and under their protection.

entries.definition: The gospel’s gathering of all kinds out of the sea of peoples.
entries.citations: (Matt 13:47-48) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A fishing net most commonly symbolizes the gathering of people into God’s kingdom through evangelism and apostolic mission—especially the calling to become “fishers of men.”

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching the net most commonly symbolizes the gospel and the kingdom of God as an instrument for gathering people: the work of evangelism by which souls are drawn into the church. This flows from Jesus' call to make his disciples 'fishers of men' and from the parable of the dragnet, where the net cast into the sea gathers fish of every kind, representing the kingdom's ingathering of all peoples pending final separation of righteous and wicked at judgment.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Evangelism, the gathering of souls, and the expansion of the Kingdom of God.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The kingdom of heaven (or the church/gospel) cast into the world to gather people of every kind, who are later separated at the final judgment

entries.definition: A newly conferred covenant identity under its giver — known, received, and kept only by the one who bears it.
entries.commonView: Commonly taught: a new God-given identity and character bestowed on the overcomer.
entries.citations: (Gen 32:28; Isa 62:2-5; 65:15; Rev 2:17) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A “new name” most commonly symbolizes a new, God-given identity and status—often associated with transformation, belonging to God, vindication, and a new vocation or destiny.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian interpretation, a 'new name' symbolizes the new identity, character, and status God confers on a redeemed person or people. Receiving a new name marks a decisive change wrought by God—conversion, covenant relationship, adoption, and transformation—so that the person's God-given identity replaces the old one. In eschatological contexts (Revelation), the new name signifies the believer's final vindication, personal belonging to God/Christ, and secure membership in the New Jerusalem.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: A transformed identity, new character, and change in status signifying divine ownership and a new destiny ordained by God.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: A new spiritual identity or transformed character bestowed by God on the faithful/overcomer, signifying redemption, intimate belonging, and eternal status before Him

entries.definition: The renewed moon — chodesh, from chadash, to renew: the phase of the moon that serves as the sign of the start of the month, and so the name of the month itself. A sign must be watched for: the east gate opens on it for worship, commerce resents it, and Paul files it among the shadows of things to come; which phase renews the month, the Pearl chapter weighs from the letters.
entries.citations: (Ps 81:3; 1 Sam 20:5, 18; Isa 66:23; Ezek 46:1-3; Amos 8:5; Col 2:16-17) · see The Pearls of Wisdom, ch. 31

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: There is no settled, specifically Christian symbolic meaning of “new moon.” When treated symbolically, its most common association is renewal or a fresh beginning, especially the recurring renewal of worship and covenantal devotion at the start of each month.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching the 'new moon' is understood primarily as part of Israel's ceremonial calendar of appointed times, and its symbolic significance is defined by Colossians 2:16-17: it is a 'shadow of things to come,' a type pointing forward to Christ, in whom the ceremonial observance finds its fulfillment. Because it marks the beginning of a month, it is commonly given the associated sense of renewal and new beginnings, with the fulfillment located in the newness of life in Christ rather than in continued calendrical observance.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: A symbol of cyclical renewal, sacred time, and the marking of God's appointed seasons, viewed typologically in the New Testament as a temporary shadow of the spiritual reality found in Christ.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: A ceremonial observance that functions as a shadow or type pointing forward to the substance found in Christ

entries.definition: The time of darkness — hiding and sleep, when opportunity closes; the children of the night sleep and are drunken, doing their deeds in the dark.
entries.citations: (Gen 1:5; 1 Thess 5:5-7) · see Light and Darkness, ch. 21

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual and moral darkness: a condition or sphere associated with sin, unbelief, ignorance of God, evil, danger, and separation from divine light. Christian interpretation commonly treats night as the contrasting counterpart to Christ, truth, holiness, and salvation as “light.”

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'night' primarily symbolizes spiritual darkness—the realm of sin, evil, unbelief, and separation from God—standing in contrast to 'day' and 'light,' which symbolize God, Christ, truth, and salvation. Believers are described as 'children of the day, not of the night,' and the consummated new creation is portrayed as having no night at all.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual darkness, sin, ignorance of God, divine judgment, and a period of earthly trial or death, often contrasted with the 'day' of salvation and light.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual darkness, evil, sin, ignorance, or the absence of God's light and presence (in contrast to day/light)

entries.definition: A great city of the sea — gentile peoples who repent and rise in judgment.
entries.citations: (Matt 12:41) · see The Sign of Jonah, ch. 4

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Nineveh is most commonly treated as an emblem of a wicked, pagan society that stands under divine judgment but may receive divine mercy through repentance.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, Nineveh functions primarily as the great symbol of repentance and of God's mercy extended even to the most wicked of pagan peoples. The city that repented at Jonah's preaching becomes the paradigm of a sinful people turning to God and being spared, and Jesus himself invokes the 'men of Nineveh' as exemplars of repentance who will condemn an unrepentant generation. Closely bound up with this is Nineveh's role as a sign that God's compassion reaches beyond Israel to the Gentile nations.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: A symbol of the quintessential wicked and oppressive pagan city, representing both the extreme depths of worldly depravity and the universal scope of God's mercy when its inhabitants repent, as well as the certainty of divine judgment upon arrogant empires.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: A wicked Gentile city that repents at God's warning and receives mercy, exemplifying repentance, divine compassion for the nations, and a model that will judge unrepentant hearers

entries.definition: The hidden quarter — tsaphon, from the root to hide, to lurk: the dark side of the sky, the door the ambush comes by. In the north country the spoilers of Babylon gather — “an assembly of great nations,” the ten allied kings who turn on the seven the whore rules — and in its uttermost recesses, the “sides of the north,” the enemy set his seat.
entries.citations: (Jer 1:14; 50:9, 41; 51:48; Ps 48:2; Isa 14:13; Rev 17:16-18) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35, and Lucifer's Declared Plan, ch. 30

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The north most commonly signifies the quarter from which hostile invasion and divine judgment come, especially through Babylon and other northern armies. This symbolism reflects Israel’s geography: major eastern empires normally approached Judah from the north along established routes.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian interpretation, 'the north' or 'the north country' symbolizes the direction from which divine judgment, invasion, and calamity come upon Israel/Judah — concretely identified with Mesopotamian powers (Assyria and especially Babylon), which, because of the Syrian desert, invaded the land from the north. By extension, 'the north country' also denotes the land of exile from which God will regather his scattered people, so the term carries a paired sense: the source of judgment and the place of captivity from which restoration comes.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: A source of impending divine judgment, hostile invasion, and disaster, often associated with destructive empires like Babylon or Assyria.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: source/direction of invasion, calamity, and divine judgment (prototypically Babylon or other northern powers used as instruments of judgment)

entries.definition: The commandment's truth and correction received and laid up inwardly until they govern the life — the tested, pressed fruit of the Spirit stored as proven obedience; light is that obedience made visible as an example to others.
entries.commonView: Commonly taught: the Holy Spirit — anointing, consecration, and empowering.

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The Holy Spirit—especially the Spirit’s sustaining presence, empowering grace, and illumination that enable believers to bear spiritual light and remain ready for Christ.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In popular Christian teaching, lamp oil is most commonly taken as a symbol of the Holy Spirit (and, closely related, the inner spiritual life or grace supplied by the Spirit that keeps one's 'light' burning). This reading is driven above all by the Parable of the Ten Virgins, where possessing oil marks readiness for the Bridegroom's coming, and it is reinforced by the broader biblical association of anointing oil with the Spirit's presence and empowerment.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The Holy Spirit, encompassing His indwelling presence, empowering, and illuminating grace.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: the Holy Spirit (empowering presence that fuels spiritual light, witness, and anointing)

entries.definition: Israel, the covenant people.
entries.citations: (Jer 11:16; Hos 9:10) · see Trees, ch. 41

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Israel—or, more broadly, God’s covenant people—is the most common shared symbolic referent assigned to the olive, vine, and fig in Christian interpretation. The plants often depict Israel’s election, spiritual condition, fruitfulness, or exposure to judgment, although their meaning varies by passage.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching and biblical interpretation, the olive tree, the vine, and the fig tree are most commonly understood—individually and as a trio—as symbols of Israel, God's covenant people, and their expected spiritual fruitfulness (or failure to bear fruit) before God. The vine typically represents Israel planted and tended by God; the fig tree represents the nation of Israel (often in contexts of judgment or restoration); and the olive tree represents the covenant people of God, with special prominence in Paul's image of Gentile believers grafted into Israel's olive tree. Prophetic use of these trees regularly frames national blessing, judgment, and restoration.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: God's covenant people (Israel) and the divine blessings of peace, prosperity, and spiritual fruitfulness associated with the Promised Land.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Israel (or God's covenant people/nation) in its various aspects

entries.definition: The covenant made whole — shalom, from a root meaning to complete, restore, repay: the work of righteousness, the great peace of them that love the law — not the world’s truce and not a feeling (“not as the world giveth”). What the gospel publishes is this peace restored; the counterfeit pronounces it twice over an unkept covenant — “Peace, peace; when there is no peace.”

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Restored wholeness and right relationship—especially reconciliation with God through Christ—which extends to harmony with others and ultimately to the renewal of creation. Christian interpretation commonly stresses that biblical peace (Hebrew shalom; Greek eirēnē) is more than the absence of conflict.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'peace' (Hebrew shalom, Greek eirēnē) primarily symbolizes reconciliation with God accomplished through Jesus Christ — a state of wholeness, well-being, and right relationship rather than the mere absence of conflict. It is presented as a gift of God, secured by the atonement, experienced inwardly through the Holy Spirit, and personified in Christ himself as the 'Prince of Peace.'

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Wholeness, flourishing, and the comprehensive restoration of relationships, specifically reconciliation between God and humanity and cosmic harmony, rooted in the Hebrew concept of shalom.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual reconciliation and harmonious relationship with God (and resulting inner wholeness/tranquility) accomplished through Jesus Christ

entries.definition: The one complete light — under the KJV's “rubies” (peninim, Strong's pearl), wisdom and the bride are priced above pearls; and the night sky's one pearl is the full moon (keseh, “fulness,” the letters under “throne” and “time appointed”), governor of the appointed times, the one-pearl gates of the city — the merchant's entry at the King's gate.
entries.commonView: Commonly taught: the kingdom of heaven, worth surrendering everything to gain — or the church, purchased by Christ.
entries.citations: (Prov 3:15; 31:10; Ps 81:3; Prov 7:20; Job 26:9; Ps 104:19; Rev 21:21) · see The Pearls of Wisdom, ch. 31

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The pearl most commonly symbolizes the incomparable worth of the kingdom of God—and, by extension, salvation or life in Christ—worth surrendering everything else to obtain.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: The pearl primarily symbolizes the Kingdom of Heaven (or the salvation/gospel found in it) as a treasure of supreme, surpassing worth — something so valuable that a person should gladly give up everything else to obtain it. By extension it stands for sacred, precious spiritual truth.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The Kingdom of Heaven, salvation, or ultimate spiritual truth which is worth sacrificing all earthly possessions to obtain.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The kingdom of heaven (or the gospel of salvation/Christ) as a treasure of supreme, inestimable worth for which everything else should be sacrificed

entries.definition: The bowed-humble before God — one Hebrew word family behind “poor” and “meek,” and “needy” (evyon) its constant companion; empty-handed toward Him, and so able to receive: the gospel’s hearers and heirs of the kingdom.
entries.citations: (Ps 37:11/Matt 5:5; Isa 61:1/Luke 4:18; Isa 66:2; Jas 2:5; Ps 72:12-13) · see Orphans, Widows & the Fatherless, ch. 14

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Those who are humble, powerless, afflicted, or conscious of their dependence on God, and who therefore look to God for protection, justice, and salvation. In Christian teaching, the terms often symbolize spiritually receptive people rather than merely a social or economic class.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'poor, meek, needy' is most commonly read as a composite description of the humble faithful — those who recognize their spiritual poverty and total dependence on God rather than on their own resources, status, or power. This is the 'anawim' concept from the Hebrew Bible: the lowly ones who wait on God, whom God defends, vindicates, and promises to exalt. In the Beatitudes this is spiritualized as 'poor in spirit' and 'meek' — the humble who mourn their sin, submit to God, and will inherit the kingdom/earth. The terms thus symbolize the true people of God characterized by humility and trust, in contrast to the proud, self-sufficient, and oppressive.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual humility, absolute dependence on God, and a faithful posture of receptivity to God's grace and deliverance, often corresponding to the Hebrew concept of the 'anawim' (the faithful remnant who rely on God rather than their own strength).

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual humility and total dependence on God (the 'anawim' ideal): those who recognize their own spiritual poverty/need and meekly trust God rather than wealth, power, or self-sufficiency

entries.definition: The faithful few who glean the edge — widow, fatherless, stranger, as Ruth did; small by design, refined like gold out of dross, at a fixed ratio traceable from the gleaning law's own geometry to Elijah's seven thousand.
entries.citations: (Ruth 2; 1 Kgs 19:18; Zech 13:8-9; Rom 11:5) · see The Remnant, ch. 15

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The “remnant” most commonly symbolizes the surviving and often faithful portion of God’s covenant people whom God preserves through judgment, exile, apostasy, or calamity and from whom the community is renewed or restored.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the 'remnant' symbolizes the faithful minority of God's people whom He graciously preserves through judgment, exile, or widespread apostasy, guaranteeing the continuity of His covenant purposes. The remnant is understood as both a sign of judgment (only a small portion survives) and a sign of hope and grace (God does not utterly destroy His people but keeps a seed alive through whom salvation history continues). In New Testament interpretation, especially in Paul, the remnant becomes the believing minority 'chosen by grace,' demonstrating that God's promises have not failed even when the majority rejects them.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: A small, faithful minority of people who survive divine judgment and through whom God preserves His covenant promises, often representing true believers or the elect within a broader visible community.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: A small, faithful core of God's people preserved by divine grace after judgment, disaster, exile, or widespread apostasy

entries.definition: The self-sufficient who “have need of nothing” — full of self, and so unable to receive; Laodicea's boast, and Smyrna's opposite. The true wealth is being “rich toward God”: faith tried in the fire, and the garment of righteousness.
entries.citations: (Rev 3:17-18; Rev 2:9; Prov 13:7; Luke 12:21) · see Orphans, Widows & the Fatherless, ch. 14

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Worldly wealth, privilege, and self-sufficiency—often symbolizing attachment to temporal goods and the spiritual danger of trusting possessions rather than God.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'rich' most commonly functions as a symbol of misplaced trust and spiritual danger: the rich person represents self-sufficiency, reliance on worldly possessions rather than God, and the deceptive security of material wealth. To be 'rich' in this symbolic sense is to be spiritually imperiled or even spiritually poor while materially full — wealth as an obstacle to entering the kingdom of God and a rival object of devotion ('mammon').

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual wealth, encompassing an abundance of faith, God's grace, salvation, and heavenly treasure.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Material wealth as a spiritual hindrance or danger that fosters self-reliance, pride, and worldliness, making entrance into God's kingdom difficult

entries.definition: Right-living. God is Right-Living by definition — His ways and works are the measure of right. For those under His authority, right-living is the doing of His commandments: the law kept, worn as the garment of righteous acts. Romans 4 excludes wage-work that would put God in debt, not obedience; even complete obedience earns no wage because the servant has only done his duty. Righteousness is given and reckoned by grace, but the gift never renames wrong-living right.
entries.commonView: Commonly taught: primarily right standing before God — Christ's imputed righteousness received by faith apart from works — with right-living as its subsequent fruit and evidence.
entries.citations: (Deut 32:4; 6:25; Ps 119:172; 145:17; Luke 17:7-10; Rom 4:4-8; Phil 3:9; Heb 11:8; 1 John 3:7) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6, for the dependent definitions; The End of the Law for Paul's wage, debt, law, and obedience vocabulary; and Garments & Armor, ch. 43, for righteousness given and worn

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Moral and spiritual rightness before God: conformity to God’s character and will, including just conduct and, in salvation contexts, a right standing with God granted by grace.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'righteousness' primarily signifies right standing before God — a state of being in right relationship with Him and conformed to His moral character and standard. In its most prominent (especially Protestant) doctrinal use, it refers to the righteousness of God credited or imputed to believers through faith in Christ (justification), rather than righteousness achieved by human works. Symbolically it is frequently pictured as a garment or robe (clothing the sinner), a breastplate (protection), and a crown or reward, all conveying a status conferred by God that covers, protects, and vindicates the believer.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Conformity to God's character, standard, and will, encompassing both a right relational and legal standing before God and moral uprightness in conduct.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Right standing with God (justification) and conformity to God's moral standards/will, often as a gift received by faith rather than earned by works

entries.definition: The covenant — the Rock that followed Israel “was Christ,” the covenant in person; the stone the builders refused, made the cornerstone.
entries.citations: (Deut 32:4; Isa 42:6; 1 Cor 10:4; Ps 118:22) · see Mountain, ch. 39

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: God—and, in explicitly Christian interpretation, Christ—as a firm, dependable foundation, refuge, source of strength, and salvation.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'rock' primarily symbolizes God (and, in Christian typology, Christ) as an unshakable foundation, refuge, and source of salvation — connoting stability, permanence, protection, and trustworthiness. The New Testament extends this explicitly to Christ, both as the spiritual rock that accompanied Israel (1 Cor 10:4) and as the sure foundation on which faith and the church are built.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: God or Jesus Christ as a firm, immovable foundation, ultimate protector, and source of salvation.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: God (and specifically Christ) as firm foundation, strength, refuge, and source of salvation/security

entries.definition: The countless multitude — grains of the shore beyond number; and so a shifting foundation: to build on the sand is to build on the crowd, not the covenant-rock.
entries.citations: (Gen 22:17; Hos 1:10; Rev 20:8; Matt 7:26) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: An innumerable multitude or immeasurable abundance, especially numerous descendants, peoples, armies, or other things beyond ordinary counting.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: Sand most commonly symbolizes an innumerable multitude — a quantity beyond counting — used especially of the promised descendants of Abraham and, by extension, of vast peoples or armies. In Christian teaching this is tied to God's covenant promise and its fulfillment in the many children of faith.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: An innumerable multitude, specifically referring to the vast, uncountable number of Abraham's descendants as promised by God.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: vast or innumerable multitude

entries.definition: The complete seven — six-and-one as a single whole, at every scale the law counts it: the week whose seventh day is the rest, the seventh year that rests the land, the seven-sevens that ring in jubilee. Scripture counts “seven sabbaths complete” and calls the week itself the sabbath; the rest-day is the crown of the unit, one-seventh of what the word names.
entries.citations: (Lev 23:15 with Deut 16:9; Lev 25:2-8; 2 Chr 36:21; Luke 18:12; Matt 28:1; Heb 4:9) · see The Sabbath, ch. 32 | (Lev 23:15 with Deut 16:9; Lev 25:2-8; 2 Chr 36:21; Luke 18:12; Matt 28:1; Heb 4:9) · see The Sabbath, in the free digital edition at TimeTested.Bible

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Sacred rest in God: the Sabbath most commonly symbolizes participation in God’s completed work and gracious rest, understood in much Christian interpretation as fulfilled in Christ and as anticipating final, eternal rest.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching the Sabbath is most commonly interpreted symbolically as God's rest — a type or foreshadowing of the spiritual rest believers find in Christ and, ultimately, of the eschatological rest of the people of God (salvation rest / heavenly rest). The weekly Sabbath, grounded in God's rest at creation, is read as pointing beyond itself to ceasing from one's own works and entering God's rest through faith in Christ.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual rest and salvation in Christ, as well as the ultimate eschatological rest for the people of God in the new creation. It symbolizes the cessation of striving for one's own justification and entering into the finished work of God.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Rest (God's rest after creation and the spiritual rest believers enter through Christ)

entries.definition: Covenant blood made wearable — and counterfeited by those who wear the form without the substance.
entries.citations: (Isa 1:18; Josh 2:18; Heb 9:19; Rev 17:4) · see Garments & Armor, ch. 43 — derived in the digital edition’s symbol study at TimeTested.Bible

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Sin and guilt, pictured as a deep, conspicuous stain that requires cleansing or forgiveness.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, scarlet most commonly symbolizes sin — deep-dyed, conspicuous guilt — with the closely paired idea that such sin can be cleansed and made 'white as snow.' The color's fastness as a dye (kermes/tola'at shani) is often cited to explain why it images sin's ingrained, seemingly permanent stain.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Sin and deep-seated guilt, as well as the typological counterpart of redemption, salvation, and the atoning blood of Christ (often conceptualized as the scarlet thread of redemption).

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: the deep stain or guilt of sin

entries.definition: Peoples and nations — the restless, unrooted mass below the firmament; and, above it, the gathered waters of heaven: the still sea of glass where the angels and the redeemed stand.
entries.citations: (Rev 17:15; Gen 1:6-8; Ps 148:4; Rev 4:6; 15:2) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The sea or deep waters most commonly symbolize primordial chaos, danger, death, and hostile powers that God restrains or defeats. This is especially prominent in poetic, prophetic, and apocalyptic texts.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching and biblical scholarship, the sea and the waters most commonly symbolize chaos, disorder, and the powers of evil hostile to God — the untamed, threatening realm that God alone subdues and from which opposition to God's people arises. Closely joined to this, in apocalyptic and prophetic literature the sea/waters frequently stand for the restless mass of the nations or peoples of the world, out of which hostile empires and the beast emerge. God's sovereignty over the sea (creating, bounding, calming, or drying it) signifies his victory over chaos and evil, culminating in Revelation's declaration that in the new creation 'the sea was no more.'

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Chaos, death, the abyss, and hostile cosmic forces that oppose God; a realm of restless evil and danger.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: chaos, disorder, and the forces of evil opposed to God's order

entries.definition: The NAME impressed on its owner — the signet-plate the law sets on the priest's forehead (HOLINESS TO THE LORD), the law bound on hand and between the eyes, stamped by the Spirit on God's servants before judgment; the inscription is quoted: the Lord knoweth them that are his — let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity. The counterfeit takes the same two places.

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A sign of belonging to God: divine ownership, authentication, and identification of God’s faithful people, often including God’s spiritual protection and preservation. The forehead location emphasizes openly marked identity and allegiance, in contrast to allegiance to the beast.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian interpretation, the seal or mark in the forehead symbolizes God's ownership of, identification with, and protection over His faithful people. It marks believers as belonging to God, secures them against divine judgment poured out on the wicked, and is commonly identified with the indwelling Holy Spirit and/or the name of God written on His servants, signifying allegiance, security of salvation, and consecration to God. Its placement on the forehead is widely read as signifying the mind—one's conscious loyalty, thought, and character being given to God (in deliberate contrast to the mark of the beast in Revelation 13).

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Divine ownership, spiritual protection from judgment, and the identifying presence of the Holy Spirit marking believers as God's faithful people.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Divine ownership, protection, and identification of God's faithful servants, shielding them from judgment

entries.definition: The word of God, sown in the hearts of men.
entries.citations: (Luke 8:11) · see Grass, ch. 42

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The word or message of God—especially the gospel—which is sown in human hearts and may produce spiritual life and fruit.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'seed' most commonly symbolizes the Word of God — the gospel message sown into human hearts, which germinates and bears spiritual fruit depending on the condition of the hearer. This meaning is treated as authoritative because Jesus himself supplies the interpretation within the parable of the sower ('the seed is the word of God').

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Offspring or descendants, specifically pointing typologically to Jesus Christ as the promised Messiah (the 'seed of the woman' and 'seed of Abraham'), and by extension, believers as spiritual descendants.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The Messiah/Christ as the singular promised offspring who fulfills the covenant promises made to the woman, Abraham, and David

entries.definition: The deceiver; the one who strips the covenant covering.
entries.citations: (Gen 3:1) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40 — derived in the digital edition’s symbol study at TimeTested.Bible

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Evil expressed through Satan, especially deception, temptation, sin, and opposition to God.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the serpent primarily symbolizes Satan (the devil) and, by extension, evil, temptation, deception, and sin. The serpent of Eden is traditionally identified as Satan or as an instrument of Satan, making the serpent the archetypal image of the tempter and adversary of God and humanity.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Satan, the Devil, temptation, deception, and the origin of evil

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Satan/the Devil as the embodiment of evil, deception, and temptation

entries.definition: The covering of a greater presence — refuge under the Almighty's wings, a kingdom's protection over its people, the outline a coming body casts ahead of itself. Good to dwell in — not the gloom it is read as; the KJV itself renders the word “defence”.
entries.citations: (Ps 91:1; Num 14:9; Col 2:17) · see Shadow, ch. 17

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A preliminary, incomplete foreshadowing or type of the greater spiritual reality fulfilled in Christ. Christian interpretation especially describes the Mosaic law, sacrifices, festivals, priesthood, and earthly sanctuary as “shadows,” while Christ and the new-covenant realities are the substance.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, 'shadow' most commonly symbolizes divine protection and refuge — being sheltered under God's presence, pictured as resting in the shadow of His wings or of the Almighty. God's shadow represents nearness, covering, and safety for those who trust Him.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Protection, refuge, and the comforting presence of God, often depicted as the shadow of wings or a great rock offering shelter from the heat.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: A temporary, incomplete, or typological foreshadowing of a greater spiritual reality (especially Christ, the gospel, or heavenly things)

entries.definition: The covenant people, who hear the Shepherd's voice and follow.
entries.citations: (John 10:27) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: God’s people—especially Israel, Christ’s disciples, or the church—pictured as dependent, vulnerable, and in need of divine or pastoral guidance, protection, and care from God or Christ as shepherd.

judges.label: Claude
