judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, sheep primarily symbolize God's people (believers, the church, or Israel) in their relationship of dependence on God or Christ as their Shepherd. The image carries connotations of belonging to and being cared for by God, vulnerability and helplessness without guidance, the need for protection and provision, and a tendency to wander or go astray. Believers are the 'sheep of his pasture' who know the Shepherd's voice and follow him.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: God's people or the followers of Christ, characterized by their dependence, vulnerability, and need for a guiding shepherd.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: God's people (Israel in the OT; the Church/believers in the NT) as the flock under the care, guidance, and protection of the divine Shepherd (God or Christ)

entries.definition: The demanding place — from sha'al, to demand: mortality's claim on all flesh, swallowing righteous and wicked alike, personified with a mouth, gates, and bars. Its dead sleep in silence until it is made to give them back; then it is itself destroyed — “O grave, I will be thy destruction.” Distinct from Gehenna, the judgment.
entries.citations: (Gen 37:35; Ps 16:10; Eccl 9:5; Isa 5:14; Hos 13:14; Rev 20:13-14) · see Heaven and Hell, ch. 16

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Sheol most commonly denotes the grave, death, or the shadowy realm of the dead—the common destination of the deceased. Symbolically, it represents death, separation from ordinary earthly life, darkness, silence, and human powerlessness. Modern biblical interpretation generally distinguishes Sheol from the later Christian concept of final hell or eternal punishment.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching and biblical scholarship, Sheol is most commonly understood as the Old Testament's term for the realm or abode of the dead — the grave or underworld to which all the dead, righteous and wicked alike, descend. It symbolizes the shadowy, silent condition of death itself rather than a place of active punishment. Modern translations therefore typically render it 'the grave,' 'the pit,' 'the realm of the dead,' or transliterate it as 'Sheol,' while older versions (notably the KJV) often rendered it 'hell,' contributing to popular conflation with the place of final punishment. In Christian theology Sheol is usually treated as the intermediate state of the dead prior to resurrection, corresponding to Greek 'Hades' in the New Testament, and is distinguished from Gehenna (the place of final judgment).

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The shadowy realm of the dead, the underworld, or the grave, symbolizing mortality, the finality of physical death, and separation from the land of the living.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: the underworld or shadowy realm of the dead (the grave) to which all people go after death, prior to any final judgment

entries.definition: An earthly kingdom, city, state, or governed political body riding upon the sea of peoples: its rulers guide it, its inhabitants and servants crew it, its armies defend it, and its wealth is carried as cargo. Christ needs no constructed body beneath Him: He walks upon the sea directly, and when He sails with His disciples the vessel comes under its true Head. The ship may be broken while its people survive.
entries.commonView: Commonly taught: the Church — a vessel of salvation carrying believers through the dangers of the world.

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The Church—often called the ship or Barque of Peter—carrying believers through the dangers of the world toward salvation, with Christ as protector or pilot.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: The ship most commonly symbolizes the Church — the vessel of salvation that carries believers safely through the storms and dangers of the world (the 'sea') toward the safe harbor of eternal life. This reading is deeply rooted in patristic writing (e.g., Tertullian, Hippolytus, Cyprian, Augustine), in liturgical architecture (the main body of a church building is called the 'nave,' from Latin navis, ship), and in the typological link between Noah's ark and baptism/the Church.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The Church, often traditionally conceptualized as the 'Barque of Peter' or typologically linked to Noah's Ark, which carries the faithful safely through the turbulent and dangerous waters of the world toward salvation.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The Church as the vessel of salvation navigating the waters of the world, storms of trial, or judgment (often linked to Noah's ark as type)

entries.definition: A prophecy given in advance — often a prophet's lived story — whose fulfillment testifies; not a wonder performed on demand.
entries.commonView: Commonly taught: a miraculous act pointing to God's power and Christ's identity.
entries.citations: (Isa 7:14; Ezek 24:24; Luke 11:30) · see Signs and Similitudes, ch. 3

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A “sign” is most commonly understood functionally as a visible event, act, object, or miracle that points beyond itself to divine activity and confirms God’s message, promise, presence, or the authority of God’s messenger. It does not have one fixed symbolic referent across Scripture.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching and biblical scholarship, a 'sign' (Hebrew 'oth; Greek semeion) is understood as a divinely given event, act, or object that points beyond itself to God's presence, power, and purpose — an attesting pointer that authenticates God's revelation, covenant, or messenger. In the Gospel of John especially, 'signs' are Jesus' miracles understood not as ends in themselves but as revelations of his identity and glory, intended to lead observers to faith. More broadly, a sign functions as a symbol of divine attestation: it confirms a promise (covenant signs), validates a prophet or apostle, or discloses a coming reality (eschatological signs).

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: An event, miracle, or object that points beyond itself to authenticate a divine messenger, reveal God's glory, or validate a divine message, most prominently used in the Gospel of John to describe Jesus' miracles as proofs of his divine identity.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: A miraculous deed, wonder, or token performed by God or His authorized messengers that authenticates divine authority, reveals God's glory or presence, and is intended to produce faith or obedience

entries.definition: The transgression of the law — Scripture's own definition: “sin is the transgression of the law”; where no law is, there is no transgression, and by the law is the knowledge of sin.
entries.citations: (1 John 3:4; Rom 4:15; 3:20; 7:7) · see Grace, Mercy & the Gift, ch. 24

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Sin most commonly signifies human rebellion against, disobedience to, and estrangement from God—an evil condition expressed in wrongful acts and resulting in corruption and death. Strictly speaking, biblical and Christian teaching usually treats sin as a theological and moral reality rather than as a symbol with one fixed symbolic referent.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'sin' primarily denotes transgression of God's law and rebellion against God — a moral failure or 'missing the mark' (Greek hamartia) that separates humanity from God, incurs guilt, and requires atonement. It functions both as individual wrongful acts and as a universal fallen condition inherited from Adam (original sin), with death as its consequence and Christ's atoning work as its remedy.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Rebellion against God, transgression of His law, and missing the mark of His holy standard, resulting in alienation.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Any thought, word, deed, or disposition that transgresses God's law, misses the divine standard (hamartia), or rebels against God, producing guilt and separation from Him

entries.definition: A spiritual name of Jerusalem — the prophets address her rulers so to their faces: “Hear the word of the LORD, ye rulers of Sodom… ye people of Gomorrah”; Ezekiel calls Sodom her sister and Jerusalem the worse; and Revelation writes the name on “the great city… where also our Lord was crucified.”
entries.citations: (Isa 1:10; Ezek 16:46-48; Rev 11:8) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Sodom and Gomorrah most commonly symbolize extreme communal wickedness brought under catastrophic divine judgment. In traditional Christian teaching, their wickedness is frequently associated especially with sexual immorality, including attempted sexual violence and, in many historic interpretations, homosexual conduct; the broader and more stable symbolism is that of flagrant sin and its punishment.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: Sodom and Gomorrah function as the Bible's paradigmatic symbol of extreme human wickedness and of sudden, total divine judgment. Across Christian teaching the cities serve as the proverbial example of what happens when sin reaches full measure: complete, irreversible destruction from God. They are invoked as a warning-type — a byword for depravity and a standing image of eschatological judgment — such that to compare a people or city to Sodom is to declare it ripe for condemnation.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The ultimate archetype of extreme human wickedness, unrepentant sin (often specifically associated with sexual immorality), and sudden, total divine judgment.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Symbol of divine judgment and fiery destruction upon extreme wickedness, especially sexual immorality and homosexual acts (sodomy)

entries.definition: The righteous, who rule the night with the Son — “they that be wise shall shine… as the stars for ever”; the twelve stars are the twelve tribes, gathered into the twelve constellations, the Mazzaroth.
entries.citations: (Dan 12:3; Ps 136:9; Gen 37:9; Rev 12:1; Job 38:32) · see Sun, Moon & Stars, ch. 29

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: In symbolic and especially apocalyptic interpretation, stars most commonly represent heavenly beings—particularly angels or angelic messengers—and, by extension in some contexts, spiritual powers.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching and biblical studies, the most commonly assigned symbolic meaning of stars is angels or heavenly beings (the 'host of heaven'). This is the one symbolic identification the Bible itself makes explicit (Rev 1:20, where the seven stars 'are the angels of the seven churches'), and it is reinforced by passages where stars and angels are interchangeable or parallel (Job 38:7; Rev 9:1; Rev 12:4; Judg 5:20). Fallen or falling stars are correspondingly read as fallen angels or Satan (Isa 14:12; Luke 10:18 by association; Rev 12:4).

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Angels, heavenly beings, or spiritual authorities (both faithful and fallen), particularly in prophetic and apocalyptic literature.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Angels or heavenly/spiritual beings

entries.definition: A covenant cut by God — for a covenant is cut (Hebrew karat) — grown into the kingdom that breaks the world-empires and fills the earth.
entries.citations: (Dan 2:34-35, 44-45; Gen 15:17-18; Deut 9:10; Col 2:11) · see Mountain, ch. 39

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The stone cut without human hands most commonly symbolizes the divinely established messianic kingdom of God, often identified personally with Christ as its king. It overthrows earthly kingdoms and becomes universal and enduring.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian interpretation, the 'stone cut out without hands' from Nebuchadnezzar's dream in Daniel 2 symbolizes the Kingdom of God—established by divine action rather than human effort—and, by close extension, Christ the Messiah himself, whose kingdom shatters the succession of worldly empires (represented by the statue of gold, silver, bronze, iron, and clay) and grows to fill the whole earth. The phrase 'without hands' is consistently read as denoting supernatural, non-human origin.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Jesus Christ and His eternal Kingdom of God, which is established by divine power rather than human agency and will ultimately crush and replace all worldly empires.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The Messianic kingdom of God (Christ and/or His kingdom) of supernatural/divine origin that destroys all human kingdoms and fills the whole earth

entries.definition: The nations in turmoil — the raging sea, stilled at Christ's word, “Peace, be still”.
entries.commonView: Commonly taught: divine judgment, and the trials of life which Christ has power to calm.
entries.citations: (Ps 65:7; Isa 17:12-13; Mark 4:39; Luke 21:25) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Divine judgment or wrath arriving as overwhelming calamity. In prophetic and apocalyptic imagery, a storm or tempest commonly portrays God’s forceful visitation against sin, nations, or false security.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In the mainstream of Christian teaching and biblical interpretation, the storm or tempest most commonly symbolizes divine judgment and the overwhelming power of God — God's wrath breaking in upon the wicked and, correlatively, God's sovereign command over chaos. Closely fused with this in traditional exegesis is the storm as theophany: the tempest as the vehicle or accompaniment of God's presence and speech.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Trials, tribulations, chaotic distress, and overwhelming life circumstances that test faith; also widely seen as a manifestation of divine judgment or power.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: adversity, trials, tribulations, or times of distress that test faith

entries.definition: A non-citizen of God's commonwealth — one outside the covenant, drawn in, or, once in, made a stranger to the world.
entries.citations: (Eph 2:12, 19) · see Orphans, Widows & the Fatherless, ch. 14

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: An outsider or alien—especially someone separated from God’s covenant people, but capable of being welcomed and incorporated into the community. In many passages “stranger” is first a literal social category rather than a fixed symbol; Christian interpretation often extends it to spiritual alienation and reconciliation.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the 'stranger' (Hebrew ger, sojourner; Greek xenos) primarily symbolizes the vulnerable outsider in whom God—and specifically Christ—is encountered, so that hospitality to the stranger is treated as a test and expression of covenant faithfulness and love of God. The stranger stands for the marginalized person whom God commands his people to welcome, protect, and love, grounded in Israel's own memory of being strangers in Egypt and culminating in Jesus' identification of himself with the stranger.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Believers living as temporary residents or pilgrims in the earthly world, signifying that their ultimate citizenship, allegiance, and home belong to the Kingdom of Heaven.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The Christian believer (or people of God) as a temporary sojourner, pilgrim, or exile on earth whose true citizenship and home are in heaven

entries.definition: The Father, the source of light, from which every lesser light is drawn; the righteous shall shine as the sun in His kingdom.
entries.citations: (Ps 84:11; Gen 37:9; Matt 13:43) · see Sun, Moon & Stars, ch. 29

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: God or Christ as the source of divine light, glory, righteousness, life, and healing—especially the traditional Christological image of the “sun of righteousness.”

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching the sun is most commonly taken as a symbol of God and, especially, of Jesus Christ — his divine glory, righteousness, and light-giving presence. The classic anchor is Malachi's 'Sun of Righteousness,' which patristic and later Christian interpreters overwhelmingly read as a messianic title for Christ, who rises with healing, dispels the darkness of sin, and illumines the world. By extension the sun signifies God's radiant glory, favor, and unfailing constancy.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The glory, presence, and righteous revelation of God, most specifically fulfilled in Jesus Christ as the Sun of Righteousness who brings salvation and illumination.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Jesus Christ as the Sun of Righteousness (divine light, glory, and healing presence)

entries.definition: The unclean beast par excellence — the one beast in the law wearing the outward sign without the inward work: the hoof parted, the cud never chewed. The nation outside the covenant that tramples what is holy — pearls under their feet, the holy city under the Gentiles, the washed sow back in the mire.
entries.citations: (Lev 11:7; Deut 14:8; Matt 7:6; Rev 11:2; Isa 66:17; 2 Pet 2:22) · see The Other White Meat, ch. 48

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Ritual and moral uncleanness—by extension, what is profane, degraded, sinful, or unfit for holy use.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, swine primarily symbolize uncleanness and spiritual impurity — the unholy, the profane, and those who reject or are incapable of valuing sacred things. Because the pig is the archetypal unclean animal of the Mosaic law, it became a standing figure for defilement, and in Jesus' usage ('do not cast your pearls before swine') for people who scorn or trample what is holy. By extension it commonly represents the unregenerate or profane person who returns to sin and filth.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Uncleanness, moral and ritual impurity, spiritual depravity, and the profane or unholy.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: spiritual uncleanness or impurity (including moral filth, sin, and the reprobate who return to it)

entries.definition: War and the word of judgment — the great sword that takes peace from the earth; the flaming sword that guards the way.
entries.citations: (Rev 6:4; Gen 3:24) · see The Four Winds, ch. 34

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The Word of God—God’s powerful, penetrating truth or speech, often portrayed as a spiritual weapon and an instrument of discernment or judgment.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, the sword most commonly symbolizes the Word of God — Scripture and the spoken word of God as a penetrating, discerning, and powerful spiritual weapon. This is the dominant interpretation in sermons, commentaries, devotional literature, and systematic treatments of biblical imagery.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The Word of God, functioning as a spiritual weapon of truth that convicts the heart, exposes inner thoughts, and defeats spiritual opposition.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: the Word of God (as a living, piercing spiritual weapon of truth, conviction, and judgment)

entries.definition: The prophet that teacheth lies — Isaiah's own decode, with head and tail already defined by the covenant: obedience makes Israel “the head, and not the tail,” and the curse inverts it. The dragon fells a third of the stars with its tail — the led destroyed by the misleading — and the trumpet armies' serpent-tails “had heads”: the liar enthroned. Moses is told to seize the serpent exactly there.
entries.citations: (Isa 9:15-16; Deut 28:13, 44; Rev 12:4; 9:19; Ex 4:4) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A false or deceitful prophet—more broadly, religious leadership or teaching that spreads lies. This is the strongest conventional symbolic assignment because Scripture itself explicitly identifies “the tail” with “the prophet who teaches lies.”

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching the tail most commonly symbolizes falsehood and deception, specifically the false prophet or lying teacher. This rests on the Bible's own explicit equation in Isaiah 9:15, 'the prophet who teaches lies, he is the tail,' and the image is frequently extended to Satan's deceptive power in Revelation, where the dragon's tail sweeps away a third of the stars and demonic locusts and horses inflict harm with their tails.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Subordination, defeat, or the lowest and least significant position, often contrasted with the head which represents leadership and prominence.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: subordinate, inferior, or last place (as opposed to the head/leadership)

entries.definition: The counterfeit sown among the wheat by the enemy — a weed that mimics the true grain until the harvest, then is bound in bundles and burned; the children of the wicked one, distinct from the winnowed chaff.
entries.citations: (Matt 13:25-30, 38-40) · see Grass, ch. 42

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The tares (darnel) symbolize people aligned with evil—identified by Jesus as “the sons of the evil one”—who coexist with the righteous until their final separation and judgment at the end of the age.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: The tares (darnel, Lolium temulentum) symbolize the 'sons of the evil one' — false believers or counterfeit Christians sown by the devil among the genuine 'sons of the kingdom' (the wheat). They look nearly identical to true believers until maturity, coexist with them until the end of the age, and are then separated out and destroyed at the final judgment by the angels. This meaning is unusually settled because Jesus himself supplies the interpretation within the Gospel text.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: False believers, hypocrites, or 'sons of the evil one' who coexist alongside true believers in the world or the visible church until the final judgment.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The wicked (children of the evil one/devil) who are sown among the righteous (true believers) and left to grow together until the final judgment/harvest, when they will be separated and destroyed

entries.definition: The stronghold raised by a Name around its house — refuge, watchtower, and lighthouse in one: high to see danger, giving light to guide the house, and covered to shelter those who come inside. A strong tower is an intact Name protecting its people; an unfinished tower is a Name begun without depth to endure its cost; a fallen tower is a covenant stronghold broken, emptied, or judged.
entries.citations: (Prov 18:10; Ex 13:21; Isa 4:5-6; Hab 2:1; Gen 11:1-8; Luke 14:28-30; Matt 13:20-21; Luke 13:4-5) · see The Tower | (Prov 18:10; Ex 13:21; Isa 4:5-6; Hab 2:1; Gen 11:1-8; Luke 14:28-30; Matt 13:20-21; Luke 13:4-5) · see The Tower

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Strength, protection, and secure refuge—especially God as the believer’s “strong tower.”

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: Strength, protection, and refuge — most specifically, God himself as a place of safety to which the righteous flee. The tower functions as an image of divine security and defense, drawn from the ancient function of watchtowers and fortified towers as places of refuge and vigilance.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Divine protection, strength, and a secure refuge for believers.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Human pride, hubris, and rebellion against God leading to confusion, division, and judgment

entries.definition: A nation or people.
entries.citations: (Dan 4:22; Rom 11:17) · see Trees, ch. 41

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Life, flourishing, rootedness, and fruitfulness under God. In Christian teaching, a thriving tree commonly represents a person or community sustained by God and producing good fruit; the tree of life intensifies this symbolism into divine or eternal life.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching a tree most commonly symbolizes a person (or a people) whose inner spiritual condition is made visible in outward 'fruit' — especially the righteous person who, rooted in God, flourishes like a well-watered tree. Closely intertwined with this is the tree as a symbol of God-given life itself, epitomized by the Tree of Life.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Eternal life, spiritual flourishing, and the Cross of Christ, often linking the Tree of Life in Eden to the cross of Calvary and the New Jerusalem.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The cross of Christ (as the tree on which he was crucified, bringing redemption from the curse)

entries.definition: God's law — the standard.
entries.commonView: Commonly taught: Christ Himself, and God's word — the gospel that sets free.
entries.citations: (Ps 119:142; 2 John 4) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: God’s revealed reality—supremely embodied in Jesus Christ and expressed in God’s word—standing in opposition to falsehood, deception, and sin.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'the truth' is understood first and foremost as the self-revelation of God in Jesus Christ — Christ himself is 'the truth' — and, by extension, God's word and the gospel message that reveals him. Knowing and abiding in this truth brings salvation and freedom, and it stands opposed to falsehood, deception, and the devil, who is 'the father of lies.' Thus 'truth' in Scripture is treated as personal and relational (embodied in Christ, communicated by the Spirit) rather than merely propositional accuracy.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Jesus Christ as the ultimate, incarnate revelation of God, alongside the Gospel message and the written Word of God.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Jesus Christ as the personal embodiment and full revelation of divine truth

entries.definition: The tassels bound to the corners of the garment; looking upon them reminds the wearer of all the LORD's commandments, to do them.
entries.citations: (Num 15:38-39) · see Wings, ch. 13

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Tzitzit—the tassels or fringes attached to the corners of a garment—are most commonly understood as a visible reminder of God’s commandments and of Israel’s covenant calling to holiness and obedience.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, tzitzit (the tassels or fringes worn on the corners of garments) are primarily understood as a divinely commanded visual reminder of God's commandments and of Israel's covenant identity—an aid to remembering and obeying the Lord rather than following one's own heart and eyes. Christian interpreters generally take over this plain-sense meaning from the Torah itself: the fringes symbolize remembrance of, and obedience to, God's word, and consecration/holiness to God.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: A physical reminder to remember and obey God's commandments, representing holiness, covenant loyalty, and devotion to God.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: A visual reminder to remember and obey all of God's commandments and to live a holy life set apart from sin

entries.definition: Discernment of good from evil, gained by departing from evil — “a good understanding have all they that do his commandments”.
entries.citations: (Job 28:28; Ps 111:10) · see The Fool and the Wise, ch. 20

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: God-given spiritual discernment: the capacity to comprehend, distinguish, and rightly apply divine truth, rather than merely possess information.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'understanding' (Hebrew binah/tebunah; Greek synesis) is most commonly read as God-given spiritual discernment: the divinely granted capacity to perceive, grasp, and rightly apply God's truth and moral order. It is closely paired with wisdom, rooted in the fear of the Lord, and treated as illumination that comes from God rather than a merely natural intellectual faculty. It denotes insight into the meaning of God's word and will, enabling right living and the discernment of good and evil.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual discernment and the God-given ability to comprehend divine truth, properly applying wisdom to life and grasping the moral reality of God's will.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Divine gift of spiritual insight and discernment enabling comprehension of God's truths and mysteries

entries.definition: The low and humbled — the opposite of the mountain-kingdom; “every valley shall be exalted”.
entries.commonView: Commonly taught: the low seasons of trial and death, set against the mountaintop.
entries.citations: (Isa 40:4) · see Mountain, ch. 39 — derived in the digital edition’s symbol study at TimeTested.Bible

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A low place of suffering, danger, grief, or spiritual trial through which God accompanies and sustains his people.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the valley is primarily a symbol of trial, suffering, hardship, and spiritual low points — the dark or difficult seasons of life through which the believer passes while trusting God's presence and protection. It stands in contrast to the mountaintop, which symbolizes closeness to God, revelation, and victory. Preaching and devotional literature routinely speak of 'valley experiences' as times of testing, grief, depression, or danger that God accompanies the believer through rather than exempting them from.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: A period or place of testing, trials, spiritual darkness, sorrow, or death, often contrasted with mountaintop experiences to represent the low points of human life.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: A place or season of trial, affliction, spiritual darkness, or testing that the believer must pass through under God's care

entries.definition: The espoused — betrothed to one husband with the wedding still ahead: covenant standing, not attainment; the law counts a betrothed virgin already a wife, the prophets call the ten-tribe house re-espoused after her divorce “the virgin of Israel,” and virgins plural are the bride’s companions who follow her in — the opposite of the harlot who goes after many.
entries.citations: (Deut 22:23-24; Joel 1:8; Jer 31:4, 21; Amos 5:2; Ps 45:14-15; 2 Cor 11:2; Matt 25:1) · see The Fool and the Wise, ch. 20

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Purity, chastity, and uncorrupted or exclusive devotion to God or Christ. In corporate imagery, a virgin commonly represents the faithful people of God—especially the Church—as a pure bride pledged to Christ.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'virgin' functions symbolically as an image of purity and undivided covenant faithfulness to God. Corporately, God's people (Israel as 'virgin daughter Zion' in the Old Testament; the Church in the New Testament) are pictured as a virgin betrothed to God/Christ, with virginity signifying freedom from spiritual adultery (idolatry, apostasy) and readiness for union with the divine Bridegroom. The term is thus read primarily as a marital-covenant metaphor: the pure, faithful bride awaiting her husband.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual purity, exclusive devotion, and faithfulness to God, most notably symbolizing the Church as the pure bride of Christ or faithful Israel.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Purity, chastity, and undivided devotion/fidelity to God (most prominently embodied by Mary in the virgin birth of Christ, and secondarily by the Church or faithful as Christ's pure bride)

entries.definition: The words of the one who speaks; the Shepherd's voice is His words.
entries.citations: (John 10:27) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: When used symbolically—especially as “the voice of God”—voice most commonly signifies divine self-revelation, authoritative speech, command, calling, or guidance: God making his will and presence known.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, 'voice' (especially 'the voice of the LORD' or 'a voice from heaven') most commonly symbolizes God's direct self-revelation and authoritative communication to humanity—the audible manifestation of divine presence, power, and command that calls for hearing and obedience.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Divine revelation, authority, and active communication, often representing God's power, presence, or the guidance of the Holy Spirit.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Divine revelation, authority, and guidance (the speech of God or Christ addressing humanity)

entries.definition: Covenant conduct — the walk.
entries.commonView: Commonly taught: Jesus Himself as the one way to the Father; the narrow way against the broad.
entries.citations: (Jer 6:16; Matt 7:14) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The way of salvation and life with God, centered in Jesus Christ: Christ is the way to the Father, and following “the way” means trusting him and living as his disciple.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'the Way' primarily symbolizes Jesus Christ himself as the sole path or means of access to God the Father — salvation understood not as a technique or map but as a person to be followed. By extension it denotes the whole life of discipleship: following Jesus is walking 'the way' to God.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Jesus Christ as the exclusive path to God and salvation, and by extension, the Christian faith, lifestyle, and the early Christian community itself.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Jesus Christ as the exclusive path/means of access to God and salvation

entries.definition: Salvation — the covenant's enclosure: “thou shalt call thy walls Salvation”; God Himself “a wall of fire round about.” The counterfeit is self-built — wealth's high wall “in his own conceit,” and the whitewashed wall of false peace that the storm flattens.
entries.citations: (Isa 60:18; Zech 2:5; Prov 18:11; Ezek 13:10-15) · see The Parable of the Vineyard | (Isa 60:18; Zech 2:5; Prov 18:11; Ezek 13:10-15) · see The Parable of the Vineyard, in the free digital edition at TimeTested.Bible

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Protection, security, and a boundary preserving the integrity of a city or community; in theological imagery, a wall often represents God-given safety, salvation, or defense.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the wall most commonly symbolizes protection, security, and salvation—especially the defense God himself provides for his people. Ancient city walls were the primary guarantee of a city's safety, so the wall becomes an image of divine safeguarding: God is a 'wall of fire' around Jerusalem, salvation itself is called walls and bulwarks, and the walled New Jerusalem pictures the perfect security and inviolability of God's redeemed people. Conversely, a broken or missing wall symbolizes vulnerability, judgment, and defenselessness.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Protection, security, and divine salvation, representing God's defense of His people.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: protection, security, or defense (often divine protection around God's people or city)

entries.definition: A seven — shavua, a unit of sevens, and not only of days: Laban decodes it in the text — “Fulfil her week… yet seven other years” — and Jacob serves seven years for the week named; the jubilee is counted as “seven sabbaths of years,” and Daniel’s seventy weeks are sevens of years — unpointed, seventy sevens that open into seventy jubilees. The Feast of Weeks runs the same count in days — seven sevens to the fiftieth — the jubilee modeled a day for a year.
entries.citations: (Gen 29:27-28; Lev 23:15-16; 25:8; Dan 9:24-25) · see Daniel Unsealed, ch. 36

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: In prophetic Christian interpretation—especially Daniel 9—a “week” is most commonly understood as a heptad (“seven”), usually a symbolic period of seven years rather than seven days. More broadly, its sevenfold structure can signify a complete or divinely appointed cycle.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian interpretation the term 'week' (Hebrew shabua, literally 'a seven' or 'heptad') is most commonly treated symbolically as a unit of seven years rather than seven days, especially in Daniel's prophecy of the seventy weeks, where nearly all traditions—dispensationalist, historicist, and most critical scholars alike—read each 'week' as seven years (seventy weeks = 490 years). More broadly, the week functions as a symbol of divine order and completeness rooted in the seven-day creation pattern, culminating in the Sabbath rest.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: A period of seven years (a 'heptad' of years) in prophetic literature, and more broadly, a symbol of divine completeness and perfect timing.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: A complete cycle of time patterned on the six days of creation plus the seventh-day Sabbath rest, symbolizing divine order, work completed, and sacred rest

entries.definition: The sea at the back — the Hebrew for west is “sea” (yam): Israel faces east, so the west is “the hinder sea,” what lies behind; and as far as the east is from the west, so far are the transgressions removed.
entries.citations: (Zech 14:8; Joel 2:20; Ps 103:12) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: There is no settled biblical symbolism for “west.” When Christian teaching does assign it a general symbolic value, the most recognizable association is with the setting sun and therefore with ending, decline, darkness, mortality, or death, often contrasted with east as dawn, resurrection, or new beginning.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In most Christian teaching, the west is understood as the direction of the setting sun and therefore symbolizes endings, completion, decline, or death — the close of day as opposed to the east's new beginning. It is very frequently invoked in tandem with the east to express totality or infinite distance, most famously in the assurance that God removes believers' sins 'as far as the east is from the west,' an immeasurable, unrepeatable distance signifying complete forgiveness. A closely related homiletical point notes that in the tabernacle and temple the entrance faced east and the Holy of Holies lay at the west end, so that movement westward pictured drawing nearer to God's presence, whereas movement eastward (as in the expulsion from Eden) pictured departure from Him.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Approaching the presence of God, restoration, and returning from exile. In biblical spatial symbolism, moving west contrasts with eastward exile, representing a return to God's dwelling place.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: darkness, night, death, or the realm of evil/Satan (as the counterpart to the east)

entries.definition: The children of the kingdom — the good grain gathered into the barn at the harvest.
entries.citations: (Matt 13:38; 3:12) · see Grass, ch. 42

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: God’s faithful people—the righteous or true members of the kingdom—who are gathered and saved, often in contrast with weeds or chaff that face judgment.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, wheat most commonly symbolizes the genuine people of God—true believers or 'children of the kingdom'—especially as distinguished from false or unrighteous people (tares/chaff) at the final judgment. The wheat harvest imagery represents the eschatological gathering of the righteous into God's kingdom.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: True believers, the righteous, or the elect who are gathered into God's kingdom at the final judgment.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: the righteous / true believers (children of the kingdom) who are gathered by God at the final harvest/judgment

entries.definition: God's covenant people cut off from their Husband.
entries.citations: (Lam 1:1; Isa 54:5) · see Orphans, Widows & the Fatherless, ch. 14

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The widow most commonly signifies vulnerability, bereavement, social powerlessness, and material need, together with dependence on God and special entitlement to the community’s protection and justice.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the widow functions primarily as the archetype of the vulnerable and defenseless person who is under God's special protection and care. Alongside the orphan and the sojourner/stranger, the widow symbolizes the socially powerless whom God defends, and treatment of widows serves as a measure of true religion and covenant faithfulness. The widow is thus a symbol of dependence on God, of the poor whom the community is obligated to protect, and of the justice God demands.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Vulnerability, defenselessness, and total dependence on God, representing the marginalized who are objects of God's special protection and justice.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The vulnerable, desolate, and marginalized under God's special protection, for whom true religion requires care and justice

entries.definition: Spirit — ruach.
entries.citations: (Zech 6:5) · see The Four Winds, ch. 34

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The Holy Spirit, especially the Spirit’s invisible, sovereign, powerful, and life-giving activity.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, wind most commonly symbolizes the Holy Spirit — the invisible, sovereign, life-giving breath/Spirit of God. The link is built into the biblical languages themselves: Hebrew 'ruach' and Greek 'pneuma' each mean wind, breath, and spirit, so interpreters routinely treat wind as the standing image of the Spirit's unseen but powerful activity in creation, regeneration, and empowerment.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The Holy Spirit, the breath of God, or the invisible, life-giving, and sovereignly directed power of God.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The Holy Spirit (or Spirit of God), as an invisible, sovereign, life-giving, and empowering presence

entries.definition: The vineyard's reckoning — where the fruit a people has borne is pressed out and rendered to the Owner, in one of two vintages: presses that “burst out with new wine” when the grapes are good; the growers themselves trodden — “the great winepress of the wrath of God” — and blood for wine, when the vintage is wickedness.
entries.citations: (Isa 5:2, 7; Prov 3:10; Joel 2:24; 3:13; Lam 1:15; Isa 63:3; Rev 14:19-20) · see The Parable of the Vineyard | (Isa 5:2, 7; Prov 3:10; Joel 2:24; 3:13; Lam 1:15; Isa 63:3; Rev 14:19-20) · see The Parable of the Vineyard, in the free digital edition at TimeTested.Bible

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Divine judgment and wrath, especially final or eschatological judgment: the wicked or hostile nations are portrayed as grapes crushed underfoot, with the flowing juice evoking bloodshed.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the winepress functions primarily as a symbol of divine wrath and eschatological judgment: the crushing of grapes and the flow of red juice picture God (or the Messiah) trampling the wicked, whose blood flows out like wine. The image is treated as one of the Bible's most vivid pictures of God's final judgment on the nations.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The wrath, judgment, and severe punishment of God poured out upon his enemies and the wicked.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Divine judgment or the outpouring of God's wrath upon the wicked (often depicted as treading/trampling grapes that yield blood)

entries.definition: The covenant edge — wing, skirt, border, corner — where the reminder of the law is bound and refuge is found.
entries.citations: (Ezek 16:8) · see Wings, ch. 13

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Protective refuge and care—especially God sheltering, preserving, and gathering his people “under his wings.”

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching and biblical interpretation, 'wings' (Hebrew kanaph) most commonly symbolizes God's protective care, refuge, and covering — the believer finds shelter 'under the shadow of his wings,' with the image drawn from a mother bird (especially an eagle or hen) sheltering her young. It expresses divine protection, tenderness, and covenantal safekeeping.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Protection, refuge, and divine sheltering care, often representing God's loving provision and deliverance.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Divine protection, shelter, and refuge (as a bird covers its young)

entries.definition: The fear of the LORD lived out — the doing of the commandments; “the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom”.
entries.citations: (Prov 9:10; Ps 111:10; Deut 4:6) · see The Fool and the Wise, ch. 20

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: God-given understanding that perceives divine order and leads to righteous, skillful living, grounded in reverence for God. In personified form, Wisdom represents God’s active instruction and ordering purpose.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, personified Wisdom (especially 'Lady Wisdom' of Proverbs 8) is most commonly read as a symbol, type, or foreshadowing of Jesus Christ — the eternal Word/Wisdom of God through whom all things were made. Christ is identified as the Wisdom of God incarnate, so that the figure of Wisdom in the Old Testament wisdom literature is taken christologically. At the practical level, wisdom also stands for godly, skillful living rooted in the fear of the Lord, but the dominant symbolic interpretation of the personified figure is christological.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Jesus Christ, the Second Person of the Trinity (the Logos or Word), representing God's mind and active agent in creation.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Jesus Christ (the divine Logos/Son), as the personal embodiment and personification of God's wisdom

entries.definition: One who hears God's word and does it, who fears the LORD.
entries.citations: (Matt 7:24; Ps 111:10) · see The Fool and the Wise, ch. 20

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Those who possess God-given spiritual discernment and therefore hear, obey, and faithfully respond to God, often contrasted with the foolish, disobedient, or unprepared.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'wise' primarily denotes the person who fears God and orders life according to His word — practical, moral-spiritual skill in godly living rather than mere intellect. The wise person hears and obeys God's instruction, and this wisdom is repeatedly said to begin with 'the fear of the LORD.' In the New Testament this is sharpened into hearing and doing the words of Christ, and into possessing the 'wisdom from above' that is given by God rather than the wisdom of the world.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: One who fears the Lord, possesses divine insight, and practically applies God's truth to live righteously.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Godly wisdom or spiritual discernment expressed in prudent, obedient living that fears the Lord and builds on His word

entries.definition: To bow down and serve — homage in the body, allegiance in the life; the fear of the LORD made visible, kept at His appointed times, on His terms. Not the song service: Scripture separates worship from singing in single scenes.
entries.citations: (Ex 20:5; Matt 4:10/Deut 6:13; 2 Chr 20:18-19; Rev 14:7) · see Worship, ch. 22

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Reverent devotion, honor, and self-surrender directed to God. In Christian teaching, worship signifies acknowledging God’s supreme worth and sovereignty through praise, prayer, thanksgiving, service, obedience, and sacrificial dedication.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, 'worship' most commonly signifies reverent adoration, homage, and self-surrender directed exclusively to God — the act of ascribing supreme worth ('worth-ship') to God, expressed outwardly in bowing down or prostration (Hebrew shachah, Greek proskuneo, literally 'to bow/kiss toward') and inwardly in submission of the whole self. It symbolizes the creature's acknowledgment of the Creator's absolute worthiness, glory, and lordship, and by extension the total orientation of one's life toward God rather than idols or rivals.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: Total submission, reverence, and the attribution of ultimate worth and glory to God, representing the surrender of the believer's entire life and will.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The act of ascribing supreme worth to God alone through heartfelt reverence, adoration, praise, thanksgiving, and obedient submission

entries.definition: A turning — shanah, written on the root to change, repeat, return: one complete cycle of time, at whatever scale the count is running — Jeremiah’s seventy “years” close only as seventy jubilees, and a thousand years pass as a day.
entries.citations: (Jer 25:11-12; Dan 9:2, 24; Ps 90:4) · see Daniel Unsealed, ch. 36

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: “Year” has no single settled biblical symbolic meaning. When used figuratively or typologically, its broadest conventional association is a complete or divinely appointed season—especially a time of favor, judgment, release, or restoration.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, 'year' most commonly carries the symbolic sense of a complete, divinely appointed period of time — above all 'the acceptable year of the Lord,' i.e., the era of God's favor, salvation, and release. This draws on the Jubilee year (a fiftieth-year proclamation of liberty, debt release, and restoration) as a type of messianic redemption, which Jesus applies to his own ministry in the Nazareth synagogue. Thus 'year' symbolizes the full season or epoch of God's saving activity rather than a mere calendar unit.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: A divinely appointed era of redemption, grace, and liberation, frequently rooted in the Year of Jubilee and fulfilling the 'acceptable year of the Lord'.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: No single settled symbolic meaning; most often denotes a complete cycle of time or a designated period of divine action (favor, judgment, testing, or release), especially the 'acceptable/favorable year of the Lord' as the messianic era of salvation and grace
